title: Food Tokens
new_elements: Magnetic program pucks (Chunky shaped tokens (cup, soup bowl, snowflake) snap onto the fascia. The magnet pattern selects the program.); Hall-sensor token recognition (A magnet pattern on each token is read by a few Hall sensors.)
rationale: Choosing a program becomes as easy as picking up the picture of your food.
judge_comment: Magnetic pictorial tokens replace menus and buttons with a zero-learning, tangible interface using simple Hall sensors, though token loss and food-specific accuracy are concerns.

title: Container-Key Presets
new_elements: Magnet-coded containers and reed switch array (Mug, bowl and plate each carry magnets that select a preset.)
rationale: The dish is the program, so there are zero controls to operate.
judge_comment: Dish-coded presets remove controls entirely and are quite radical, though they require special containers and magnets must be microwave-safe.

title: +30 Seconds Mega Button
new_elements: Single large +30 s push button (Each press adds 30 s and starts the oven immediately; it is the only control.)
rationale: One button that needs no explanation: press more for hotter.
judge_comment: A single button needing no instruction directly removes the learning curve and is cheap and easy to build, though it has less control over power.

title: Close-the-Door-to-Start
new_elements: Door-closure start switch with default 60 s cycle (Closing the door starts a fixed one-minute heat. Closing it again adds another minute.); Starts cooking implicitly on door close (Shutting the door is the only action needed to start cooking.)
rationale: Replacing the timer knob with the door itself means the user only has to do what they already do: put the food in and shut the door.
judge_comment: Very simple: closing the door starts a fixed cycle, with no learning curve, though a fixed 60 s may not suit all foods and the accidental-start safety logic needs care.

title: Close-to-Cook Door
new_elements: Door-close start sensor (Closing the door starts a default reheat cycle; opening it stops cooking.); Zero-button start (The door is the only control.)
rationale: Every user already knows how to close a door, so cooking needs no instruction.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start is trivially simple and cheap, though accidental starts and a one-size default cycle limit it.

title: Tap-Top Gesture
new_elements: Piezo tap sensor in lid (Each knock on the top adds 30 s, and a double-knock stops cooking.)
rationale: The whole box becomes one giant button.
judge_comment: Tap-to-add-time with a double-tap to stop is highly intuitive and needs no learning, and a piezo sensor is cheap and feasible, though accidental knocks are a risk.

title: Weight-Activated Start
new_elements: Starts only when food is present (The load cell prevents empty running and auto-starts on door close.)
rationale: Removes the 'never run it empty' rule and the start button.
judge_comment: A load cell that auto-starts when the door closes removes both the start button and the empty-run risk, though it needs a default cook time and must handle low-weight foods.

title: Keyed Smart Bowls
new_elements: Notch-coded cookware set (Bowls and plates have base notches that press cam pins in the turntable to select a program.)
rationale: Choosing the soup bowl is the whole setting, so there are no controls at all.
judge_comment: Notch-coded bowls that select the program remove the controls entirely, which is a radical, zero-learning-curve idea, though it requires proprietary cookware and a robust cam-pin mechanism.

title: Say-a-Number Voice Chip
new_elements: Offline keyword voice chip (A low-cost chip recognises 'one minute', 'two minutes', 'stop'.)
rationale: Speaking a duration needs no learning and no fine motor skills.
judge_comment: Offline keyword chips are cheap and proven, and speaking a duration is natural, though noisy kitchens may cause errors.

title: Linear Food Slider
new_elements: Big slider with food zones (A slider with zones labelled drink, leftovers and frozen meal replaces both knobs.); Spatial setting (Slider position encodes both time and power.)
rationale: One labelled motion replaces two abstract controls.
judge_comment: Food-labelled zones make operation intuitive and cheaply replace two knobs, though it is less radical.

title: RFID Smart Dishware
new_elements: Microwave-safe tagged bowls (Each dish carries a shielded tag such as 'soup bowl' or 'pasta plate'.); Floor RFID reader (Reads the dish identity through the glass plate.); Dish-defined cooking program (The bowl selects the program.)
rationale: Choosing which bowl to use is the only decision the user makes.
judge_comment: The dish selects the program, so the user makes no choices at all. It is very novel, though it needs a tagged dish ecosystem and shielding from microwave energy.

title: Picture Card Slot
new_elements: Punched picture cards (Slide a laminated card showing a food photo into a slot; the punch pattern sets the program.); Card-based programming (A mechanical, low-cost replacement for the knobs.)
rationale: Users insert the card of what they're eating; nothing else is required.
judge_comment: Insert-a-picture programming is nearly zero-learning and mechanically cheap, though it limits flexibility and needs cards to be kept on hand.

title: Big +30s Button
new_elements: Single palm button (Each press adds 30 s and starts heating immediately.); Incremental time by tapping (Replaces the twist-and-wind timer knob.); Clockwork knob imprecise below 1 min (Short times are hard to set on a 0-30 min scale.)
rationale: Tapping one big button is the simplest interaction possible.
judge_comment: A single big +30s button is very easy to use and cheap to make, though it is already familiar from existing microwaves.

title: Hand-Crank Timer Spring
new_elements: Pull-cord timer (Pulling a cord out sets the time by length (longer pull = longer heat) and it retracts as time passes.); Visible physical countdown (The cord length shows the remaining time.); Invisible remaining time (The clockwork position is hard to read.)
rationale: A longer pull means more time, a playful and self-explanatory mapping.
judge_comment: A pull-cord timer maps pull length to time intuitively, shows the countdown visibly and needs no learning, which makes it very relevant.

title: Close-the-Door Default Minute
new_elements: Door-wound default timer (Closing the door winds 1 minute and starts heating; turning the knob only adds time.)
rationale: The most common task needs zero inputs beyond shutting the door.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start a default minute needs no learning and is cheap to build, a strong fit for the need.

title: Handle-Twist Controls
new_elements: Rotating door handle timer (Pull the handle to open the door, or twist it to set time. The handle is the only control on the oven.)
rationale: Every interaction happens at the single point the hand already touches.
judge_comment: A single handle that opens the door and sets the time is very simple, with a plausible mechanical or encoder build, and it directly replaces the control panel.

title: Smart-Dish Coding
new_elements: Coded cookware with embedded magnet pattern (Each bowl or mug carries a magnet code that sets the time and power automatically.); Hall-effect pattern reading (Sensors under the cavity floor read the dish code.)
rationale: The container is the program: put the soup mug in and it heats soup correctly.
judge_comment: The dish itself sets the program, which removes nearly all operation, though it needs special cookware and the magnets must be microwave-safe.

title: Big +30s Button
new_elements: Single large +30 s push button (Each press adds 30 s to a cheap RC/microcontroller countdown and starts heating.)
rationale: Pressing more for more heat is self-explanatory, and short times become precise.
judge_comment: A single +30s button is extremely simple and cheap to build with no learning curve, though some microwaves already have a similar quick-start button.

title: Recipe Token Slot
new_elements: Notched recipe token reader (Plastic tokens with notch patterns set time and power cams when dropped into a slot.)
rationale: Caregivers can hand an elderly user a 'soup token': insert it and it is done.
judge_comment: A mechanical token that sets time and power is very simple to use, cheap to build and easy for caregivers to manage, though the token library is limited.

title: Pictogram Food Dial
new_elements: 5-step power knob (Existing numbered power knob from base_product meta); Pictogram dial (Icons for cup, plate, soup, frozen and popcorn instead of numbers); Select by food picture (Maps directly to what the user is holding)
rationale: Pictures of food are understood instantly, unlike abstract power numbers.
judge_comment: Replacing numbers with food icons is simple, cheap and very intuitive, though it is a modest innovation and gives less precise control.

title: Pull-String Toy Timer
new_elements: Pull-cord spring timer (Replaces the rotary clockwork knob: the further you pull the cord, the longer it heats, and the cord slowly retracts.); Visible remaining time (The length of cord still out shows the time left.)
rationale: A physical length maps intuitively to duration, so no numbers need to be read.
judge_comment: A pull cord with a retracting spring gives an intuitive physical mapping of time to length and is mechanically plausible, similar to wind-up timers.

title: One-Button +30
new_elements: Single +30 s button (Replaces both knobs: each press adds 30 seconds and starts heating.); Incremental heating (Press again if the food is not hot enough.)
rationale: One button with one meaning leaves nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single +30 s button that also starts heating removes nearly all learning and is trivially buildable, though similar buttons already exist.

title: Handle-Is-the-Timer
new_elements: Rotary door handle timer (Turning the handle locks the door and winds the time in one motion.)
rationale: Closing and setting merge into one intuitive gesture.
judge_comment: Combining door locking and timer winding in one twist gesture is intuitive, mechanically plausible and directly removes steps.

title: Detent Dish-Size Knob
new_elements: Haptic three-stop knob (Clicks into cup, plate or bowl stops, each with a fixed time and power cam.)
rationale: A cheap mechanical knob gives feel-based choices with no numbers to interpret.
judge_comment: A detented mechanical knob with cams replaces the keypad and directly removes the need to learn; it is plausible, cheap and clear, though not very radical.

title: Colour-Coded Bowl Set
new_elements: Tagged blue/red/yellow bowls (Blue bowl means defrost, red means reheat, yellow means boil, detected by an NFC tag in the base.)
rationale: Choosing a bowl is the setting, so a child could use it.
judge_comment: Bowl choice becomes the setting through NFC, so there is no learning curve; it is cheap and feasible, though it requires proprietary bowls.

title: Keyed Smart Containers
new_elements: Shape-keyed container set (Mug, soup bowl and defrost box each have a foot shape that presses a different program pin through the tray.); Auto-selects program from container (The container itself acts as the control input.)
rationale: Picking the right container is the whole setup, so there are no settings to learn.
judge_comment: Container shape as the control input removes settings entirely and is radical, though it needs proprietary containers and a reliable mechanical pin interface through the tray.

title: Talk-To-It Microwave
new_elements: Offline voice keyword chip (Recognises phrases like 'warm my coffee' or 'defrost' and sets time and power.); Edge keyword-spotting speech recognition (A low-cost DSP running a small neural network.)
rationale: Saying what you want is the most natural interface there is and needs no learning.
judge_comment: Voice input removes the controls and the learning curve entirely, and offline keyword spotting is practical, though noisy kitchens and a limited vocabulary are drawbacks.

title: Food Token Slot
new_elements: Shaped food tokens and keyed slot (Dropping in a mug-shaped or pizza-shaped token sets a cam profile for time and power.); Programs cooking via physical token (The token's shape encodes the program.)
rationale: Like posting a coin, you pick the picture and drop it in.
judge_comment: A physical token that selects the program is a radical, coin-like interface with zero learning, and it is mechanically plausible with keyed cams.

title: Magnet-Coded Containers
new_elements: Containers with embedded magnet codes (Reed switches under the floor read the container's code and set the program.); Reed-switch magnetic code reading (A cheap, passive identification method.)
rationale: The bowl tells the oven what to do, so the user just puts it in.
judge_comment: Container-coded programs remove all input, though it requires dedicated containers and the substitution is not obviously cheaper.

title: Slider Lever Timeline
new_elements: Linear slider with food icons along track (Slide to 'coffee' or 'leftovers'; the slider returns as time elapses.)
rationale: Remaining time is shown as physical position.
judge_comment: A slider with food icons that moves back as time elapses substitutes for the keypad, needs no learning, and shows remaining time physically.

title: Pull-Cord Wind-Up
new_elements: Retractable pull cord (Replaces the timer knob; the length pulled sets time, retracting like a toy.); Proportional time gesture (A longer pull gives more time.); Spring-motor escapement (Reuses the clockwork mechanism.)
rationale: More pull means more heat, a mapping anyone understands immediately.
judge_comment: A pull cord with a proportional gesture needs no learning, and a spring-and-escapement mechanism is cheap and plausible.

title: Solid-State Self-Finishing Oven
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Low-voltage RF source that measures reflected power.); Detects doneness from absorbed-power signature (Ends cooking when dielectric response flattens.)
rationale: The oven itself knows when food is done, so the user sets nothing.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with reflected-power doneness sensing removes the need to set anything, but reliable detection across varied foods is unproven.

title: Cup-Pocket Program
new_elements: Mug-shaped tray recess with microswitch (Setting a mug in the recess automatically selects the drink time.)
rationale: Where you put the food is the instruction, so no reading is needed.
judge_comment: Placement of a mug directly selects the program, removing all reading and button choices, though it only covers the drink use case.

title: Food-Shaped Buttons
new_elements: Tactile food-silhouette keys (Raised cup, pizza-slice and snowflake buttons that can be found by touch.)
rationale: Shape tells the meaning, even to blind users.
judge_comment: Shape-coded tactile buttons make operation intuitive and accessible, are easy to build, and directly serve the no-learning-curve need.

title: Hold-to-Heat Button
new_elements: Momentary hold button (Heats only while held, giving precise short bursts without a timer.)
rationale: Short reheats work the way a kettle switch does: hold to heat, let go to stop.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat is intuitive with zero learning curve and easy to build, though it is tiring for longer cooks and not truly a substitution radical leap.

title: Lid-Keyed Containers
new_elements: Shape-coded container lids (Lid tabs press floor pins that select the right program.)
rationale: The container itself tells the oven what to do.
judge_comment: Container lids that mechanically select the program remove the need for any input, which is a radical substitution of the controls, though it needs a dedicated container ecosystem.

title: Food Token Slot
new_elements: Timer and power knobs (Base-product components being substituted); Shaped physical tokens (Drop a 'pizza slice' token into the slot to run that program); Select a program by inserting an object (Child- and elder-friendly)
rationale: Matching a token to the food is as simple as a child's shape-sorter toy.
judge_comment: Shape-sorter tokens make program selection near-zero learning and are simple to build with RFID or mechanical sensing, though tokens can get lost.

title: One Dial, Food Pictures
new_elements: Single pictogram dial (One knob with food icons (mug, plate, frozen block); each detent sets both time and power via a combined cam.)
rationale: The user picks a picture of their food instead of translating it into minutes and power levels.
judge_comment: Pictogram dial removes time/power translation and is easy to build with a cam, though similar to existing preset knobs.

title: Twist-Handle Timer Lock
new_elements: Rotating door handle timer (Twisting the handle to lock the door also sets the time; it unwinds back to open.)
rationale: Closing and setting become one gesture with a single control.
judge_comment: Combining door closing and time setting in a single twist is a radical, intuitive gesture, though the mechanical complexity and precision are challenging.

title: Recipe Punch Cards
new_elements: Notched pictogram card reader (Slide in a 'popcorn' card, and its notches set time and power mechanically.)
rationale: Users pick a picture card, a zero-literacy interface.
judge_comment: A mechanical card reader replaces the keypad with pictures, which directly removes the learning curve and is easy to build, though it adds cards to keep track of.

title: Tagged Smart Containers
new_elements: RFID-tagged containers (Soup bowl, mug and rice box each carry a tag holding their heating program.); Cavity RFID reader (Shielded antenna that reads the tag when the door shuts.); Container-driven program (The vessel tells the oven what to do.)
rationale: Choosing the right bowl is the only decision the user makes.
judge_comment: A container that carries its own program is radical and needs no decisions, but it requires proprietary vessels and tags that can be affected by microwaves.

title: Toaster Lever
new_elements: Spring-return lever (Push down to start; the lever rises as time elapses and the door pops open at the end.); Visible remaining time (The lever height shows the countdown.)
rationale: It borrows the toaster's universally understood mental model.
judge_comment: The toaster-lever mental model is universally familiar and shows remaining time visibly, which makes it very intuitive, though it is mechanically tricky and imprecise for varied foods.

title: Pictogram Food Dial
new_elements: Single pictogram food dial (One knob with icons (cup, plate, frozen block, butter) whose cam sets both duration and duty-cycle at once); Dual-track profile cam (One cam shaft with two tracks: timer contact and power-cycling contact)
rationale: Users pick what they are heating, not minutes and watts, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Pictogram dial with a dual-track cam is intuitive and mechanically plausible, though similar to existing auto-cook presets.

title: Toaster-Lever Start
new_elements: Push-down toaster-style start lever (Lever pressed down along a scale latches the circuit and pops up with a clunk when time is over.); Escapement-damped lever return (A spring and air-dashpot return the lever at a fixed speed, giving the cooking time.)
rationale: Every user already knows how a toaster works: push it down, wait for the pop.
judge_comment: A toaster-style lever relies on a metaphor users already know and is mechanically plausible, though an air-dashpot gives only a fixed time per lever travel.

title: Food Picture Cards
new_elements: Picture-card slot (Slot that accepts cards for soup, popcorn, defrost and similar foods, read by notches in the card.); Program by picture (Each card sets both time and power.)
rationale: Choosing a picture of your food needs no reading and no settings.
judge_comment: Picture cards with notch-coded slots directly remove the need to read or set anything, and the mechanism is simple and cheap, though it is a variation on preset buttons.

title: Food-Icon Dial
new_elements: Icon dial (One knob marked with food icons instead of minutes, set by a cam that controls both time and power.); Select food, not parameters (Merges the timer and power knobs into one.)
rationale: Users think in terms of foods, not watts, so they can just point at what they have.
judge_comment: A single food-icon dial with a cam replaces two knobs with a simpler mechanical part and is directly intuitive, though food-based presets are not new.

title: Token Timer
new_elements: Wooden minute tokens (Dropping in tokens adds one minute each, and they fall back into a tray at the end.); Tangible time units (Makes time something you can count.)
rationale: Counting objects is understood by children and users with dementia.
judge_comment: Tangible tokens replace the keypad with an intuitive, inclusive interface, which is radical and simple to build, though it is slower for longer times.

title: Toaster Lever Microwave
new_elements: Rotary clockwork timer knob (Base timer being substituted.); Spring-loaded push-down lever (Press depth sets the time; the lever pops up when done.); Familiar toaster-style operation (Reuses an interaction model almost everyone already knows.)
rationale: Borrowing the universally known toaster gesture removes the learning curve.
judge_comment: Reusing the toaster lever gesture gives an instantly familiar interface and a mechanical, cheap implementation.

title: Popcorn Ear
new_elements: Timer guessing for popcorn (Base manual method being substituted.); MEMS microphone pop counter (Stops heating when the gap between pops exceeds 2 s.)
rationale: Ends burnt popcorn with no setting needed.
judge_comment: Acoustic pop counting removes all settings for popcorn and is concrete and feasible, though it only covers one food.

title: Food-Picture Single Dial
new_elements: Pictogram combo dial (One knob with food icons (cup, plate, frozen, butter); one cam sets both duration and duty cycle.); Dual-track cam (time + duty) on one shaft (Two cam profiles on the same shaft, so each icon position encodes a time and power pair.)
rationale: The user makes one choice by pointing at a picture of their food, with no numbers or power settings to understand.
judge_comment: A pictogram dial with a dual-cam mechanism is simple, cheap and plausible, though similar preset dials already exist.

title: One Big +30s Button
new_elements: Single giant +30 s ratchet button (Each press adds 30 s at full power, and pressing it again while cooking adds more time.)
rationale: One button with one rule is the shortest learning curve possible.
judge_comment: A single +30s button is the simplest possible operation and is easy to build, but similar quick-start buttons already exist.

title: IR Thermometer Instead of Timer
new_elements: Ceiling infrared food thermometer (Stops heating when the food surface reaches eating temperature.); Stops when food is hot (Uses a temperature target instead of a time target.)
rationale: The user never has to guess a duration because the oven stops when the food is hot.
judge_comment: Goal-based heating by temperature is intuitive, but IR only reads the surface and food in covered or uneven loads makes it unreliable.

title: Picture-Button Power
new_elements: Three pictogram buttons (cup, plate, snowflake) (Replaces the 5-step duty-cycle cam with food-type choices.)
rationale: Users pick what they are heating, not an abstract power percentage.
judge_comment: Pictogram buttons directly deliver zero-learning operation and are easy to build, though not very radical.

title: Tangible Food Tokens
new_elements: Magnetic food-shaped pucks (Dropping a cup- or pizza-shaped puck into a slot selects the program.)
rationale: A physical shape match works for children, elderly users and non-readers.
judge_comment: Physical shape-matching tokens are accessible and simple to build, though they can be lost and cover limited foods.

title: Auto-Popping Door
new_elements: Solenoid door kicker (Pops the door open a few centimetres when cooking ends.)
rationale: An open door unmistakably means 'done', and food is never forgotten inside.
judge_comment: A door that pops open gives an intuitive done signal with no learning, and a solenoid kicker is easy to build, though it may be startling and interact awkwardly with the latch.

title: RFID Smart Containers
new_elements: RFID-tagged microwave containers (Each container tells the oven what program to run.)
rationale: The container is the interface, so the user just puts the box in.
judge_comment: A container that tells the oven what program to run removes the interface entirely, which fits the zero-learning goal well, though it needs a container ecosystem and the reader hardware.

title: Door-Wound Clockwork
new_elements: Door-closing spring motor (Closing the door winds a spring that drives a fixed 1-minute cycle and the turntable.)
rationale: Close the door and it heats for one minute; there is nothing else to understand.
judge_comment: Radically simple: closing the door starts a fixed cycle with no electronics, though a fixed one-minute cycle limits usefulness and the spring and safety interlock are tricky.

title: Steam-Says-Done Sensor
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor (Cheap capacitive humidity sensor in the vent stops the magnetron when the steam rate spikes.)
rationale: The oven stops itself when the food is hot, so the user never has to guess a time.
judge_comment: Humidity-based auto stop removes time guessing and is plausible, as sensor cooking exists, but it works poorly for dry foods.

title: Single GO Button Auto-Cook
new_elements: Single GO button (One large button replaces the clockwork timer knob and the 5-step power knob.); Steam humidity sensor (Detects the steam burst from the food and ends the cycle.); Automatic doneness detection (Ends heating without the user choosing a time or power level.)
rationale: One button with no settings leaves nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single button with steam-sensor doneness detection is simple and workable (sensor-cook exists), though not very radical.

title: Toaster Lever Microwave
new_elements: Push-down lever (A familiar toaster-style lever replaces both knobs and springs up when the food is done.); Borrowed mental model (Reuses a control everyone already knows how to use.)
rationale: No new interaction has to be learned.
judge_comment: The toaster-lever metaphor is a clever, familiar mental model, but with no time or power input it needs a timer or sensor logic behind it.

title: Kettle-Style Auto Click-Off
new_elements: IR food thermometer (Replaces the clockwork timer by stopping when the food reaches 70°C.); Temperature-terminated heating (Ends the cycle on food temperature rather than on time.)
rationale: It works like a kettle: switch it on and it stops by itself.
judge_comment: Switch-on, auto-stop at food temperature removes all settings, but an IR sensor reads only the surface and struggles with uneven heating and with covered or frozen food.

title: Colour-Coded Lids
new_elements: Coloured container lids (Red means reheat and blue means defrost, replacing the power knob.); Colour sensor (Reads the lid colour to pick the program.); Object-as-setting (The container itself carries the cooking setting.)
rationale: Choosing a lid replaces choosing a power level.
judge_comment: Encoding the setting in the container is a wild, intuitive idea that removes menus, though it requires buying special lids and sensors.

title: Printed Antenna Food Packs
new_elements: Chipless RFID conductive ink (Printed patterns are read by the cavity's RF field.); Self-describing food (The food tells the oven how to cook it.)
rationale: Placing the pack inside is the only step.
judge_comment: Chipless RFID printed in conductive ink read by the cavity RF is radical and truly one-step, but reading inside a high-power cavity and arcing risks make it hard.

title: Magnetic Time Tokens
new_elements: Tokens with Hall sensor pad (Placing a "2 min" token on top sets the time.); Tangible presets (Physical tokens replace the timer dial.)
rationale: Children and elderly users can use tokens without reading.
judge_comment: Tangible tokens read by Hall sensors are workable and need no reading, but tokens can get lost and it adds a part.

title: Top-Loading Rice-Cooker Form
new_elements: Hinged top lid with one switch (Replaces the side door and both knobs.); Appliance familiarity (Copies the form of rice cookers, a single-switch appliance people already use.)
rationale: A familiar form brings familiar operation.
judge_comment: Borrowing the single-switch rice cooker form directly removes the learning curve and is plausible, though top-loading microwaves need a safe seal and a defined cook program.

title: Weight-Sensing One-Button Microwave
new_elements: Load-cell turntable base (Strain-gauge scale under the plate weighs the food automatically.); Auto-compute time and power from mass (Replaces both the clockwork timer and power knobs with a single GO button.); User must guess minutes and power level (The two-knob interface forces users to estimate settings.)
rationale: Users press one button and never have to pick a time or power level.
judge_comment: A load cell with one GO button removes settings, though weight alone doesn't identify food type and the load cell adds cost compared with a clockwork timer.

title: Package NFC Tap
new_elements: NFC tap pad on door (Tap the meal package on the pad and the program loads.); Tap-to-program (No reading of the package instructions.)
rationale: It works like a contactless payment, which users already know.
judge_comment: Tapping the package to load the program removes the need to read instructions, though it needs package data and ecosystem support.

title: Pull-Cord Start
new_elements: Bead pull-cord (Each pull adds one heating increment, like an old lamp switch.); Tactile incremental heating (Replaces the clockwork timer spring.)
rationale: Users pull more for hotter; the logic is self-evident.
judge_comment: A pull cord with one increment per pull is intuitive, cheap and tactile, but it is slow for long cook times and gives imprecise control.

title: One Button +30s
new_elements: Single +30 s push button (Each press adds 30 s at full power and starts immediately.)
rationale: One button with one meaning gives zero learning curve.
judge_comment: A single +30s button gives a near-zero learning curve and is easy to build, though it is hardly radical and offers limited control.

title: Thermal-Eye Auto Stop
new_elements: Ceiling IR thermal sensor (Reads the food surface temperature and stops at a target such as 70 °C.)
rationale: Heating ends at the right temperature without user input.
judge_comment: IR sensing with automatic stop removes time and power decisions, directly serving no-learning-curve operation, though surface-only readings and existing sensor models limit novelty.

title: Program Token Drop
new_elements: Magnetic food-token slot (Drop a picture token (soup, rice, milk) into the slot to select the program.)
rationale: Physical, tangible choices work even for kids and the elderly.
judge_comment: Tangible picture tokens are accessible to kids and the elderly and are easy to build with magnets or RFID, though the preset programs are limited.

title: Stick-In Probe Stop
new_elements: RF-safe wireless food probe (Push it into food; heating stops at the safe-to-eat temperature.)
rationale: Stick it in and walk away, with no timing knowledge needed.
judge_comment: A probe that stops heating at a safe temperature removes any need for timing knowledge, though wireless probes inside a microwave are challenging and the idea exists in part already.

title: Weighing Turntable Autotimer
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (A strain gauge under the turntable weighs the food and computes the cooking time.); Strain-gauge mass sensing (Low-cost load cell paired with an ADC.)
rationale: Putting the food in is all the setting that is required.
judge_comment: Weighing the load to auto-set time achieves true zero-setting operation, though mass alone is an imperfect proxy for food type and heating needs.

title: Toaster Lever Start
new_elements: Push-down start lever with pop-up release (Pushing the lever down latches the door and starts cooking; when time ends the lever pops up.)
rationale: It borrows the toaster metaphor that nearly everyone already understands.
judge_comment: The toaster lever is a familiar metaphor that makes starting obvious, but a cook time still has to be set, so it only partly removes the need to learn.

title: Recipe Card Slot
new_elements: Notched recipe card reader (Inserting a punched card mechanically sets the cam timer and power, with no electronics.)
rationale: Pushing in a picture card is as easy as posting a letter.
judge_comment: A punched picture card that mechanically sets a cam timer is a radical, electronics-free substitution that is easy to use, though cards must be sourced and mechanical precision is a challenge.

title: Pull-Cord Timer
new_elements: Retractable pull-string timer (The length of string pulled out sets the time, and the string slowly retracts as it counts down.)
rationale: Remaining time is a physical length anyone can see and understand.
judge_comment: A pull-cord whose length shows remaining time is simple, visible and cheap, and it substitutes the dial or keypad well.

title: Food-Icon Slider
new_elements: Linear pictogram slider (A single slider runs along a strip of food pictures from 'drink' to 'frozen meal'.)
rationale: One linear motion is matched to familiar images.
judge_comment: A single slider along food pictures needs no learning and is easy to build, though the presets are only approximate.

title: Meal Pod Capsules
new_elements: Coded meal pod dock (Sealed pods carry a notch code that sets the whole heating cycle, like coffee capsules.)
rationale: Operation is insert-and-forget, as with a capsule coffee machine.
judge_comment: Coded pods remove all settings and make operation insert-and-forget, but they need a pod ecosystem and the code reader adds cost.

title: Popcorn Ear
new_elements: Acoustic pop-rate microphone (Stops cooking when the popping slows down, or when sizzling starts.)
rationale: The oven listens for doneness as a person would, so popcorn needs no guesswork.
judge_comment: Acoustic popcorn detection already exists in some ovens and works, and extending it to sizzle makes doneness guessing unnecessary.

title: Toaster Lever Start
new_elements: Single push-down lever (Spring lever like a toaster's: pushing it further gives more time, and it pops up at the end.)
rationale: Everyone already knows how a toaster lever works, so there is no learning curve.
judge_comment: A familiar toaster-lever metaphor gives zero learning curve and is cheap, though pop-up timing control in a microwave is a little crude.

title: Draining Colour Bar Timer
new_elements: Shrinking light-bar timer (An LED bar across the door shortens as time runs out, like an hourglass.)
rationale: Remaining time is understood instantly, without reading numbers.
judge_comment: A shrinking light bar shows remaining time at a glance and is simple to build, but it is not very radical.

title: Hold-to-Heat
new_elements: Hold-to-heat paddle (The oven heats only while the paddle is pressed, like a kettle tap, with a safety maximum.)
rationale: Direct control lets the user stop when they see the food is done.
judge_comment: A hold-to-heat paddle removes the need to set a time at all and is intuitive, though it is tiring over long cook times and the safety max adds complexity.

title: Food-Photo Dial
new_elements: Picture ring dial (A single knob ringed with food photos (drink, soup, leftovers, frozen, butter) sets both time and power.)
rationale: Pointing at a picture of the food replaces two abstract scales.
judge_comment: A picture-based single dial replaces abstract time and power settings, which directly eliminates the learning curve and is easy to build.

title: Popcorn Ear
new_elements: Acoustic doneness microphone (Listens for popping slowing down or boiling starting, then stops heating.)
rationale: The oven listens like a careful cook, so the user just presses start.
judge_comment: Acoustic auto-stop removes the need to choose times, which strongly serves no-learning-curve use, though it works reliably only for some foods.

title: RFID Smart Dishes
new_elements: Tagged dish set (Mug, bowl and plate each carry a microwave-safe tag encoding their heating program.); Container selects the program (The oven reads the dish and heats accordingly.); Settings must be chosen manually (Both knobs require a decision on every use.)
rationale: Put your mug in and the oven knows it is coffee; there is nothing to set.
judge_comment: It removes settings entirely by letting the dish choose the program, which is highly relevant and plausible with RFID, but it requires proprietary dishes and cannot adjust for the actual food.

title: Three Big Intent Buttons
new_elements: DRINK / MEAL / DEFROST buttons (Three large buttons replace both knobs and use sensors to finish the cycle.); Intent-based control (Covers about 90% of everyday uses in a single press.); Knob combinations overwhelm (The time and power knobs together offer too many combinations.)
rationale: Three plainly labelled choices need no learning.
judge_comment: Three labelled intent buttons directly remove the learning curve and are very feasible, though the idea is fairly familiar and not radical.

title: Food-Recognising Camera
new_elements: On-device image classification (A low-cost vision chip recognises common foods.); Cavity camera (Identifies the dish and its quantity, then sets the program.); Zero-input cooking (Replaces both knobs.); User must know settings per food (Each food requires remembered or guessed settings.)
rationale: The oven figures out what the food is, so the user decides nothing.
judge_comment: Zero-input cooking via a camera fully removes the need to learn, though recognising food and quantity reliably and cheaply is challenging.

title: Program Pucks
new_elements: Magnetic program tokens (Shaped pucks (cup, popcorn, snowflake) dropped into a dock on top select the program.); Tangible program selection (Replaces the knobs with physical objects.); Abstract dial positions (Dial positions have no obvious meaning.)
rationale: Even children understand putting the cup token on to heat a cup.
judge_comment: Tangible tokens make program choice intuitive and are easy to build, though the idea is not very radical and tokens can get lost.

title: Weigh-and-Go Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (Strain-gauge support under the glass plate weighs the food and derives cook time automatically.); Weight-to-energy cooking algorithm (Maps food mass to the energy needed for a standard reheat.)
rationale: The user only puts food in and closes the door; there are no minutes or power levels to choose.
judge_comment: Zero-input operation is ideal for no learning curve, though mass alone poorly predicts heating needs for different foods and the load cell must cope with a rotating plate.

title: Solid-State RF Self-Tuning
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF source with reflected-power sensing (Reads how much energy the food absorbs and stops when absorption changes.)
rationale: The source senses the food, so the user just presses start.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with reflected-power sensing enables true press-start-only cooking, strongly serving the need, though cost and cooking-end detection accuracy remain challenges.

title: Warmth Slider
new_elements: Lukewarm-hot-boiling slider with IR feedback (The user picks the target warmth and an IR sensor ends the cycle.)
rationale: Users express the outcome they want, not the process to get there.
judge_comment: Choosing an outcome rather than a time is an intuitive interface, but IR sensing of food temperature through the cavity is tricky and uneven heating limits accuracy.

title: Hourglass Flip Timer
new_elements: Flip-over sand-glass module with tilt switch (Three snap-in sand glasses (1, 2 and 5 min); flipping one starts heating until the sand runs out.)
rationale: Everyone understands an hourglass, and it shows remaining time visually.
judge_comment: A flip hourglass that starts heating is highly intuitive and visual, but it has limited time options and sand timing may not match the actual heating time.

title: Weigh-and-Go Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable support (Strain gauge under the turntable measures food mass and derives cooking time.); Derives cooking time from food weight (Time is proportional to mass at fixed power.)
rationale: Put the food in and the oven decides the time, so the user sets nothing at all.
judge_comment: Zero-input weight-based timing is great for usability, though time is not truly proportional to mass for all foods and it cannot tell what the food is.

title: Close-the-Door-to-Cook
new_elements: Door-actuated start switch (Shutting the door starts a fixed 60 s cycle; opening the door stops it, and shutting it again adds another 60 s.)
rationale: The only action is closing the door, which every user already does.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start is intuitive and cheap, but a fixed 60 s and the risk of accidental starts limit it.

title: Infrared Hot-Food Cutoff
new_elements: Thermopile IR food sensor (A low-cost thermopile reads food surface temperature and ends cooking at about 70 °C.)
rationale: A single 'heat it up' action replaces the whole time-setting task.
judge_comment: Single-action heat-until-hot via IR sensing directly removes the learning curve and is plausible, though surface-only reading and sensor substitution of a timer add some cost.

title: Magnet-Coded Bowls
new_elements: Coded container with base magnets (Supplied bowls and mugs carry magnet patterns read by reed switches under the floor to select the program.)
rationale: The dish is the interface: using the soup bowl means a soup program.
judge_comment: The container becomes the interface with cheap magnets and reed switches, though it locks users into proprietary dishes.

title: Three Big Buttons
new_elements: Three preset mechanical buttons (Buttons for Warm (30 s), Heat (1 min) and Cook (3 min) with no other controls.)
rationale: Three choices cover most daily use and are impossible to misunderstand.
judge_comment: Three labeled preset buttons are nearly impossible to misuse and directly serve the no-learning-curve need, though presets are not new.

title: Shrinking Light Ring
new_elements: LED ring progress bar (A ring of lights around the door goes out segment by segment as time elapses, replacing knob markings and the bell.)
rationale: Remaining time is readable at a glance from across the room without reading numbers.
judge_comment: An LED ring that counts down is intuitive and cheap, and it replaces the markings and bell, so it needs no learning.

title: Mug-Stop Plate
new_elements: Drink-zone pad (Placing a cup on a marked pad triggers a fixed 'drink' program via a weight switch.)
rationale: The most common task needs no settings at all.
judge_comment: A weight-triggered drink pad removes all settings for the most common task, and it is simple and buildable.

title: Hot-o-Meter Slider
new_elements: Cold-warm-hot target slider (The user picks the desired warmth rather than a time. An IR thermopile reads the food and ends the cycle.); IR thermopile food sensing (Non-contact surface temperature reading through a small cavity port.)
rationale: People think in terms of 'warm' or 'hot', not seconds, so the control speaks their language.
judge_comment: Choosing a target warmth matches how people think and the IR sensing is concrete, but surface-only readings and cost limit accuracy.

title: Tagged Dishes Self-Program
new_elements: RFID-tagged dish set (Each bowl or mug carries a ceramic-embedded tag telling the oven its size and typical contents.); Passive RFID through microwave-safe ceramic (Low-frequency tag read before the magnetron starts.)
rationale: The dish tells the microwave what to do, so the user only chooses which mug to use.
judge_comment: Dish-embedded tags that auto-program the oven are radical and remove all choices, but they require a proprietary dish set and tag survival in the microwave environment is questionable.

title: Reflected-Power Auto Mode
new_elements: RF directional coupler sensor (Measures how much energy the food absorbs to detect frozen, thawed and boiling states.); Detects food state from RF absorption (Automatically switches between defrost, heat and stop.)
rationale: The oven knows whether food is frozen, so the user never selects a defrost mode.
judge_comment: Auto-detecting food state from reflected RF removes mode selection entirely, though reliable sensing of varied foods is hard and it adds cost rather than substituting something cheaper.

title: Portion Dial
new_elements: Portion-count dial (Positions marked 1 cup, 2 cups, 1 plate and 2 plates map to cam durations.)
rationale: Counting portions is natural, whereas estimating minutes is not.
judge_comment: A portion dial with cam timers is simple, cheap and intuitive, though the mapping is imprecise across different foods.

title: Cup Port
new_elements: Dedicated mug slot (A small shielded side well sized for one mug. Dropping a mug in starts a fixed drink-warming cycle.)
rationale: The most common task becomes 'put the cup in the hole', with zero settings.
judge_comment: A dedicated mug well with automatic start is zero-learning for the most common task, but it is narrow in use and takes up space.

title: Slot-Machine Pull Lever
new_elements: Side ratchet pull handle (Each pull winds 30 s into a spring clockwork, and a tick-tock sound confirms it is running.)
rationale: 'More pulls = more heat' is an instantly graspable, playful mapping.
judge_comment: A mechanical pull lever replacing the keypad is playful, intuitive and cheap, and a clockwork timer is real, proven tech.

title: Steam-Sniffer Auto-Stop
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor (Detects the steam burst when food is hot and ends the cycle.); Ends cooking when food is hot (Closed-loop doneness detection.)
rationale: Put food in and press nothing; the oven decides when the food is done.
judge_comment: Humidity sensing for auto-stop exists in sensor-cook models, but it gives a truly zero-input experience and is plausible.

title: IR Thermometer Cut-Off
new_elements: Thermopile IR sensor in the cavity roof (Reads the food surface temperature and stops at 70 °C.)
rationale: The user sets nothing, because the oven stops at 'hot' automatically.
judge_comment: Automatic stopping at a target temperature removes the settings entirely and is feasible, though IR sensing exists in some ovens and reads only the surface.

title: Toaster-Lever Microwave
new_elements: Push-down start lever (A toaster-style lever starts the cycle; the lever height sets the duration and it springs up when done.)
rationale: It borrows the toaster's universally understood push-down, pop-up model.
judge_comment: Toaster-lever metaphor is instantly understood and removes the keypad; mechanical timer linkage is plausible, though the lever-height-to-duration mapping is a bit vague.

title: Door-Glass Cheat Sheet
new_elements: Printed pictogram guide on the door glass (Shows cup = 1 tap, plate = 4 taps and similar shortcuts.)
rationale: The manual is always in sight, at zero cost.
judge_comment: A pictogram guide on the door glass directly removes the need to learn the controls, and it is cheap and simple, though not radical.

title: Smart-Tag Meal Tap
new_elements: NFC reader in door handle (Reads a cooking profile printed on the meal package.); Package-defined heating profile (The ready-meal maker's program sets time and power.)
rationale: The user taps the box and puts it in, with no reading of instructions.
judge_comment: Tapping the package removes nearly all decisions, but it depends on food manufacturers adopting NFC tags and shared profile standards.

title: IR Thermometer 'Make It Hot'
new_elements: Thermopile food-surface sensor (Reads food temperature through the cavity roof.); Heats to target temperature (Uses Warm / Hot / Boiling targets instead of time.)
rationale: Users ask for 'hot', which is what they actually want, instead of minutes.
judge_comment: Choosing a target temperature instead of a time removes the learning curve, though sensing food surface temperature through the cavity is hard in practice.

title: Smart Container Shapes
new_elements: Keyed mug / bowl / plate inserts (A magnet code in the base of each container selects the program.)
rationale: Picking a container is the same as programming the oven.
judge_comment: Container-as-program is an intuitive, zero-learning interface using magnet codes, though it requires special containers and limits flexibility.

title: Mechanical Visual Countdown Ring
new_elements: Shrinking coloured disc timer (A red sector visibly shrinks as time passes, like a Time Timer.)
rationale: Remaining time is understood at a glance, even by children.
judge_comment: A Time Timer-style visual dial is intuitive and directly removes the learning curve, but it is an existing concept and not very radical.

title: Weigh-and-Go Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable hub (Strain-gauge hub under the glass plate weighs the food and derives cooking time automatically.); Weight-to-time lookup mapping (Simple lookup table converts grams to seconds at a fixed reheating energy per gram.)
rationale: The user just puts food in and closes the door; the oven picks the time, so there are no settings to learn.
judge_comment: Auto-weighing removes all settings, though weight alone poorly predicts heating needs for varied foods and the load cell adds cost.

title: Toaster-Lever Microwave
new_elements: Toaster-style push-down lever (A side lever pushed down closes and locks the door, starts heating, and pops back up when time ends.); Latching solenoid hold-down (A solenoid holds the lever down until the timer releases it.)
rationale: It borrows the toaster gesture everyone already knows, so the user does not have to learn anything new.
judge_comment: The toaster lever uses a familiar gesture and replaces the door latch and start button, but time setting is still unresolved.

title: Camera Food Recognition One-Button
new_elements: Cavity camera with on-device food classifier (Recognises the food and portion and sets time and power; one GO button.); Embedded vision classification (Low-cost MCU neural inference.)
rationale: The oven figures out what is inside, and the user just presses one button.
judge_comment: A one-button camera-based oven fits zero learning curve very well, but classification accuracy, portion estimation, and cavity steam and splatter make it hard, and it is not a cheap substitution.

title: Bimetal Exhaust Thermostat Timer
new_elements: Snap-disc bimetal on vent duct (Opens the circuit when exhaust air passes a 'food is steaming' temperature; costs cents.)
rationale: This is a no-electronics auto-stop, so cheap ovens can also skip the time-setting step.
judge_comment: A cents-cost bimetal snap-disc in the vent duct is a clever, simple substitution for a timer, though calibration and the lag from ambient temperature and food type limit its accuracy.

title: Twist-and-Push Single Ring
new_elements: 5-step power knob (Existing second knob from base_product meta); Single illuminated ring (Twist for more or less heat, push to start, with a light arc showing progress); Unified single control (Merges time and power into one control)
rationale: One control cannot be confused with another.
judge_comment: A single twist-and-push control with a light ring is very simple and buildable, but it is an incremental interface change rather than a radical one.

title: Meal Pod Insert-to-Cook
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (Existing timer from base_product meta); Coded meal pods (Notches on each pod mechanically set the cycle, like coffee capsules); Capsule-defined cooking (The program travels with the food)
rationale: It works like a capsule coffee machine: insert the pod and wait.
judge_comment: Mechanically coded pods that set the cycle remove all settings and work like capsule coffee machines, but they need a pod ecosystem and the packaging must be microwave-safe.

title: Food Token Drop Slot
new_elements: 5-step power knob (Existing power knob from base_product meta); Magnetic food tokens (Chunky picture tokens dropped into a slot select the program); Tangible program selection (Suits children and people with dementia)
rationale: Physical picture tokens can be used without reading or remembering anything.
judge_comment: Picture tokens give tangible, reading-free operation that is very intuitive, though token management and loss are drawbacks.

title: Haptic Detent Food Knob
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (Existing smooth-turning timer from base_product meta); Detented food-type knob (A firm click at each food type, with Braille and relief icons); Feel-based selection (Usable without looking)
rationale: Clicks confirm each choice by touch, which suits low-vision users.
judge_comment: Detented food-type knob with tactile icons gives intuitive, no-learning operation and is mechanically simple and cheap, though not very radical.

title: Camera Food Recognition
new_elements: 5-step power knob (Existing power knob from base_product meta); Cavity camera with on-device vision model (Identifies pizza, soup, rice and so on and picks the program); Recognise food and auto-set (No input needed at all)
rationale: The oven sees what you put in, so you don't have to tell it.
judge_comment: Camera recognition removes all input and fits the zero-learning-curve need well, though recognition accuracy and cost are concerns.

title: Large Tactile Relief Buttons
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (Existing knob with small printed numbers); Three oversized relief buttons (Drink, Meal and Defrost, each with an embossed shape); Three-choice operation (Covers the vast majority of everyday use)
rationale: Three big buttons are easy to grasp at a glance.
judge_comment: Three big embossed buttons are highly intuitive and feasible, but they are a fairly obvious simplification and not radical.

title: Infrared Done-Sensor
new_elements: IR thermopile in ceiling (Replaces the timer: watches the food surface temperature and stops at about 70 °C.); Stop when food is hot (Ends the cycle based on the food's state rather than elapsed time.)
rationale: "Hot" is the goal, so the machine targets heat directly instead of asking the user for minutes.
judge_comment: Targeting temperature directly removes all decisions and is feasible with a thermopile, though it only reads the surface and the user still has to start it.

title: Hold-to-Heat Lever
new_elements: Spring-return dead-man lever (Replaces the timer knob: heating runs only while the lever is held or latched.); Direct manual heating control (Works like a kettle switch or a tap.)
rationale: Everyone already understands "push to run, let go to stop".
judge_comment: Hold-to-run lever is instantly understood and safe, though it is tiring for long heating unless it latches, and it is not very radical.

title: Flip-Cube Timer
new_elements: Tilt-sensing cube on top (Replaces the knob: the cube's faces read 30s, 1m, 2m and 5m, and the face turned up sets the time.); Select time by orientation (Uses a tilt sensor, so there are no moving dial parts.)
rationale: Choosing a time works like setting down a die, with only four obvious options.
judge_comment: A tilt cube is playful and simple with four clear options, though the orientation-to-time mapping needs a little learning and the options are limited.

title: Resonant Food Tags
new_elements: Chipless passive RF resonator tags (Foil patterns printed on packaging that resonate at distinct frequencies.); Magnetron-sweep tag reader (Replaces the knobs: the cavity's own RF reads the tag in the first second of heating.); Zero-touch recipe identification (Identifies the food without any separate scanner.)
rationale: Putting food in is the whole interface.
judge_comment: Zero-touch identification via magnetron-read chipless tags is radical and well specified, but reading tags with a high-power magnetron is risky and hard.

title: Pop-Open Finish
new_elements: Solenoid door kicker (Replaces the end-of-cycle bell: the door gently opens when the food is done.); Self-evident completion (An open door signals the food is ready.)
rationale: An open door says "take it out" to anyone.
judge_comment: An auto-opening door is an intuitive, wordless completion cue, though it risks spills and is a mild safety concern.

title: Elderly Big Dial Auto-Start
new_elements: Oversized high-contrast dial (Replaces the small clockwork knob: turn it and heating starts, with no separate start step.); Turn-and-go (Setting the time and starting are one action.)
rationale: It keeps the familiar dial but makes it legible and one-step.
judge_comment: A big dial that starts on turning directly removes the learning curve and is easy to build, but it is incremental, not radical.

title: Weigh-and-Go Floor
new_elements: Load-cell cavity floor (Strain-gauge floor weighs the food and computes time and power automatically.); Auto-sets cook time from mass (Replaces the timer knob and power knob with one weight reading.)
rationale: The user puts food in and closes the door, and the oven works out time and power with no settings to learn.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto time and power removes all settings, though mass alone poorly predicts cooking needs and turntable load cells are tricky.

title: Steam-Sniffer Auto-Stop
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor (Detects the steam burst released when food is hot and ends the cycle.); Stops when food is done (Doneness detection replaces the clockwork timer.)
rationale: The user never has to guess minutes because the oven stops when the food is ready.
judge_comment: Humidity-based auto-stop is already used in sensor-cook microwaves, but it directly removes the need to guess time.

title: Infrared Target-Temp Stop
new_elements: Ceiling IR thermopile (Reads the food surface temperature and stops at 70 °C for food or 65 °C for drinks.); Heats to temperature not time (Ends heating at a target temperature, before liquids can superheat.)
rationale: 'Make it hot' becomes the only instruction, and there is no risk of overcooking.
judge_comment: Target-temperature heating removes the need to choose time or power, directly serving zero-learning-curve operation, and IR thermopile sensing is plausible, though it only reads the surface temperature.

title: One Pictogram Knob
new_elements: Single food-pictogram dial (One cam knob with icons (cup, plate, bowl, frozen) sets both duty cycle and time.)
rationale: Two abstract knobs become one obvious choice.
judge_comment: A cheap, mechanically simple substitution of two knobs with one pictogram dial that is clearly learnable at a glance.

title: Countdown Light Ring
new_elements: Shrinking LED halo around door (A light ring shrinks as time passes and replaces the bell and tiny dial markings.)
rationale: Remaining time is readable across the room at a glance.
judge_comment: An intuitive visual countdown is easy to build and understand, though it only simplifies feedback rather than operation as a whole.

title: Three Big Buttons
new_elements: Drink / Plate / Defrost buttons (Three large preset buttons replace both knobs.)
rationale: Three choices that cover 90% of use mean nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Replacing the knobs with three presets directly removes the learning curve, but it is a familiar approach.

title: +30 Seconds Slap Button
new_elements: Large +30 s paddle (Each slap adds 30 s at full power, replacing the imprecise short-time dial.)
rationale: Counting slaps is the simplest timer imaginable.
judge_comment: A +30 s paddle is very simple and directly cuts the learning curve, but it is not radical and it limits precision.

title: Thermochromic Done Cover
new_elements: Thermochromic splatter cover (Microwave-safe lid turns from blue to red when the food underneath reaches about 70 °C.)
rationale: A colour change replaces reading dials and guessing doneness.
judge_comment: A thermochromic lid gives an intuitive doneness cue that needs no learning, and it is feasible and concrete, though the user still has to stop the oven manually.

title: Pictogram Single Dial
new_elements: Single food-icon dial (One knob with icons (coffee, soup, leftovers, defrost) sets both time and power through a cam.)
rationale: Two abstract knobs become one picture choice.
judge_comment: A single icon dial is simple and intuitive and cheap with a cam, though presets are already common.

title: Lid-Colour Power Code
new_elements: Colour-coded container lids plus optical sensor (Red lid for high power, blue for defrost, green for gentle.)
rationale: Choosing a lid colour is the only decision.
judge_comment: A radical, intuitive swap of controls for lid colour, though it requires dedicated containers and a reliable optical sensor.

title: Push-Anywhere Door
new_elements: Push-to-open cabinet catch (Pressing the door face springs it open, like furniture.)
rationale: No hidden button to discover.
judge_comment: Push-to-open catch is cheap, proven, and removes a hidden button, a true simple substitution, though not very radical.

title: Thermal-Eye Timer
new_elements: Low-res IR thermal camera (Watches the food surface temperature and stops at the target.)
rationale: Heats to the target temperature, not to a time the user must estimate.
judge_comment: Target-temperature cooking removes the need to guess time, strongly serving zero-learning operation, though IR sensing through steam and surface-only readings is challenging.

title: Hold-to-Heat Button
new_elements: Dead-man heat button (Heats only while held, with a 3-minute maximum and a seconds counter.)
rationale: For quick reheats, holding the button is the whole interface.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat is very intuitive for short reheats and cheap to build, though it is tiring for longer cooking and the 3-minute cap limits it.

title: Dielectric Load Sensing
new_elements: S11 reflection load analysis (RF reflection reveals the food's amount and frozen or thawed state.)
rationale: The microwave senses whether the food is frozen or how much there is, removing every setting.
judge_comment: Sensing load and frozen state through S11 reflection could remove every setting, but reliably inferring that from reflection is technically hard.

title: Mug-Only Single-Purpose Oven
new_elements: Mug-cavity beverage microwave (Fits one mug or bowl and has one button that heats to drinking temperature.)
rationale: Narrowing the product to one job removes every decision.
judge_comment: A one-button mug heater cuts decisions to nearly zero and is easy to build, but it is limited to beverages and small bowls.

title: Spin-the-Plate Timer
new_elements: Turntable rotary encoder (Spinning the plate by hand sets the time, and closing the door starts it.); Turntable doubles as time input (Merges the timer knob into an existing part.)
rationale: The user spins the plate further for longer, using a physical, intuitive gesture with zero external controls.
judge_comment: Using the turntable as the time input is a radical substitution of the timer knob and is intuitive, though the encoder must be sealed and the plate is awkward to spin by hand with food on it.

title: Weigh-and-Go Tray
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (A strain gauge under the tray weighs the food and sets the heating time automatically.); Strain-gauge load sensing (A low-cost bridge sensor of the kind used in kitchen scales.)
rationale: The user just puts food in, and its weight replaces any guessing about how many minutes to set.
judge_comment: Automatic weighing removes time entry entirely and uses cheap strain gauges, though weight alone is a poor proxy for heating needs and the turntable mount is awkward.

title: Coin-Op Time Tokens
new_elements: Token chute timer (Each dropped token adds 30 s, and the stacked tokens show visibly how much time remains.)
rationale: Counting tokens is physical and countable, so even children and elderly users grasp it immediately.
judge_comment: Physical tokens make time visible and countable and are easy to build, but they are inconvenient since users need tokens and the mechanism is a bit gimmicky.

title: Hourglass Timer Window
new_elements: Flip-sand-glass interlock timer (Flipping a 1, 2 or 3-minute sand glass tilts a switch and heating runs while the sand flows.)
rationale: An hourglass is a universally understood, visible countdown.
judge_comment: Visible, intuitive sand-glass countdown is wildly different and needs no learning, but fixed durations and a mechanical-electrical interlock limit practicality.

title: Three Preset Buttons Only
new_elements: Drink / Plate / Frozen keypad (Three large buttons, each with fixed time and power.)
rationale: Three choices cover most real use and leave nothing to configure.
judge_comment: Three fixed-function buttons nearly eliminate decisions and are easy to build, but the idea is fairly conventional and inflexible.

title: +30 Big Button
new_elements: Single +30 s push button (Each press adds 30 seconds at full power, replacing the clockwork timer.)
rationale: One button and one rule: press more for longer.
judge_comment: A single +30 button is very simple, cheap and easy to build, but it is a modest idea and some microwaves already have a similar quick-start button.

title: Pull-Cord Start
new_elements: Lamp-style pull cord (Each pull adds a minute; a long pull cancels.)
rationale: A familiar, tactile gesture that also works in the dark or with poor eyesight.
judge_comment: A pull cord is a familiar, tactile control that works without sight, and it is cheap and unusual, though it is awkward to place and gives little feedback.

title: Thermal-Eye Auto Stop
new_elements: IR thermopile food sensor (Measures the food surface temperature and stops heating at the eating temperature.)
rationale: The food reaches 'just right' without the user setting anything.
judge_comment: Auto-stop on temperature removes the need to set anything, which directly delivers zero learning, and thermopile sensors are plausible and cheap.

title: Pop-Up Done Lid
new_elements: Turkey-timer pop lid (A microwave-safe cover whose wax plug pops a red pin when the contents are hot.)
rationale: 'Pin up means done' is a known, zero-learning signal.
judge_comment: A familiar pop-up indicator gives a zero-learning done signal using a simple, cheap, passive part, though it only signals completion rather than controlling the heating.

title: Popcorn Ear
new_elements: Acoustic pop/boil microphone (Stops heating when popping slows or when rolling boil sounds are heard.)
rationale: It listens the way a cook would, with no setting needed.
judge_comment: Listening for popping and boiling removes the need to set anything for these foods and is quite novel, though noise and reliability make it hard.

title: Steam-Whistle Cutoff
new_elements: Bimetal steam vent switch (Escaping steam heats a bimetal disc that opens the magnetron circuit.)
rationale: Food stops heating when it is hot rather than when a guessed time runs out.
judge_comment: Cooking until the food is actually hot is a radical, no-input approach, but steam venting is inconsistent in a sealed cavity and cutoff safety and reliability are doubtful.

title: Package Punch-Card Programs
new_elements: Notched card slot reader (Notched tabs on food packaging set time and power mechanically.)
rationale: Users tear off the tab, slot it in and close the door, so they never read instructions.
judge_comment: Mechanical notched cards on packaging remove the need to enter settings and so cut the learning curve, though they require packaging-industry adoption and only suit supported foods.

title: Pull-Cord Timer
new_elements: Retracting pull-string clockwork (The length of cord pulled out equals cook time, marked with knots.)
rationale: Pull a little or pull a lot is a child-simple analogue of time.
judge_comment: A pull-cord timer is intuitive and mechanical, with knot markings making time easy to read, though precision is limited.

title: Pop-Up Lever Cooker
new_elements: Rice-cooker style press lever (Press down to cook; a thermal latch pops it up when the food is hot.)
rationale: The toaster or rice-cooker metaphor is known worldwide.
judge_comment: A toaster-style lever with a thermal latch is intuitive and plausible, though the latch must trip reliably on food temperature rather than just elapsed time.

title: Elastic-Band Timer
new_elements: Rubber-damped return lever (A viscous damper lever returns slowly to zero, as a cheap timer.)
rationale: Users push the lever up and watch it sink.
judge_comment: A damped lever that sinks slowly works as an intuitive, cheap mechanical timer and is a clear substitution, though precision is limited.

title: One Dial, Food Pictures
new_elements: Single pictogram dial (mug, plate, defrost, popcorn) (One cam dial whose segments encode both time and duty-cycle for common foods.); Selects a complete cooking program in one turn (Time and power are chosen together by choosing the food.)
rationale: Replacing two abstract knobs with one dial of food pictures means the user only has to recognise their food.
judge_comment: A single pictogram dial that encodes both time and power is simple and plausible, though picture dials already exist in some appliances.

title: Pull-Cord Timer
new_elements: Spring-retracting pull cord with knot marks (The length of cord pulled out sets the time; the cord slowly retracts as a visible countdown.); Escapement-governed spring reel (A toy-style governor retracts the cord at a constant speed.)
rationale: Pull more for longer is a mapping that even a child grasps, and the retracting cord shows how much time is left.
judge_comment: A pull-cord timer with a retracting countdown is a radical, intuitive mapping, though cord durability and accuracy are open questions.

title: Reflected-Power Done Sensor
new_elements: Diode detector of reflected microwave power (Rising reflection indicates water has evaporated or the load is heated.); Waveguide diode probe cut-off (Stops the magnetron automatically.)
rationale: The oven knows when to stop, so the user does not need to choose a time.
judge_comment: Zero-input automatic stop is ideal for the need, and the diode reflected-power detector is concrete, though detection reliability across loads is uncertain.

title: Temperature Dial (Warm/Hot/Boil)
new_elements: IR thermopile with three-position target dial (The user picks the desired result; the oven heats until the food reaches it.); Heats to a target temperature (Outcome-based control replaces duration-based control.)
rationale: Users state what they want ('hot') instead of translating it into minutes.
judge_comment: Outcome-based Warm/Hot/Boil dial is very easy to understand, and IR thermopiles are workable, though they sense surface temperature only.

title: Two-Button Oven
new_elements: '+30 s' and 'Stop' buttons only (Two large mechanical buttons replace both knobs.)
rationale: With two choices and nothing else, there is no way to get it wrong.
judge_comment: A two-button interface almost entirely removes the learning curve and is easy to build, though minimal-button microwaves exist.

title: Mug-Only Micro Oven
new_elements: Mug-sized cylindrical cavity with lid (A single-purpose drink reheater with a fixed 60 s cycle.); Quick drink reheat (The most frequent microwave task.)
rationale: One purpose and one action means zero learning.
judge_comment: A single-purpose mug heater is radical and needs zero learning, but it cannot replace a general microwave.

title: Descending Weight Timer
new_elements: Visible cuckoo-clock weight on the side (Lifting the weight sets the time; its slow descent counts down and trips the switch at the bottom.)
rationale: 'Higher means longer' is physically obvious, and the remaining time is visible.
judge_comment: A cuckoo-clock weight timer is a wildly intuitive and visible substitute for a keypad, though it is awkward to build and the weight's travel limits the maximum time.

title: Push-In Drawer Sets Time
new_elements: Drawer whose push depth winds timer (Pushing the drawer past its closed click adds time, and it ejects when done.)
rationale: Loading, setting and starting merge into one push, like a toaster.
judge_comment: Merging load, set and start into one push is highly intuitive, though mapping push depth to time and the drawer mechanics are tricky.

title: One Big Go Button
new_elements: Single large illuminated start button (One press runs 30 s at full power; each extra press adds 30 s.); Sets cook time by press count (Replaces the clockwork timer knob and power knob with one input.)
rationale: One button with one rule is understood on first use, with nothing to read or set.
judge_comment: Highly intuitive and very feasible, but similar to existing +30s buttons so not radical.

title: Weighing Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable base (Weighs the food and auto-scales the cook time.); Auto-sizes cook time to mass (Removes the time-setting step.)
rationale: Portion size is handled automatically, so one press suits any amount of food.
judge_comment: Weighing and auto-scaling time removes the time-setting step, though it is a fairly known concept and is not strictly a cheaper substitution.

title: Package-Coded Cooking
new_elements: RFID/QR reader in cavity (Reads the meal packaging and loads the exact program.)
rationale: The food tells the oven how to cook it, so the user does nothing.
judge_comment: Package-coded programs remove all input and are plausible, though packaged-meal scanning already exists and it adds a reader rather than substituting a cheaper part.

title: IR Food Thermometer Stop
new_elements: Ceiling IR thermopile (Reads the food surface temperature and stops at 'warm' or 'hot'.)
rationale: Users choose a result, not a duration.
judge_comment: Choosing a result instead of a time removes the main need to learn settings, and IR thermopile sensing is realistic, though surface-only readings limit accuracy.

title: Door Tap Adds Time
new_elements: Accelerometer in door (Each knock on the closed door adds 15 s.)
rationale: Knock-knock to cook is a playful gesture that is learned instantly.
judge_comment: Knocking to add time is intuitive and cheap to implement, though accidental bumps and the lack of a display or feedback could cause confusion.

title: Colour-Status Interior Light
new_elements: RGB LED cavity light (Amber while cooking, green when done, red on error; replaces the bulb and bell.)
rationale: Traffic-light colours are universally understood.
judge_comment: An RGB cavity light that replaces the bulb and bell gives universally understood status feedback cheaply and with no learning.

title: Default-Minute Auto-Ask
new_elements: Runs 1 min then blinks 'more?' (Always starts with a safe default; one press continues.)
rationale: An iterative check-and-continue loop needs no prior knowledge.
judge_comment: A one-minute default with a single 'more?' press needs no learning and is trivially feasible, though it is a modest idea.

title: Infrared Food Thermometer Cutoff
new_elements: Thermopile IR sensing (Non-contact food surface temperature measurement.); Ceiling IR eye (Replaces the timer and power knobs by heating to a target temperature.); Heat to eating temperature (Stops at about 65 °C regardless of food.)
rationale: Users want 'hot', not '3 minutes at level 4', and the sensor delivers exactly that.
judge_comment: Heating to a target temperature matches what users actually want, though an IR sensor only reads surface temperature and cannot see through steam or containers.

title: Doneness Needle Gauge
new_elements: Analog doneness meter (Replaces the time scale with a needle moving from cold to hot, driven by the humidity sensor.); Show food state not time (Displays meaningful feedback.); Moving-coil meter (Cheap analog gauge.)
rationale: Cold-to-hot is self-explanatory.
judge_comment: An analog cold-to-hot needle driven by a humidity sensor is intuitive and cheap, though accuracy across foods is questionable.

title: One Picture Dial
new_elements: Single pictogram dial (cup, plate, frozen, butter) (One knob whose cam sets both time and duty cycle for each food icon.)
rationale: The user turns one knob to a picture of their food instead of translating it into minutes and power levels.
judge_comment: A single pictogram dial removes the translation to time and power; it is plausible with a cam, but the icons are somewhat generic.

title: Magnet-Coded Dishes
new_elements: Dish with embedded ferrite code (Ceramic bowls carry ferrite pellets in a pattern that reed switches under the floor read to select a program.); Reed-switch pattern reading (Magnet positions close specific contacts.)
rationale: Choosing the soup bowl or the milk mug is the whole setting, so the dish does the programming.
judge_comment: Dish-coded programs remove settings entirely and are very novel, but they need special dishes and microwave-safe ferrite placement is questionable.

title: Toaster Lever Start
new_elements: Slide-down toaster lever (Push the lever down to start; its height on a pictogram scale sets the time; it springs up when done.)
rationale: It borrows the toaster interaction that everyone already knows.
judge_comment: Familiar toaster lever maps time to height intuitively, though microwave time ranges and a pictogram scale are less precise than a dial.

title: Color-Coded Plates
new_elements: Floor colour sensor + coloured plate rims (Cheap photodiode reads the plate colour: blue for defrost, red for reheat, yellow for melt.)
rationale: Picking a coloured plate replaces programming the oven.
judge_comment: Using plate colour to select the program is radical and needs no learning, but it forces the user to buy special plates and the sensor must work in a microwave cavity.

title: Handle-Is-the-Timer
new_elements: Rotating door handle timer (Twist the door handle to set time; closing the door starts cooking; the handle unwinds as a visual countdown.)
rationale: The one part the user must touch anyway also becomes the control, so there is no panel to learn.
judge_comment: Replacing the control panel with a twisting door handle is intuitive and a true substitution, though mechanical timing and handle-latch integration are tricky.

title: Two-Word Rocker
new_elements: WARM / HOT rocker switch (Two presets replacing both knobs and covering most daily reheating tasks.)
rationale: Two choices, each one word, leave nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A two-choice rocker is very simple and easy to build, but it is not radical and offers little control.

title: Punch-Card Recipes
new_elements: Music-box punch-card reader (Insert a printed card; the timer motor drags it past pins that switch the magnetron on and off in a recipe profile.)
rationale: Complex multi-stage cooking becomes 'insert the butter card'.
judge_comment: A mechanical punch-card reader is a quirky, cheap, concrete substitute for digital menus, and 'insert the card' needs no learning, though cards limit flexibility.

title: Look-and-Cook Camera
new_elements: Cavity camera with food-recognition chip (Recognizes soup, pizza or frozen peas and picks the program; also replaces the viewing window function.); Edge TinyML image classification (Low-cost microcontroller vision model.)
