rationale: The oven sees what is inside and decides how to cook it.
judge_comment: Auto-recognition removes the need to choose settings, directly eliminating the learning curve, though accuracy and cost are concerns and it adds rather than substitutes.

title: Shrinking Light Ring
new_elements: LED pie-ring countdown around window (A lit ring around the door window shrinks like a clock pie as time runs out.)
rationale: Time remaining is shown as an amount, not numbers, so a glance tells the user how long is left.
judge_comment: A glanceable pie-ring timer is cheap and easy to understand, but it addresses only the display, not the operation.

title: Picture Dial
new_elements: Food-icon preset dial (Detented dial with icons (cup, plate, popcorn, frozen block); each detent drives a pre-shaped time and duty cam.); Selects cooking program by food type (Maps what the food is directly to time and power.)
rationale: Users point at a picture of their food instead of translating it into minutes and watts.
judge_comment: Food icons directly remove the need to translate to time and power, and the mechanical cam implementation is plausible, though similar presets already exist.

title: Steam Snap-Disc Stopper
new_elements: Exhaust-duct bimetal snap disc (Cheap thermostat in the vent trips when steam temperature rises, ending the cycle.); Detects food is hot via steam (Closed-loop end-of-cook.)
rationale: The microwave decides when the food is hot, so users never have to guess a time.
judge_comment: A closed-loop steam-sensing stop removes time guessing entirely and uses a cheap part, though a single trip threshold and covered food limit reliability.

title: Toaster Lever
new_elements: Push-down toaster-style lever (Push the lever down to start; its depth sets the time and it rises as time elapses.)
rationale: It borrows the one appliance gesture nearly everyone already knows.
judge_comment: The toaster lever uses a familiar gesture and is very easy to learn, though depth-based timing is imprecise for longer durations and the idea is not especially radical.

title: Dish-Coded Power
new_elements: Magnet-coded cookware with reed switches (The supplied defrost dish carries a magnet that a reed switch under the floor detects, selecting low duty.)
rationale: Choosing the right dish is the power setting, so there is no knob to misunderstand.
judge_comment: Dish-coded power removes the power-level concept using cheap reed switches, though it requires users to use the right dish.

title: Say It To Heat It
new_elements: Offline keyword voice chip (A $1 recognizer for about 10 fixed phrases such as 'warm tea', 'defrost', 'stop'.)
rationale: Users say what they want in plain words and need no interface at all.
judge_comment: A cheap offline keyword chip removes the interface and directly serves zero learning, though voice control in microwaves already exists.

title: Infrared Warm/Hot Button
new_elements: Thermopile IR food sensor (A cheap thermopile looks at the food and stops at a target of warm (50°C) or hot (70°C).); Heats to target temperature (Replaces time with result.)
rationale: Users choose the outcome (warm or hot) instead of an abstract duration.
judge_comment: Outcome-based warm/hot control removes time guessing and is a strong simplification, though IR sensing of food through a door and in a microwave cavity is challenging and accuracy varies.

title: Just-One-Button +30
new_elements: Single +30 s mega button (One large button: press once to start 30 s, press again to add 30 s; open the door to cancel.)
rationale: A single control means no wrong choice is possible.
judge_comment: A single +30 s button has essentially no learning curve and is trivial to build, though it is slow for long cook times and not very radical.

title: Safe-Handle Timer
new_elements: Rotating door handle timer-latch (Turning the door handle latches the door and winds the time; turning it back opens the door.)
rationale: Closing and starting become one continuous natural gesture.
judge_comment: Merging closing and starting into one gesture removes steps and is truly radical, but winding time through a latch handle raises safety interlock and mechanical complexity.

title: Fridge-Magnet Programs
new_elements: Magnetic program tokens on front panel (Stick the 'soup' magnet on the start zone; Hall sensors read its code.)
rationale: Tangible picture tokens are understood even by people with cognitive decline.
judge_comment: Tangible magnet tokens replace menus and keypads, which makes them intuitive and plausible with Hall sensors, though the token set is limited.

title: Humidity One-Touch Reheat
new_elements: Capacitive humidity sensor in vent (Stops a 'Reheat' cycle when a steam humidity spike is detected.)
rationale: One button with the end decided by the food means no guessing.
judge_comment: One button with a humidity sensor ending the cycle is truly zero-learning; sensor reheat already exists, and it is less reliable for some foods.

title: Pressure-Plate Start
new_elements: Floor pressure plate auto-start (With the door closed and food weight detected, a fixed 1-minute cycle runs; open the door to add more.)
rationale: Put food in, close the door, and it cooks: there are literally no controls.
judge_comment: Zero-control auto-start removes all learning, though a fixed 1-minute cycle and the risk of accidental starts limit it, and weight sensing is plausible.

title: Toaster Lever
new_elements: Push-down start lever with bimetal release (The user presses the lever down and it pops up when the cavity air reaches serving temperature.)
rationale: It copies the toaster gesture almost everyone already knows.
judge_comment: The familiar toaster lever removes the learning curve, though sensing food readiness from cavity air temperature is unreliable and could be unsafe.

title: Package Tells the Oven
new_elements: NFC reader under tray (Reads a cooking program from a tag on the food package.)
rationale: The user does nothing except insert the food.
judge_comment: A tag-driven program directly removes all input, though it needs packaging ecosystem adoption and a way to handle non-tagged food.

title: Picture Cards
new_elements: Card slot with punched-hole program cards (Picture cards such as 'soup' or 'milk' encode the program in holes.)
rationale: Children and elderly users just choose a picture and slot it in.
judge_comment: Picture-coded punched cards are very intuitive for children and the elderly and are mechanically simple, though they require physical cards that can get lost.

title: Metal Forgiveness
new_elements: Reflected-power arc detector (Senses arcing and cuts RF within milliseconds, then flashes a spoon icon.)
rationale: No rules about metal have to be memorised; the oven protects itself.
judge_comment: Arc detection that removes the need to remember metal rules directly eliminates a learned behavior, and it is plausible though it needs reliable sensing and protection.

title: Smart Vessels
new_elements: Coded companion containers (A mug, bowl and defrost box each have a magnet code the base reads.)
rationale: Choosing the container chooses the program.
judge_comment: Magnet-coded containers make choosing the vessel choose the program, which is clever and workable, but it requires proprietary containers and offers limited flexibility.

title: One Big Go Button with Humidity Auto-Cook
new_elements: Steam/humidity sensor + single GO button (Detects escaping steam to decide when food is done, replacing the timer and power knobs.); Determines doneness automatically (Ends heating when the steam curve indicates the food is hot.)
rationale: The user presses one button and never chooses a time or power level.
judge_comment: A single button with steam-sensing auto-cook removes every choice and substitutes sensors for timer and power knobs; sensor cooking exists in some models but is still strong.

title: Weighing Floor Sets Time
new_elements: Load cell under floor (Weight determines the heating energy.)
rationale: Putting food in is the only input needed.
judge_comment: Weight-based automatic heating directly removes inputs, though weight alone poorly predicts the needed energy for different foods.

title: Turn the Plate to Set Time
new_elements: Turntable acts as the input dial (Twisting the plate by hand sets the cook time, then it auto-rotates.)
rationale: The input sits right where the food is, so there is no separate control panel.
judge_comment: It truly substitutes the control panel with the turntable and is intuitive, though it is mechanically tricky and a bit ambiguous to use.

title: Tap +30 s Button
new_elements: Single +30 s tap button (Each tap adds 30 s and starts heating immediately.)
rationale: Short times become precise and obvious to set.
judge_comment: It replaces the keypad with one button that is instantly understandable and cheap, though similar buttons already exist.

title: Punched Recipe Cards
new_elements: Card slot with mechanical hole reader (Insert a printed food card whose holes set the time and power cams.)
rationale: The user picks a picture card, slides it in and the oven cooks.
judge_comment: A mechanical card reader that sets time and power cams replaces the keypad with a picture-and-insert action, which is intuitive, novel and buildable, though it needs a card for every food.

title: Toaster-Lever Microwave
new_elements: Door push-release button (Base-product component being substituted); Spring lever and lift tray (Pushing the lever lowers the food into a choked slot cavity; the tray pops up when the food is done); Load, start and finish using a familiar toaster gesture (Borrowed mental model)
rationale: Everyone already knows how to use a toaster, so the microwave inherits a learning curve of zero.
judge_comment: The toaster-lever metaphor is radical and instantly familiar, but a choked-slot cavity with a lift tray is hard to build, and the tray pops up on completion only if sensing works reliably.

title: Tap-Once +30 Button
new_elements: Mechanical clockwork timer knob (Base-product component being substituted); Single giant +30 s button (Each press adds 30 seconds and starts heating); One-button operation (No other controls)
rationale: With only one button there is literally nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single +30 button is very simple and cheap, though it offers limited control and similar ideas already exist.

title: Auto Power Modulation
new_elements: 5-step power knob with duty-cycle cam (Base-product component being substituted); Inverter with temperature feedback loop (Continuously adjusts power to the food's state); Self-choose power level (Removes the power decision)
rationale: Power level is the least understood microwave setting, and here it simply disappears.
judge_comment: Removing the power-level decision through inverter feedback directly cuts the learning curve, though food-state sensing is hard to get reliable.

title: Haptic Detent Knob
new_elements: Mechanical clockwork timer knob (Base-product component being substituted); Coarse-click knob with 1-2-3 min stops (Only three feelable positions); Blind, error-free setting (Usable by touch alone)
rationale: Few, tactile choices remove fine-adjustment confusion and help visually impaired users.
judge_comment: Coarse tactile detent knob is highly intuitive and feasible, but similar to old mechanical microwaves, so not very radical.

title: Close-the-Door-to-Cook
new_elements: Door-actuated start switch with fixed reheat cycle (Closing the door starts a 60 s cycle; opening the door stops it; closing it again adds another 60 s.)
rationale: There are no controls to learn: the door is the only interface.
judge_comment: The door is the only interface, which is very simple, though a fixed 60 s may suit few foods and the door-open stop and restart behavior needs care.

title: Colour-Coded RFID Plates
new_elements: RFID-tagged colour plates and reader (Blue plate = drink, green = reheat, white = defrost; the oven reads the tag and runs the matching program.)
rationale: Choosing a plate is the only decision the user makes.
judge_comment: Choosing a colour plate is simple and removes menus, and RFID readers are cheap, but it adds a plate the user must own and does not replace a part with something cheaper.

title: One-Pull Lever
new_elements: Side lever with fixed preset stroke (A slot-machine-style pull charges a spring timer; a half pull gives 1 min and a full pull gives 3 min.)
rationale: A big lever is easy to grip and its stroke length is self-explanatory.
judge_comment: A spring-timer lever with two preset strokes is intuitive, mechanical and cheap, though it offers only two durations and the slot-machine metaphor is a little gimmicky.

title: Thermopile Target Heat
new_elements: IR thermopile with Warm/Hot switch (Senses the surface temperature of the food and stops at the chosen setting.)
rationale: Users choose an outcome (warm or hot) instead of a process (minutes and watts).
judge_comment: Choosing an outcome (warm or hot) instead of time and power removes the learning curve, and IR thermopiles are cheap and plausible, though sensing the surface of food inside a microwave is imperfect.

title: Three Big Picture Pads
new_elements: Capacitive pads: Drink / Plate / Frozen (Three large icons replace both knobs.)
rationale: Three choices that match how people think about food cover most daily uses.
judge_comment: Three large icon pads are immediately understandable and easy to build, but similar preset buttons already exist, so the idea is not very radical.

title: Meal Key Inserts
new_elements: Shaped mechanical program keys (Plastic keys shaped like a cup or bowl whose notches set the cam time and power.)
rationale: Caregivers prepare the keys and users just insert the matching shape.
judge_comment: Shaped mechanical keys that set a cam are a simple, plausible substitution for a keypad, but they depend on caregiver preparation and a stock of keys.

title: Printed Time Sticker Code
new_elements: Optical dot-code reader (Reads colour-dot stickers that caregivers print or stick on leftovers.)
rationale: Programming is moved to the food itself, so the user only presses go.
judge_comment: Moving the programming onto the food is a radical idea and the user only presses go, but it needs a sticker printing workflow and a reader.

title: Kettle-Style Single Switch
new_elements: Kettle-type press-down switch with auto-off sensor (Push down to heat; the switch clicks up when the steam sensor trips.)
rationale: It borrows the kettle interface that everyone already knows.
judge_comment: A kettle-style push-down switch with steam-triggered auto-off substitutes the whole control panel with a familiar interface, though sensing doneness for varied foods is challenging.

title: One-Button Steam Sensing
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor (Detects the steam burst that signals the food is hot.); Ends cooking at doneness (Stops heating when steam appears, replacing guessed timer settings.)
rationale: A single Go button replaces both knobs because the oven decides when the food is done.
judge_comment: Humidity sensing for doneness is proven (sensor-cook modes), and a single Go button gives a very simple operation.

title: Three Picture Buttons
new_elements: Pictogram buttons (drink, plate, frozen) (Three icon buttons replace the 5-step power cam and time dial.)
rationale: Users pick what they see, not watts or minutes.
judge_comment: Three pictogram buttons directly remove the learning curve and are very feasible, though similar presets are common and not radical.

title: Food-Icon Dial
new_elements: Pictogram clockwork dial (Coffee, soup, popcorn, and frozen icons are printed around the existing timer cam.)
rationale: This is a cheap reprint of the current dial that users understand instantly.
judge_comment: A cheap pictogram dial directly removes the learning curve and is trivially feasible, though it is an incremental idea rather than a radical one.

title: Thermal Eye
new_elements: Low-res IR thermopile array (Maps the food surface temperature through the cavity roof.); Heat to target temperature (Stops when the food reaches about 70 °C everywhere.)
rationale: "Hot enough" replaces minutes, which is the result users actually want.
judge_comment: Outcome-based heating removes the need to choose a time, though IR sensing through a shielded cavity and the cost of the array are real challenges.

title: Curie-Point Safe Plate
new_elements: Curie-point ferrite susceptors (Stop absorbing microwaves above a set temperature.); Self-limiting ceramic plate (Food on it cannot exceed about 75 °C regardless of the time set.); Overheat-proof heating (Makes time setting non-critical.)
rationale: If too long is harmless, there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A radical substitution of control with passive physics that makes timing non-critical; the 75 °C cap and uneven heating limit real-world use.

title: Ice-Sensing Defrost
new_elements: RF reflection dielectric sensing (Ice and water reflect microwaves differently.); Directional coupler sensor (Measures reflected power to detect when thawing is complete.); Automatic defrost end (No defrost tables needed.)
rationale: Defrosting, the most confusing task, becomes automatic.
judge_comment: Automatic defrost detection removes the most confusing task, and RF reflection sensing is plausible though hard to make reliable across foods.

title: Toaster Lever Microwave
new_elements: Push-down toaster lever (Pressing a lever latches heating on; a solenoid pops it up with a clack at the end.)
rationale: It reuses the toaster gesture, which everyone already knows.
judge_comment: A familiar toaster-lever gesture makes operation intuitive and is easy to build, though it only handles a fixed-duration cycle and is not very radical.

title: Plus-30 Single Button
new_elements: Single big '+30 s' button (Each press adds 30 s at full power; holding it cancels.)
rationale: The whole interface is one button, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single +30 s button is nearly zero-learning and trivial to build, but it is an incremental simplification rather than a radical idea.

title: Twist-Handle Timer
new_elements: Rotary door handle timer (Twisting the door handle after closing sets the time; it unwinds as it cooks.)
rationale: Closing and timing merge into one hand motion at one spot.
judge_comment: Merging door closing and time-setting into one twist is intuitive and plausible, though it needs a mechanical timer linkage and gives limited cooking-power control.

title: Braille Click Detents
new_elements: Tactile detent timer knob (one click = 30 s) (Audible and tactile clicks with raised marks at 1, 2 and 5 min.)
rationale: Users count clicks instead of reading tiny printed numbers.
judge_comment: Detented knobs with tactile marks are simple and accessible, but they are close to existing mechanical timers and so not very radical.

title: IR Eye Auto-Stop
new_elements: Thermopile array in the cavity roof (Reads food surface temperature and stops at 'hot'.)
rationale: The user presses 'heat' and the oven finishes the thinking.
judge_comment: IR sensing with automatic stop is plausible, is already partly on the market, and directly removes the need to set a time.

title: Probe Stick Target
new_elements: Microwave-safe fiber-optic temperature probe (Stick it in the food; cooking stops at 'warm' or 'hot'.)
rationale: Users choose the outcome they want, not the method to get there.
judge_comment: Outcome-based cooking with a probe removes the need for settings and strongly fits zero learning, though a probe in a microwave and the need to insert it add cost and some friction.

title: Toaster-Lever Microwave
new_elements: Push-down start lever with slide scale (Toaster-style lever: slide along a short-to-long scale, push down to start, pops up when done); Solenoid/escapement lever hold-down (Lever is held down by a catch and released when the timer expires)
rationale: It borrows the toaster's universally known gesture, so anyone can use it on sight.
judge_comment: The toaster lever gesture is familiar and the catch/release mechanism is simple, but the time scale still needs some judgment.

title: Twist the Plate to Set Time
new_elements: Wind-up turntable timer (User twists the turntable itself to wind it; it unwinds back to zero while rotating, and a marked rim shows time left); Spring-wound turntable escapement (Mainspring plus a governor drives rotation and timing together)
rationale: Turning the food means 'cook this much longer', which is an immediately intuitive gesture.
judge_comment: A wind-up turntable that sets the time through a familiar twist gesture is radical and intuitive, though mechanical coupling and load on the plate are awkward.

title: Food Tokens
new_elements: Shaped token slot (Drop in a chunky token shaped like a mug, a soup bowl or an ice cube; its notches set the program)
rationale: Matching a shape needs no reading or numeracy, which suits children and elderly users.
judge_comment: Physical shape-matched tokens remove reading and numeracy, though losing tokens and limited food coverage are drawbacks.

title: Temperature, Not Time
new_elements: IR thermopile food thermometer (Roof sensor watches the food surface temperature); Warm/Hot/Boiling dial (User chooses a target state instead of minutes)
rationale: People think 'I want it hot', not '2:30 at 600 W'.
judge_comment: Matches the user's mental model of wanting food hot, though IR sensing of the surface is imperfect in a microwave.

title: Absorption-Sensing Stop
new_elements: Reflected-power diode detector (Senses RF reflected back up the waveguide; a rise means the water is gone or the food is done); Waveguide reflectometry (Measures standing-wave ratio to infer load state)
rationale: The oven listens to the food and stops by itself, so there is nothing for the user to set.
judge_comment: Auto-stop from reflected-power sensing removes the need for any settings, but reliably detecting doneness is hard in practice.

title: Solid-State 'Just Start' Engine
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Low-voltage semiconductor RF source with continuous power and built-in load sensing); Gallium-nitride RF power transistors (Wide-bandgap transistors producing 2.45 GHz at tens of volts)
rationale: Closed-loop sensing makes a single start button sufficient for any food.
judge_comment: A solid-state RF source with closed-loop sensing is a true component substitution that enables one-button use; it is plausible but costly at the needed power.

title: Door-Tap Timer
new_elements: Door knock sensor (Piezo sensor counts taps on the closed door; each tap adds 30 s)
rationale: 'Knock twice for a minute' is a playful rule that can be learned in seconds.
judge_comment: Tapping the door to add time is playful and learnable in seconds, though accidental knocks and the lack of power-level control are drawbacks.

title: Portion Dial
new_elements: Portions dial (1 cup, 2 cups, 1 plate, family dish) (Quantity scale mapped internally to time)
rationale: People know how much food they have, not how long it needs.
judge_comment: A portion dial maps what users already know (how much food) to cook time, so it directly removes the learning curve and is easy to build.

title: Photo Drum Selector
new_elements: Rotating photo drum (Roll a drum until the picture of your food appears in a window; the drum's cam encodes the program)
rationale: Matching a picture is all the skill required.
judge_comment: A picture-matching drum with a cam-encoded program is highly intuitive and radical, though it limits the number of programs and needs mechanical care.

title: Phone-Charger-Style Base
new_elements: Dock-to-cook pod base (Seating the bowl on the base is the start command; lifting it off is stop)
rationale: Placement equals action, a gesture already learned from wireless chargers.
judge_comment: Placing the bowl to start and lifting it to stop removes the controls entirely and is intuitive, though it needs a preset time or power and weight sensing.

title: Toaster Lever Microwave
new_elements: Push-down start lever with pop-up release (Pushing the lever down latches the door and starts heating. The lever pops up at the end.)
rationale: It borrows the toaster interaction that everyone already knows.
judge_comment: Leverages a familiar toaster mental model so there is zero learning, and is easily built with a mechanical latch and timer.

title: Just Make It Hot Button
new_elements: IR thermopile food thermometer (Watches the food's surface temperature and stops at about 70 °C.); Single 'HOT' button (The only control on the panel.)
rationale: One button with an obvious meaning leaves nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single HOT button with IR temperature sensing is a truly zero-learning interface, though surface-only sensing and steam/container interference limit accuracy.

title: Food Tells the Magnetron
new_elements: Reflected-power sensing (Tracks the shift in RF absorption as water heats or thaws to estimate when food is done.); Directional coupler in waveguide (Cheap sensor that measures the RF power coming back from the cavity.)
rationale: The microwave decides when to stop, so the user only presses start.
judge_comment: Sensing reflected power to auto-stop makes operation one-touch, though accuracy across different foods is difficult.

title: Packaging Conductive Code
new_elements: Contact pads that read conductive-ink codes on food trays (Ready meals carry a printed pattern that sets time and power when the tray sits on the pads.); Auto-programs cooking from the food package (No user input is needed.)
rationale: The food tells the oven what to do, so the user just puts it in.
judge_comment: Zero-input cooking from package codes removes the learning curve entirely, but requires industry-wide packaging adoption and reliable contacts in a microwave environment.

title: Single Mug Slot
new_elements: Mug-sized shielded slot with a fixed 90 s program (Inserting a cup presses a switch that runs one preset.)
rationale: The most common task needs zero decisions.
judge_comment: Zero decisions gives a true no-learning-curve experience and it is easy to build, but it is limited to one task.

title: Piano-Key Presets
new_elements: Three large mechanical piano keys: Drink, Reheat, Defrost (Each key latches a fixed cam profile.)
rationale: Three labelled keys cover most tasks with one press.
judge_comment: Three labelled mechanical keys are very easy to use and quite feasible, though the idea is not very radical.

title: Ceiling IR Eye
new_elements: Thermopile IR sensor in the cavity ceiling (Stops cooking when the food surface reaches serving temperature.)
rationale: 'Heat until warm' is the only mode, and it needs no input.
judge_comment: A single 'heat until warm' mode with an IR sensor removes all input, though a thermopile can't reliably read food surface temperature through steam, and it's not cheaper than a timer.

title: Magnet-Coded Cookware
new_elements: Dishes with embedded ferrite codes read by reed switches (A mug, bowl or plate each select their own program.)
rationale: Choosing the dish is the whole interface.
judge_comment: Dish selects the program, which removes the interface, though it requires special cookware and fixed programs.

title: Passive Temp-Tag Plate
new_elements: Plate with a Curie-point ferrite tag that detunes a coil at serving temperature (A coil under the turntable detects the change and stops cooking.)
rationale: The plate decides when the food is done.
judge_comment: Plate-driven auto-stop removes all settings, but Curie-point detection of a tag under a turntable with food variability is tricky and it requires special plates.

title: One Big +30s Button
new_elements: Single +30s push button (One large button that starts at 30 s; each extra press adds 30 s at full power.); Set time by repeated presses (Cooking time is set by counting presses, with no dial or menu.)
rationale: One button that you press more for longer is understood instantly, with no settings to learn.
judge_comment: Very simple and clear, but many microwaves already have a +30s button, so it is a modest substitution.

title: Pull-Cord Timer
new_elements: Retracting pull cord (Pulling the cord out sets the time by length, and the cord slowly rewinds as it counts down.); Physical length equals time (The remaining time is visible as the length of cord still out.)
rationale: Pulling further for longer is a toy-like mapping that children and older users understand at once.
judge_comment: A pull cord that maps length to time is a wild and intuitive idea, though the mechanism is gimmicky and gives only coarse precision.

title: Self-Identifying Dishes
new_elements: Magnet-coded containers (Each container type carries magnets that a Hall sensor reads to select power and time.); Container selects program (The dish tells the oven what to do.)
rationale: Using the right bowl is the whole interface, so nothing has to be set.
judge_comment: Containers that tell the oven what to do is a radical idea and needs no settings, but it requires special dishes and microwave-safe magnets, which limits practicality.

title: RFID Meal Packs
new_elements: RFID reader in cavity (Reads cooking instructions stored in tags on ready-meal packaging.); Package-driven cooking (The user only has to press start.)
rationale: There is nothing to read on the box and nothing to set on the oven.
judge_comment: Package-driven cooking removes nearly every decision, but it needs tagged packaging across the industry and covers only ready meals.

title: Egg-Timer Top Knob
new_elements: Kitchen egg-timer knob on top (A familiar twist-and-tick timer that switches the oven on directly.); Familiar countdown (Uses an object people already know.)
rationale: It reuses a mental model nearly everyone already has.
judge_comment: A familiar egg-timer knob gives near-zero learning and is easy to make, though similar mechanical dials already exist.

title: One Giant Go Button
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob + 5-step power knob (Base controls being substituted (from product meta).); Single oversized Go button (Each press adds 30 s at full power; long-press cancels.); Start heating with one action (One control replaces two knobs and their combined settings.)
rationale: One button with one meaning leaves nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Very simple and highly feasible with no learning curve, but similar to existing +30s buttons and not radical.

title: Infrared Eye Thermostat
new_elements: Power knob + timer knob (Base controls being substituted.); Ceiling IR thermopile (Reads food surface temperature and stops at about 70 °C.); Non-contact infrared thermometry (Low-cost thermopile sensor array.)
rationale: "Make it hot" becomes the only instruction, and the sensor handles the rest.
judge_comment: An IR thermopile that targets a temperature makes 'make it hot' the only instruction and is cheap and plausible, though surface-only readings and uneven heating are drawbacks.

title: Food Pictogram Dial
new_elements: 0-30 min numeric timer scale (Base dial markings being substituted.); Picture dial (Icons for mug, plate, bowl, popcorn and frozen meal replace the minute marks.)
rationale: Users point at what they are heating instead of converting it into minutes.
judge_comment: Pointing at the food type removes time conversion and is easy to build, though presets already exist on many microwaves.

title: Say "Warm It"
new_elements: Timer and power knobs (Base controls being substituted.); Offline keyword voice module (Understands only "warm", "hot", "defrost" and "stop".); On-device keyword spotting (Microcontroller speech recognition with no network needed.)
rationale: Users just say what they want in plain words.
judge_comment: A small offline voice vocabulary removes the learning curve, but noise and misrecognition could cause problems.

title: RFID Smart Plates
new_elements: Timer and power knobs (Base controls being substituted.); Tagged dish set (Mug, soup bowl and dinner plate each carry an RF-shielded tag naming its program.)
rationale: The container chooses the program, so the user does nothing.
judge_comment: Container-driven programs remove all user input, though they need a dedicated dish set and a tag reader, and tag shielding adds complexity.

title: Mug-Fit Pod
new_elements: 20 L cavity + turntable (Base cavity and plate being substituted.); Mug-sized heating well (Dropping in a mug starts heating; lifting it out stops.)
rationale: Put the mug in and it heats; take it out and it stops.
judge_comment: Drop-in mug heating with automatic stop is extremely intuitive, though it limits the microwave to mugs and needs reliable sensing of the mug's presence.

title: Fridge-Magnet Presets
new_elements: Knob programming (Base setting method being substituted.); Magnetic preset tiles (Sticking a soup, pizza or milk tile on the door sets the program.)
rationale: Tangible pictures replace any settings memory.
judge_comment: Magnetic tiles that sense and set the program make operation tangible and learning-free, and are plausible with Hall sensors, though the cooking guidance is limited to the preset tiles.

title: Shrinking Light Bar
new_elements: Clockwork dial readout (Base time display being substituted.); LED countdown bar (A bar of light shrinks as time runs out.)
rationale: Time remaining is understood without reading numbers.
judge_comment: A shrinking light bar makes remaining time intuitive and is easy to build, though not very radical.

title: Rice-Cooker Steam Cutoff
new_elements: Vent steam bimetal switch (A bimetal disc in the exhaust path snaps open when sustained steam signals the food is hot.); Steam-temperature sensing via exhaust bimetal (Reuses snap-disc technology to detect the food reaching its boiling plateau.)
rationale: Like a rice cooker, the user just presses go and the oven decides when the food is done.
judge_comment: A steam-sensing bimetal cutoff gives press-and-go operation and is plausible, though it works poorly for dry or covered foods.

title: Magnet-Coded Vessels
new_elements: Magnet-coded cup, bowl and defrost box set (Each vessel's base magnet pattern trips floor reed switches that select a preset time and power.)
rationale: The container itself is the program, so choosing a cup is the only decision the user makes.
judge_comment: Magnet-coded vessels make the container the program, which is feasible with reed switches but requires proprietary cookware and limits flexibility.

title: Close-the-Door-to-Start
new_elements: Starts a default 1-minute cycle on door close (The door striker winds the timer cam to a default one-minute position.)
rationale: The most common reheat needs zero controls: put the food in, shut the door, and wait.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start a default cycle removes all controls for the most common use, though it risks accidental starts and is a known concept in some designs.

title: Package Barcode Scan
new_elements: Door-mounted barcode reader (Holding the ready-meal pack to the door window loads the maker's time and power profile.)
rationale: There is no need to read tiny print on the package or translate it into knob settings.
judge_comment: Scanning the pack removes the need to read instructions or set anything, which directly serves zero-learning-curve use, though it is not far from existing smart-oven scanning and relies on a barcode database.

title: Infrared Food-Temperature Stop
new_elements: Thermopile IR food sensor (A roof sensor watches the food surface and stops at about 65 °C.); Thermopile infrared radiometry (Non-contact temperature measurement of the food.)
rationale: 'Heat until hot' replaces guessing minutes.
judge_comment: 'Heat until hot' removes the need to choose a time, which fits zero learning curve well, though IR sensing of surface temperature is imperfect.

title: Two-Floor Power Cavity
new_elements: Upper gentle shelf behind attenuating grid (The top compartment receives reduced field for melting and thawing, while the bottom gets full power.)
rationale: Where you put the food is the power setting: up for gentle, down for hot.
judge_comment: Using food position as the power setting removes the need for any controls and is very intuitive, but achieving reliable field attenuation by shelf is technically hard.

title: Pocket Timer Puck
new_elements: Detachable wind-up timer puck (A magnetic egg timer docks on the front to run the oven, and the user can carry it away to hear it ring.)
rationale: It reuses the familiar kitchen egg timer as the whole user interface.
judge_comment: Reusing a familiar egg timer as the whole interface gives virtually no learning curve, is cheap and substitutes a simple part for the electronics, and it is feasible with a magnetic dock and a mechanical switch.

title: Punched Recipe Card Slot
new_elements: Jukebox-style punched card reader (Inserting a picture card (e.g. 'porridge') sets the time and power via its punched holes over feeler switches.)
rationale: Users pick a picture card and slot it in, so programs become physical objects.
judge_comment: Picture cards with punched holes make presets tangible and need no learning, and feeler switches are workable, though the cards are extra items to keep.

title: Steam Sniffer Auto-Off
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor (Detects the burst of steam released when food is heated through.); Steam-triggered shutoff (Ends the cycle once steam is detected.)
rationale: A cheap humidity sensor replaces the user's judgement about timing.
judge_comment: A humidity sensor for auto-off is cheap and already used in sensor-cook modes, but it works poorly for dry foods.

title: Barcode Scan Cooking
new_elements: Door-mounted barcode reader (Reads the packaging and loads the manufacturer's cooking program.)
rationale: Showing the box replaces reading and interpreting package instructions.
judge_comment: Barcode reader is cheap and feasible and simplifies operation, but it depends on a program database and on packaged food only.

title: Camera Food Recognition
new_elements: Cavity camera with food classifier (Identifies the food and portion size, then picks time and power.)
rationale: The oven recognises the food, so the user gives no input at all.
judge_comment: Zero-input operation fits the need perfectly, though camera cost, steam on the lens, and classifier accuracy are real challenges.

title: Talking End Signal
new_elements: Speech synthesis (Recorded voice prompts.); Voice chip replacing bell (Says 'Done - stir and wait 1 minute'.)
rationale: It tells the user what to do next instead of just ringing.
judge_comment: Spoken instructions are easy to build and plainly reduce confusion about what to do next, though talking appliances are not new.

title: Metal-Detector Door Frame
new_elements: Eddy-current coil in door frame (Refuses to start and shows a spoon icon if metal is inside.)
rationale: Mistakes are prevented by the oven instead of by user knowledge.
judge_comment: Eddy-current metal sensing is feasible and the spoon icon gives clear feedback, but it blocks rather than removes the rule and may false-trigger on foil-trimmed dishes.

title: Progress Light Ring
new_elements: LED ring around door (Shrinks like a clock pie as time runs out and replaces the timer markings.)
rationale: Remaining time is understood at a glance without reading numbers.
judge_comment: An intuitive visual countdown replaces numeric reading and is cheap and easy, though only a modest improvement.

title: Single Smart Knob
new_elements: Unified food-amount knob (One dial, from small cup to big plate, sets both power and time electronically.)
rationale: It halves the controls and describes food amount, not physics.
judge_comment: A single knob for food amount simplifies the controls and is feasible, but it is a fairly familiar approach and doesn't say how food type is handled.

title: One Picture Dial
new_elements: Single pictogram food dial (One knob showing drawn icons (cup, plate, frozen meal, popcorn), each detent mapped by cam to a fixed time and power pair.)
rationale: Users point at a picture of their food instead of translating it into minutes and power levels.
judge_comment: Pictogram dial with a cam is simple and cheap, but icon-based presets are already seen and not radical.

title: Close-Door-to-Cook
new_elements: Door closure starts auto cycle (The interlock switch doubles as the start trigger and the sensor ends the cycle.)
rationale: Shutting the door, an action everyone already performs, becomes the only control.
judge_comment: Zero-control door-close start is radical and has no learning curve, but it risks accidental starts, empty runs and safety concerns, and it depends on reliable sensing.

title: Package-Reads-Itself
new_elements: NFC/barcode food reader (Reads a code on packaged meals and applies the manufacturer's time and power.)
rationale: Users never read or type the package instructions.
judge_comment: Removes all input for packaged meals, though it depends on manufacturer codes and doesn't cover non-packaged food.

title: Two-Position Rocker
new_elements: Heat/Defrost rocker switch (Replaces the 5-step cam with two clear states: 100% or 30%.)
rationale: Two choices match the only decisions most users actually make.
judge_comment: Very simple and cheap, but it is an incremental simplification and gives limited control.

title: Pull-Cord Timer
new_elements: Retracting pull-cord timer (Pull out a cord marked with food icons; it retracts slowly and the remaining length is the remaining time.)
rationale: Users can see and feel how much time is left without reading numbers.
judge_comment: The pull-cord is an intuitive, tactile timer with a visible countdown, though a retracting mechanism needs a damper and is imprecise.

title: Temperature Knob, Not Time
new_elements: IR thermopile + Warm/Hot/Boiling knob (A ceiling IR sensor reads the food surface temperature and stops at the chosen level.)
rationale: People think in 'hot', not in minutes, so the control speaks their language.
judge_comment: A temperature-level knob matches the user's mental model and removes time guessing, though IR surface sensing through steam and varied foods is imperfect.

title: Wind-Up Spring Timer
new_elements: Escapement clockwork kitchen timer (A spring escapement replaces the synchronous motor and is mains-frequency independent.)
rationale: It works exactly like the egg timer users already own, the same in every region.
judge_comment: A mechanical wind-up timer is the familiar egg-timer interface and very feasible, though it is already the classic microwave dial and not radical.

title: Gravity-Drop Weight Timer
new_elements: Visible descending weight timer (Lift a weight up a front column; it sinks through a damper and its height shows the time left.)
rationale: Remaining time is shown as plain height, readable from across the kitchen.
judge_comment: A visible gravity-damper timer is wildly novel and intuitive to read, but lifting a weight and damping it accurately over varied durations is awkward and it is not obviously simpler to operate.

title: Token Slot Programs
new_elements: Shaped token slot (Drop a chunky 'mug', 'plate' or 'frozen' token; its shape sets the cam program.)
rationale: It works like a toy shape sorter: impossible to get wrong.
judge_comment: A shape-sorter token that sets a cam program is nearly foolproof, though loose tokens get lost and the mechanism adds complexity.

title: Portion Knob
new_elements: Portion-size knob (1 cup / bowl / plate / family) (The cam sets both power and time from the portion size.)
rationale: 'How much food' is a question everyone can answer instantly.
judge_comment: Choosing by portion size removes the need to know power or time, directly serving zero learning curve and being easy to build with a cam.

title: Revolving Drum Cavity
new_elements: Half-open rotating drum (Rotate the cavity drum 180° to face the food inward; the solid back wall shields, with no door.)
rationale: One turn both closes the oven and starts it, like a bank teller drawer.
judge_comment: A one-turn rotating drum that closes and starts the oven is radical and very simple to use, though microwave shielding and sealing are hard.

title: Knee Bump Panel
new_elements: Lower-front bump bar release (A wide bar under the door releases the latch with a hip or knee nudge.)
rationale: Hands-full operation needs no precision or instructions.
judge_comment: Simple, cheap mechanical substitute that is intuitive, but it only simplifies opening the door.

title: RFID Plate Rims
new_elements: Microwave-safe RFID-tagged plates (A tag in the rim glaze tells the oven the dish type and preset.)
rationale: Users pick a plate and the setting is done.
judge_comment: Plate-driven auto setting is clever and zero-input, but requires proprietary plates and an RFID reader, which limits practicality.

title: Hourglass Flip Microwave
new_elements: Tilt-switch flip timer module (Flip a sand-glass-shaped module on top; a tilt switch runs the oven while the sand falls.)
rationale: Turning an hourglass is a centuries-old, self-explanatory action.
judge_comment: The hourglass flip is a radical, self-explanatory interface that replaces the timer and buttons, though the tilt-switch safety and the fixed durations need work.

title: Squeeze-and-Hold Handle
new_elements: Pressure handle (Holding the handle counts up the time, shown on a light strip.); Hold-to-set (Release when the bar looks right.)
rationale: It is a continuous, intuitive gesture with no reading required.
judge_comment: Hold-to-set is an intuitive gesture that removes number reading, though it is a bit imprecise and a continuous hold is tiring for long times.

title: Infinite Smart Knob
new_elements: Single haptic encoder knob (One knob that turns to set time and is pushed to start; power is auto-derived.); Merged controls (Two knobs become one.)
rationale: Fewer controls means fewer things to learn.
judge_comment: Merging controls into one knob is simple and highly feasible, but it is a familiar, incremental design rather than a radical one.

title: Steam-Sniffing Auto-Stop
new_elements: Humidity/steam sensor in exhaust (Detects the vapour burst released when food is hot.); Stop when food is actually hot (Replaces the 0-30 min clockwork timer.); Capacitive humidity sensing (Low-cost polymer RH sensor.)
rationale: The machine knows when food is done, so users never learn timing.
judge_comment: Steam sensing is plausible, as sensor-cook already exists, and it removes the need to choose a time, though it is not a full no-input interface.

title: Food-Picture Dial
new_elements: Single pictogram dial (Positions show a mug, a plate, a frozen block and popcorn instead of minutes and power steps.); Select by food type, not by parameters (Each picture maps internally to a preset time and duty cycle.)
rationale: Pointing at a picture of your food needs no literacy and no reasoning about numbers.
judge_comment: A pictogram dial is cheap and easy to understand but is incremental and already common, and the presets are inflexible.

title: Toaster-Lever Microwave
new_elements: Spring-loaded push-down lever (Push the lever down to start; it pops up with a clunk when done, like a toaster.); Familiar start/stop affordance (Borrows a mental model everyone already has.)
rationale: Reusing toaster muscle memory removes any learning curve.
judge_comment: A familiar toaster-style lever makes starting intuitive, but it only addresses start/stop and leaves the question of how long to cook unresolved.

title: Magnetic Recipe Pucks
new_elements: Magnetic program tokens (Chunky picture pucks are dropped onto a top recess to select the program.); Tangible program selection (Replaces the dials with physical objects.)
rationale: Children and elderly users simply place a picture puck.
judge_comment: Picture pucks are easy for children and elderly users and simple to build, but the user still has to pick a program, and the idea resembles existing tangible interfaces.

title: Heat-Colour Cavity Glow
new_elements: RGB LED cavity lighting (Interior light shifts from blue (cold) to red (hot) following the IR sensor.); Intuitive heat progress display (Replaces the timer pointer and the bell.)
rationale: Blue to red is a universally understood signal.
judge_comment: A blue-to-red glow is an intuitive, cheap LED substitution for timer and bell that is easy to understand, though it relies on an IR sensor.

title: Solid-State RF with Self-Tuning
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF generation (Replaces the magnetron and the duty-cycle cam.); Multi-antenna RF array (Senses reflected power to know the food state.); Self-regulating even heating (Removes the power knob entirely.)
rationale: The oven chooses power itself, so the user never touches a power setting.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with reflected-power sensing could auto-select power and remove the knob, though cost and reliable doneness sensing are still open problems.

title: Auto Mass-Temperature Defrost
new_elements: Frost-detecting IR sensor (Recognises frozen food by surface temperature.); Automatic defrost mode switch (No defrost setting to find.)
rationale: The oven notices frozen food and handles it automatically.
judge_comment: Auto-detecting frozen food removes a confusing setting directly, though surface IR is an imperfect proxy for frozen mass and it is more an addition than a substitution.

title: Haptic Detent Knob
new_elements: Detented food-category knob (Strong clicks with raised Braille-like icons at each food type.); Eyes-free selection (Replaces the smooth clockwork scale.)
rationale: Vision-impaired and hurried users can operate it by feel.
judge_comment: A detented tactile knob is simple, cheap and intuitive, and it is a true substitution, but it is not radical.

title: Close-the-Door-to-Start
new_elements: Starts cooking on door closure (The interlock closing event triggers the preselected program, so no start button is needed.)
rationale: Shutting the door is the only action required, which removes a whole step from operation.
judge_comment: Starting on door closure removes a step and is easy to implement with the existing interlock, though it risks accidental starts and needs a default program.

title: Steam-Sniffer Auto Stop
new_elements: Humidity/steam sensor in exhaust (Detects the moment food releases steam and ends the cycle.)
rationale: The timer is replaced by a sensor that knows when the food is done.
judge_comment: A steam sensor replacing the timer is highly relevant and feasible, but sensor-cook is already common in higher-end models.

title: Package Barcode Programs
new_elements: Door-frame barcode/NFC reader (Reads the ready-meal packaging and runs the manufacturer's program.)
rationale: Students simply insert the meal and the package instructions program themselves.
judge_comment: Package-driven programs are novel and truly zero-learning, but they depend on manufacturers adopting a standard and on a limited set of supported packages.

title: Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Push-pull RF-sealed drawer (A sliding drawer with a choke rim replaces the hinged door and latch lever.)
rationale: Everyone already knows how to open a drawer.
judge_comment: A drawer is an intuitive interaction that removes the latch, though RF sealing and a drawer-sized cavity are challenging.

title: Built-In Boil Nucleator
new_elements: Porous ceramic nucleation stud (A microwave-transparent stud on the turntable on which cups sit, seeding bubbles.)
rationale: The user does not need to know the stir-before-heating rule.
judge_comment: It removes a hidden safety rule the user would otherwise have to learn, though its effectiveness is uncertain.

title: Auto-Pop Door When Done
new_elements: Solenoid door kicker (Releases the latch at the end of the cycle, venting steam and signalling done.)
rationale: An open door means ready, which is unmistakable.
judge_comment: A door that pops open is an unmistakable done signal with no learning needed, but it substitutes a beep rather than a part and could startle users or let food spill.

title: Clockwork Turntable
new_elements: Spring drive wound by timer knob (Winding the timer also stores energy that spins the turntable, replacing the motor.)
rationale: One twist does everything.
judge_comment: A spring drive wound by the timer knob is a clever, tangible substitute for the motor, but its link to a no-learning-curve interface is mild, and spring runtime would need to match the timer.

title: Zero-Control Microwave
new_elements: Fully autonomous heat-to-eat (Senses weight, temperature and steam, heats to eating temperature and opens; it has no controls.)
rationale: No controls means nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A microwave with no controls removes the learning curve entirely and is truly radical, but reliably sensing food state and heating safely and evenly is very hard, and the mechanisms are only loosely specified.

title: One Picture Dial
new_elements: Single food-pictogram dial (One knob with icons (mug, plate, popcorn, frozen) whose cam sets both duration and duty cycle together.)
rationale: The user picks what the food is rather than translating it into minutes and watts, so one choice replaces two.
judge_comment: Pictogram dial is simple and plausible, though presets on dials exist already and it isn't very radical.

title: Tap-Count Button
new_elements: Single +30 s press button (Each press adds 30 s of cooking time and the first press also starts the oven.)
rationale: The interface is one button where more presses means more heat, so it is learnt in seconds.
judge_comment: One-button +30s is trivially learnable and cheap, but it is already common on many microwaves.

title: Steam-Sniffer Auto-Off
new_elements: Humidity sensor in exhaust vent (Detects the steam spike from heated food and ends the cycle.)
rationale: The oven decides when the food is done, so the user never has to guess a time.
judge_comment: Humidity-sensor auto-cook exists in some high-end microwaves, but it removes the time decision and so fits the no-learning-curve need well.

title: Fixed-Power Simplicity
new_elements: Single defrost toggle (The power knob is removed; the oven runs at full power except for one 'snowflake' switch that sets 30% duty.)
rationale: Five power levels collapse to a single clear 'frozen or not' decision.
judge_comment: Dropping the power knob in favor of one defrost switch is simple and easy to build, but it is a modest idea and full power can overcook delicate foods.

title: Color-Keyed Containers
new_elements: Shape-keyed cookware set (Each bowl or mug has a molded foot whose shape presses cavity switches to select a program.)
rationale: The dish itself is the program, so nothing has to be set.
judge_comment: Cookware whose foot shape triggers cavity switches makes the dish the program and removes setting entirely, though it forces users to buy a proprietary set and the cavity switches add hygiene and wear concerns.

title: IR Food Thermometer
new_elements: Ceiling thermopile sensor (Reads the food's surface temperature and stops at the target heat.)
rationale: The oven cooks to a temperature rather than a time, so the user has nothing to estimate.
judge_comment: Cooking to a target temperature removes time estimation, and IR sensing is plausible, though surface-only readings and the lack of a way to set the target limit it.

title: NFC Phone Tap
new_elements: NFC tag reader pad (Tapping a phone or food package on the pad loads the cooking cycle.)
rationale: A single tap is all the programming the user does.
judge_comment: A tap-to-load cycle is very simple to use, but it depends on a phone or tagged packaging and is not a true substitution.

title: Self-Opening When Done
new_elements: Signals completion by opening door (The cam end-stop trips the latch so the door swings ajar, replacing the bell.)
rationale: An open door unmistakably means the food is ready, even for users with hearing loss.
judge_comment: The door opening on completion is an intuitive signal that substitutes for the bell, though an unexpectedly ajar door has safety and heat-retention drawbacks.

title: Mug Hole Microwave
new_elements: Top-entry mug-shaped cavity with choke collar (The mug drops into a cylindrical well and a quarter-wavelength choke at the rim contains the field.)
rationale: Dropping the cup in is the whole operation for the most common use.
judge_comment: A drop-in mug well removes controls and door for the dominant use case, and a choke collar is a plausible containment approach, though limited to mugs and still needs heating logic.

title: How-Hot Single Knob
new_elements: Combined cam with warm/hot/very-hot scale (One cam profile ramps time and duty cycle together.)
rationale: Users choose the outcome they want rather than technical parameters.
judge_comment: A single outcome-based cam knob replaces the keypad and timer and is cheap and intuitive, though it is not radical.

title: Mode Stirrer Instead of Turntable
new_elements: Ceiling metal mode stirrer fan (A rotating reflector spreads the field, so there is no glass plate to drop, misplace or seat.)
rationale: The flat floor means there is no assembly and nothing can go wrong.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are proven and cheaply replace the turntable, removing a misplaceable part, though they do little for operating the controls.

title: Frozen-Detect Auto Defrost
new_elements: Detects frozen food and auto-lowers power (An IR sensor reading below 0°C switches the oven to defrost duty.)
rationale: Users never need to know about a defrost setting.
judge_comment: Removes the need to understand defrost, and IR surface sensing is plausible, though it only reads the surface and may misjudge.

title: Dish-Weight Door Lock
new_elements: Weight-triggered auto-closing door (Placing a dish on the turntable makes a motor close the door and start a load-based cycle.)
rationale: Putting the food in is the user's only action.
judge_comment: Truly zero-step operation, but an automatic door closing and starting on its own raises safety, cost, and misfire concerns.

title: Weigh-and-Go Scale Floor
new_elements: Load-cell cavity floor (Strain-gauge scale under the tray weighs the food and sets cook time automatically.); Strain-gauge weighing (Low-cost bridge load cell with a simple microcontroller lookup table.)
rationale: The user puts food in and closes the door, and the weight decides the time, so there is nothing to set.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto time removes input, but weight poorly predicts heating needs (food type, starting temp), and the load cell must cope with the turntable and a hostile microwave environment.

title: Steam-Sniffer Auto Stop
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor (Capacitive humidity sensor in the vent air detects the steam burst when food is hot.); Senses food doneness (Closes the loop by stopping heating at the onset of steam.)
rationale: The user presses start and the oven itself works out when the food is done.
judge_comment: Humidity-based sensor cooking exists in premium ovens, but it is effective, simple for the user, and plausible; it works poorly for dry foods.

title: Thermochromic Ready Plate
new_elements: Thermochromic glaze tray (Tray glaze turns from blue to red when the food above it is hot.); Leuco-dye thermochromism (Reversible colour change at about 60 °C.)
rationale: Ready is shown by a colour anyone understands at a glance.
judge_comment: A thermochromic tray gives an intuitive done signal, though the tray heats by conduction from the food rather than the microwaves, and the colour reads food contact temperature unevenly.

title: One Button +30 s
new_elements: Single +30 s button (Each press adds 30 s at full power, and cooking starts immediately.)
rationale: With one control there is only one thing to learn.
judge_comment: A single +30 s button is very easy to learn and trivial to build, but it offers limited functionality and many microwaves already have a similar button.

title: Solid-State RF Heart
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (A transistor amplifier with continuous power control replaces the magnetron and HV chain.); GaN RF power amplification (Semiconductor amplification at 2.45 GHz using low-voltage DC.)
rationale: The oven adapts power to the food automatically, so the user never sets a power level.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with automatic power control directly removes the need to choose settings, though cost and maturity are still limiting.

title: Set Temperature, Not Time
new_elements: IR thermopile food sensor (A sensor in the roof measures the food surface temperature.); Warm/Hot/Boiling dial (A three-position dial sets the desired temperature.)
rationale: Users think in terms of 'hot', not minutes.
judge_comment: Temperature-target dial matches mental model and removes time guessing, though IR surface sensing in microwaves is imperfect and the sensor is added rather than substituted.

title: Fill-Line Smart Tray
new_elements: Engraved portion tray (Rings on the tray map the food quantity to a printed time beside each ring.)
rationale: Instructions built into the tray remove guesswork at zero extra cost.
judge_comment: Printed portion rings with times remove guesswork cheaply, but they only suit certain foods and tray types.

title: Empty-Cavity Lockout
new_elements: Reflected-power empty detector (A diode probe senses high reflected RF from an empty cavity or metal and stops the oven.)
rationale: Mistakes can't hurt the oven, so users need no rules to memorise.
judge_comment: Reflected-power detection is plausible and removes the rules about empty or metal loads, though it addresses safety more than operation.

title: Two-Axis Slider
new_elements: Gentle-to-strong time slider (One slider: vertical position sets strength, and sliding length sets time.)
rationale: One physical gesture replaces two separate controls.
judge_comment: A single two-axis slider merges strength and time into one gesture, which is intuitive and feasible, though the mapping of length to time still needs some learning.

title: Ring-Light Timer Door Frame
new_elements: Clock-face LED ring (An LED ring around the window empties like a clock hand and flashes when the food is done.)
rationale: A clock-like display of time is understood universally.
judge_comment: An intuitive clock-like LED ring communicates remaining time with no learning and is easy to build.

title: Close-the-Door-to-Start
new_elements: Door-latch start switch (Closing the door starts a default 1-minute cycle; each extra open/close within 2 s adds 30 s.); Start cooking without any control (The natural act of shutting the door becomes the start command.); Timer knob must be wound to start (Users must know to twist the clockwork knob before anything happens.)
rationale: Shutting a door is already instinctive, so starting the oven requires nothing new to learn.
judge_comment: Door-close-to-start is intuitive and simple, though the default time may not suit all foods and the 'must wind knob' element reads as a contradictory problem statement; it also risks accidental starts.

title: Food Pictogram Dial
new_elements: Picture dial (One knob showing icons for a mug, plate, bowl, frozen block and popcorn instead of minutes.); Select by what you are heating (Each icon maps to a preset time and power combination.); Numeric minutes are abstract (Users must translate the food they have into a number of minutes.)
rationale: Pointing at a picture of your food needs no numeracy or prior experience.
judge_comment: A pictogram dial is very easy to use and cheap to build, though preset icons already exist on some appliances so it is not very radical.

title: Infrared Target-Temperature Knob
new_elements: IR thermopile + Warm/Hot/Boiling selector (The user picks the end state they want and the oven heats until the food surface reaches it.); Heat to desired outcome (The user states the goal rather than the process.); Power levels are meaningless to users (The 5-step duty-cycle knob has no intuitive interpretation.)
rationale: Choosing 'warm' or 'hot' is universally understood, unlike watts or duty-cycle steps.
judge_comment: Goal-based heating removes the need to understand power levels and fits the no-learning-curve need well, though IR surface sensing is limited and similar sensor ovens already exist.

title: Melting-Fuse Food Tag
new_elements: Thermal-fuse RFID label on food (The tag circuit breaks at serving temperature and the oven stops when the tag goes silent.); Food tells the oven it is done (Doneness is measured inside the package itself.); Timer unrelated to food state (The clockwork timer knows nothing about the actual food temperature.)
rationale: The user just presses start and the food itself ends the cycle.
judge_comment: Food-embedded thermal-fuse tag makes it one-press operation and is very novel, but RFID in a microwave and per-package cost are serious hurdles.

title: Acoustic Boil Detector
new_elements: Cavity microphone (Listens for popping, sizzling or boiling sounds.); Sound-based stop (Stops heating before boil-over or burning.); Boil-overs and burnt popcorn (A fixed time leads to messes when the food finishes early.)
rationale: It removes the need to babysit the microwave or learn per-food timings.
judge_comment: Sound-based stopping is plausible and cuts per-food timing knowledge, though it works only for foods that make distinctive sounds.

title: Natural Language Voice Control
new_elements: Offline voice module (Understands phrases like 'warm my coffee' or 'defrost the chicken'.); Speak your intent (Replaces the dials with ordinary speech.); Controls require interpretation (Dial scales must be understood before use.)
rationale: Talking requires no interface knowledge at all.
judge_comment: Speaking intent removes the learning curve almost entirely, and offline voice modules exist, though it is a fairly familiar concept.

title: Auto-Reset on Door Open
new_elements: Door-linked timer clutch (Opening the door returns the timer to zero automatically.); Clean state each use (No leftover time from the previous user.); Residual time surprises (A knob left mid-way restarts the oven unexpectedly.)
rationale: The oven always starts from the same predictable state.
judge_comment: A door-linked reset gives a predictable start state and is mechanically plausible, though it is a modest, not radical, change.

title: Solid-State RF Heater
new_elements: GaN RF power amplifiers (Solid-state microwave generation with closed-loop control.); RF module with reflected-power sensing (Replaces the magnetron and duty-cycle cam, adapting power to how the food absorbs energy.); Self-tuning power (Removes the need for any user power choice.); Crude on/off duty cycling (Cam-based power control heats unevenly.)
rationale: The power setting disappears because the machine optimises it.
judge_comment: Self-tuning solid-state RF removes the power choice and is truly radical, but cost and maturity of high-power GaN limit feasibility.

title: Countertop Time Projection
new_elements: Downlight LED projector (Replaces the interior bulb and projects the remaining time and a done icon onto the counter.); Ambient status display (Status is readable from across the kitchen.); Status hidden on small dial (Remaining time cannot be read from a distance.)
rationale: Large, obvious status removes guesswork.
judge_comment: Projected status is feasible and makes the time easy to read, but it only covers feedback and not input.

title: Photo Slider
new_elements: Linear slider with photo strip (Slide from 'sip-warm drink' to 'big frozen meal' with haptic detents.); Continuous intuitive scale (Replaces both rotary knobs.); Rotary knob direction ambiguity (Users are unsure which way to turn or how far.)
rationale: Left-small, right-big is an obvious mapping.
judge_comment: A photo-based slider substitutes for the knobs with an intuitive mapping, though it is less precise and only moderately radical.

title: Fill-Line Bowls
new_elements: Bundled bowls with fill lines (Each fill line matches a printed time on the door, giving standardised quantities.); Quantity-to-time mapping (Replaces guesswork about how long a given amount takes.); Unknown portion sizes (Varying portion sizes make the right time unpredictable.)
rationale: It is as simple as a measuring cup.
judge_comment: Very cheap and simple, and fill lines map quantity to time, but portion variety and food type limit it, and it is hardly radical.

title: Phone Tap Packaging
new_elements: NFC tap pad on front (Tapping a ready-meal package's NFC tag onto the pad loads the maker's program.); Tap-to-program (Replaces reading instructions and turning knobs.); Instruction translation errors (Wattage mismatches between package and oven cause mistakes.)
rationale: Tapping is as familiar as contactless payment.
judge_comment: Tapping an NFC tag on the package to load the program is familiar and workable, but it only works for tagged packaged meals.

title: Stir Reminder Rotation Pause
new_elements: Mid-cycle chime and door nudge (Pauses and slightly opens the door with a 'stir me' light, replacing user knowledge of when to stir.); Guided stirring (Prompts the user at the right moment.); Uneven heating without stirring (Novices do not know to stir halfway through.)
rationale: The appliance teaches as it goes, so prior knowledge is unnecessary.
judge_comment: A mid-cycle stir prompt with door nudge is plausible and teaches as it goes, though it adds interruptions and isn't really a substitution.

title: Mechanical Food Wheel Cam
new_elements: Combined time-power cam wheel (A single knob whose cam sets both duty cycle and duration per food sector, with no electronics.); One-knob preset cooking (Replaces the two-knob arrangement cheaply.); Mismatched power and time (Users pair the wrong power level with the wrong time.)
rationale: A single mechanical choice keeps the oven cheap and impossible to misconfigure.
judge_comment: A single cam knob that sets both time and power is simple, cheap and hard to misconfigure, though it limits flexibility.

title: Infrared Done-Sensor
new_elements: Thermopile IR food-temperature sensor (Looks at the food surface and cuts power at about 70 °C.); Stops cooking when food is hot (Closed-loop end condition instead of a time limit.)
rationale: The user asks for 'hot' rather than guessing a number of minutes.
judge_comment: A thermopile gives a 'cook until hot' interaction that is intuitive and plausible, though it senses only the surface temperature and the packaging can interfere.

title: Package Barcode Autopilot
new_elements: Door-mounted barcode reader (Reads the ready-meal barcode and loads the manufacturer's heating profile.)
rationale: The user shows the package and the microwave sets itself.
judge_comment: Scanning the package removes all settings, but it only works for packaged foods and needs a profile database.

title: Sliding Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity on rails (A drawer replaces the hinged door, hinges and latch; it is shielded by a choke flange.)
rationale: Pulling a drawer is a natural motion, and the food is reached from above with no reaching inside.
judge_comment: A drawer is a natural motion and removes hinges, and microwave drawers already exist, though the choke-flange shielding is a real engineering challenge.

title: Portion-Picture Knob
new_elements: Food-icon rotary dial (Dial positions show a cup, small bowl, big bowl and plate instead of minutes.)
rationale: Matching a picture to what is on the plate requires no knowledge of heating times.
judge_comment: Picture-based dial removes the need to know heating times and is easy to build, though the idea is somewhat incremental and fixed time presets may not suit every food.

title: Pull-Chain Timer
new_elements: Pull-cord ratchet timer (Each pull of a cord winds 30 s onto a spring escapement.)
rationale: Pulls map directly to time, with no reading of a scale.
judge_comment: A pull-cord and spring escapement is simple and mechanical, but users still have to know how much time to set and counting pulls is a small learning step.

title: Tactile Detent Knob
new_elements: Big-click knob with 30 s detents and raised dots (Each felt click equals 30 s; the knob is usable by touch alone.)
rationale: Counting clicks suits low-vision and elderly users.
judge_comment: Detented knobs with tactile dots are simple, proven and accessible, but they are an incremental improvement.

title: Popcorn Ear
new_elements: Acoustic pop-interval microphone (Stops when pops slow to about 1 per 2 s, and also detects boiling sounds.)
rationale: The oven listens, so the user never has to guess when the popcorn is done.
judge_comment: Acoustic popcorn sensing removes guesswork and is plausible, though it only serves one use case and isn't much of a substitution for a part.

title: Two-Button Start/Stop
new_elements: Green 'heat' and red 'stop' paddles (Heat runs at full power until stop or the IR sensor ends it.)
rationale: Go and stop are the simplest controls possible.
judge_comment: Very simple and directly serves zero-learning-curve use, but it is an incremental reduction of controls and full-power-only heating limits suitability for many foods.

title: Pop-Up Done Lid
new_elements: Wax-plug pop-up indicator lid (A turkey-timer-style plug pops at the target temperature and presses a cavity cut-off switch.)
rationale: Cheap closed-loop doneness with no electronics and nothing to set.
judge_comment: A wax-plug mechanical cutoff is a clever, cheap substitution that removes settings, though the plug would be hard to place in food and needs resetting and consistent calibration.

title: Tap-the-Window Interface
new_elements: Capacitive-touch door window (Each tap on the glass adds 30 s; a long hold stops cooking.)
rationale: The biggest surface on the oven becomes the only button.
judge_comment: Tapping the glass to add time is intuitive and replaces the keypad, but capacitive sensing through a shielded mesh door and condensation is tricky.

title: Plate-Down Auto Start
new_elements: Pressure-mat start trigger (Placing food and closing the door starts a 1 min heat automatically.)
rationale: There is no start action to remember.
judge_comment: Auto-start on door close removes the start step and is easy to build, though a fixed 1 min and accidental starts are concerns.

title: Big +30 Second Palm Button
new_elements: Ratchet +30 s palm button (Each press of a large button winds the mechanical timer forward by exactly 30 s.)
rationale: Pressing a button more times for more heat is self-explanatory and needs no fine dexterity.
judge_comment: Simple and clear, but it resembles existing +30 s buttons and is not radical.

title: Steam-Whistle Shutoff
new_elements: Steam-driven vent flap switch (Rising steam from heated food lifts a light flap in the exhaust duct, opening the magnetron circuit.); Passive steam-flow detection (Mechanical, unpowered sensing that food has reached boiling.)
rationale: The oven stops itself when the food is hot, so users never have to guess a time.
judge_comment: Passive steam flap that ends cooking removes time-setting entirely and is wildly inventive, but unreliable for dry foods and risky as a sole safety cutoff.

title: Boil-Listener for Drinks
new_elements: Bubble-sound boil detector (A piezo pickup on the cavity wall hears the onset of simmering in liquids and stops before boil-over.)
rationale: A mug of tea is heated correctly with zero settings.
judge_comment: Acoustic boil detection gives zero-setting drink heating and is plausible, though it only covers liquids and the sound signal may be noisy in a magnetron-driven cavity.

title: Weight-Loss Doneness
new_elements: Detects doneness by moisture mass loss (A load cell tracks evaporation and stops cooking at a target percentage of mass lost.)
rationale: Closed-loop doneness removes the need for the user to understand cooking times.
judge_comment: Closed-loop mass-loss doneness removes the need for time knowledge, but a load cell in a hot, RF-filled cavity is hard to build and mass loss is a weak proxy for doneness.

title: Pull-String Timer
new_elements: Pull-cord spring timer (Pulling a cord further gives more time; a governed spring rewinds it slowly as a visible countdown.)
rationale: Length equals time, so the remaining time is obvious just by looking at the cord.
judge_comment: A pull-cord spring timer makes time physically visible and needs no electronics, but it is a bit gimmicky and imprecise.

title: Wind-Up Egg-Timer Mechanism
new_elements: Escapement spring clockwork (A motorless kitchen-timer escapement replaces the synchronous motor.)
rationale: It is the same familiar twist-and-ding egg-timer behaviour, cheaper and identical in every region.
judge_comment: A familiar twist-to-set mechanical timer has zero learning curve and is plausible, though mechanical timers already existed in microwaves, so it isn't very radical.

title: Water-Ballast Power Cup
new_elements: Fill-line ballast cup (A water cup absorbs a share of the energy; fill lines are marked Gentle and Very Gentle.)
rationale: Analog, continuous power control needs no electronics and no instructions beyond 'fill to the line'.
judge_comment: Water load for attenuation works physically and is a simple substitute for electronic power control, though it needs a fill step and wastes energy.

title: Hourglass Window Timer
new_elements: Rotating sand-glass switch (Flipping a large hourglass tilts a mercury-free ball switch to start cooking; when the sand runs out, an optical gate stops it.)
rationale: Everyone knows how an hourglass works, so the countdown is self-explaining.
judge_comment: A flip-to-start hourglass is instantly understood and has concrete mechanisms, but fixed sand durations limit flexibility and the time resolution is coarse.

title: Wax-Actuator Thermal Stop
new_elements: Exhaust-air wax pellet cutoff (A pellet melts from hot moist exhaust air and pushes open the power contact.)
rationale: A cheap, unpowered automatic stop means users press start and walk away.
judge_comment: A wax pellet that cuts power from exhaust-air heat is a clever, cheap, unpowered substitute for a timer, though it is hard to calibrate across different foods and loads.

title: Toaster-Lever Start
new_elements: Spring push-down start lever (Push the lever down like a toaster to start. It pops up with a click when heating ends.); Starts and ends cooking with one familiar gesture (Reuses the toaster mental model that most people already know.)
rationale: Everyone already knows how a toaster lever works, so starting and finishing a heat cycle needs no learning.
judge_comment: The toaster-lever start is intuitive and cheap, but it still needs a time input, so it only partly removes the learning curve.

title: Weigh-to-Time Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (A strain gauge under the tray weighs the food and sets the heating time from that weight.); Strain-gauge weighing (Low-cost load cell with a lookup table of mass versus energy.)
rationale: The user puts food in and closes the door, and the machine works out the time, so nothing needs to be set.
judge_comment: Weighing the food to set the time is plausible and truly hands-off, though weight alone is a poor proxy for the heating needed.

title: One Pictogram Dial
new_elements: Single food-pictogram dial (One knob with icons for mug, plate, frozen and butter. Each icon is a preset cam profile combining time and power.)
rationale: One knob with pictures replaces two abstract knobs, so the user just points at what they are heating.
