judge_comment: A single pictogram dial is simple and very feasible, but it is an incremental, familiar approach and not radical.

title: Lift-Off Cloche
new_elements: Transparent ITO-coated glass dome (A conductive transparent dome lowers over the plate to form the Faraday cage. It needs no door and no lamp.); Indium-tin-oxide transparent conductive coating (Optically clear film that reflects 2.45 GHz radiation.)
rationale: Covering a plate with a dome is as obvious as a cake cover, and the food stays visible the whole time.
judge_comment: A cake-cover style ITO dome is a radical and intuitive replacement for the door, but sealing, shielding, and heat durability are major challenges.

title: Pack-Scan Cooking
new_elements: Door-mounted barcode reader (Wave a ready-meal package and the oven loads the maker's exact heating profile.)
rationale: It removes the need to read and translate the instructions printed on the package.
judge_comment: Scanning a package barcode is feasible and removes instruction reading, but it only works for compatible packaged meals and the data must come from somewhere.

title: Camera Food Recognition
new_elements: Cavity camera with on-device AI (Recognises the food type and quantity and picks the time and power automatically.); Embedded image classification (Low-cost microcontroller vision model.)
rationale: The user puts food in and the machine sees what it is, so nothing has to be selected.
judge_comment: A camera that recognises the food gives true zero-input operation, but accuracy, steam on the lens, and cost make it hard and the idea is fairly common.

title: Big Single +30 Button
new_elements: Single giant +30 s button (Each press adds 30 s at full power, and a long press cancels. This replaces both knobs.)
rationale: One button, pressed more for more heat, is the simplest possible interface.
judge_comment: A single +30 s button is extremely simple and cheap, but it is a modest idea rather than radical, and it offers limited control for different foods.

title: Turn the Plate to Set Time
new_elements: Turntable-as-dial encoder (The user twists the turntable by hand to dial in time. A rotary encoder on the coupler reads the angle.)
rationale: The setting gesture happens where the food already is, so the user never looks for a control panel.
judge_comment: Twisting the turntable to set time is intuitive and novel, though it needs a hand-accessible plate and a sealed encoder coupling, and it replaces the keypad with something simpler.

title: Solid-State RF Engine
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (A semiconductor source with continuously adjustable power and frequency and no high-voltage stage.); Gallium-nitride RF power transistors (Low-voltage DC drive that replaces magnetron vacuum electronics.)
rationale: Precise, continuous power lets the oven self-tune, removing the power setting the user would otherwise have to choose.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is real and enables self-tuning and automatic power control that removes a user decision, though cost is still high for consumer ovens.

title: Self-Labelled Glow Controls
new_elements: Backlit next-step guidance (Only the control needed next lights up: door, then dial, then start.)
rationale: The interface leads the user step by step, so there is nothing to learn up front.
judge_comment: Sequential lit guidance directly removes the learning curve and is cheap with LEDs, though not very radical.

title: One-Button Tap-to-Add Timer
new_elements: Single large 'Go' push button (Each press adds 30 s at full power; a long press cancels.); Low-cost microcontroller countdown (Cheap MCU counts presses and controls the relay.)
rationale: A single button that only means 'more time' can be learned with one press and needs no instructions.
judge_comment: Very easy to learn and cheap, but many microwaves already have a +30s button, so it is not radical.

title: Flip-Token Timer
new_elements: Magnetic flip tokens (Physical tokens labelled 1, 2 and 5 min snap onto the fascia; a Hall sensor reads them.)
rationale: Choosing a physical object is as intuitive as picking up a cup.
judge_comment: Physical tokens are intuitive and easy to build, but they replace a keypad with something users can lose and offer limited choices.

title: Dome-Over-Plate Microwave
new_elements: Lift-down shielded dome (A meshed metal cloche lowers over the plate on a choked base; the dome is the door.); Encloses food by covering it (Works like a cake cover.)
rationale: Covering a plate is a gesture everyone knows, with no door mechanics.
judge_comment: Cloche-style dome is wildly novel and intuitive, but RF leakage safety, sealing and interlock make it hard to realize.

title: Talking Ding
new_elements: Voice chip speaker (A cheap voice chip says 'Your food is ready'.)
rationale: A spoken sentence needs no interpretation, unlike a ding.
judge_comment: Spoken feedback is clear and cheap, but talking appliances are common and it only addresses completion, not operation.

title: Fill-to-Line Mug Heater
new_elements: Single-cup microwave pod (A mug-sized cavity with a fixed 90 s cycle; fill the mug to the line and close.)
rationale: There is one job and one action, so there is literally nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single-purpose fixed-cycle appliance has truly zero learning curve, though it is limited in what it can heat and is a narrow product.

title: Solid-State GaN RF Source
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (A low-voltage chip source with built-in reflected-power sensing for automatic cooking.); Gallium-nitride RF transistors (Continuous power control and absorption feedback.)
rationale: The source senses the food itself, enabling a true 'just press go' auto-cook.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with reflected-power sensing could enable real one-button auto-cooking, but it is costly and still maturing for consumer products.

title: Braille-Shape Tactile Controls
new_elements: Raised-shape tactile knob detents (Each setting has a distinct shape and click felt by the fingers.)
rationale: The controls can be understood by touch alone, with no reading required.
judge_comment: Tactile, shape-coded controls directly lower the learning curve and help accessibility, and they are easy to build, though the concept is not radical.

title: Twist-Handle Timer
new_elements: Rotating door handle timer (Twisting the door handle sets the time, so the controls sit right where the hand already is.)
rationale: Closing the door and twisting the handle is one fluid motion.
judge_comment: Putting the timer in the door handle merges steps in a natural motion, but it makes the door mechanism and interlock more complex.

title: Heat / Thaw Two-Button
new_elements: Two big buttons: HEAT and THAW (Each press adds 30 s in that mode.)
rationale: Two verbs cover 95% of microwave use.
judge_comment: Two verb buttons greatly simplify operation and are easy to build, but the idea is fairly obvious and not radical.

title: Glowing Fascia Without Knobs
new_elements: Capacitive slide strip (Slide a finger further for longer, like a volume bar.)
rationale: The familiar phone-slider gesture sets time with one swipe.
judge_comment: A familiar slider gesture replaces knobs simply, but capacitive sliders are already common and not radical.

title: Butter-Melt Cup Insert
new_elements: Shielded melting cup (A partially metal-shielded cup so delicate items heat slowly at any setting.)
rationale: Put chocolate in the special cup and it never burns, with no power knob needed.
judge_comment: A passive shielded cup removes the need for power-level choices and substitutes hardware for settings, though effectiveness and safety (arcing) need care.

title: Weigh-and-Go Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable hub (Strain gauge under the turntable spindle weighs the food.); Infers cook time from food mass (Sets time and power from weight, with no knob setting.)
rationale: The user puts food in and closes the door, and the machine works out time and power itself.
judge_comment: A load cell under the turntable that sets time and power from food mass removes the settings, though mass alone is a weak proxy for the right cook time.

title: Door Is the Start Button
new_elements: Door-close triggers auto cycle (Closing the door starts heating and opening it stops heating; the start button and timer knob are removed.)
rationale: The only action is opening and closing a door, which everyone already knows how to do.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start is very intuitive and cheap, but it needs a default time or some cooking logic, and it risks accidental starts.

title: +30 s Single Button
new_elements: One '+30s' button with LED countdown (Each press adds 30 s and starts immediately.)
rationale: One button gives an obvious, precise short duration.
judge_comment: A single +30s button is very simple and easy to build, but many microwaves already have one and it is not radical.

title: Flat Floor, Hidden Stirrer
new_elements: Rotating antenna under ceramic floor (A sealed flat floor replaces the glass turntable.)
rationale: There is no plate to align or lose, and any dish size just fits.
judge_comment: Flat-floor microwaves with a hidden antenna already exist, and they remove the plate-alignment hassle, which helps ease of use.

title: Energy Dial Instead of Time
new_elements: Cold-to-Hot single dial (One dial marked with food-temperature icons sets delivered energy.)
rationale: One dial with one meaning replaces two knobs with abstract units.
judge_comment: A single dial with food icons directly cuts the learning curve and is easy to build, though it is an incremental idea and not a radical one.

title: RF Ice Detection Auto-Defrost
new_elements: Senses frozen state via RF reflection (S11) (Ice absorbs differently from water, so the oven auto-defrosts.)
rationale: The user never has to choose a defrost setting because the oven knows.
judge_comment: Using RF reflection (S11) to detect frozen state is a clever substitution of a sensor for a user decision, and it is plausible with solid-state RF, but accuracy varies from load to load.

title: Tactile Shape Buttons
new_elements: Cup / plate / snowflake shaped buttons (Each button's physical shape signals its program.)
rationale: Buttons can be understood by touch or by sight, in any language.
judge_comment: Shape-coded buttons directly cut the learning curve and are easy to build, but they are an incremental idea rather than a radical one.

title: Hold-Until-Steam Button
new_elements: Tap = 30 s, hold = cook until steam (One button has two intuitive gestures.)
rationale: A single control covers both quick warm-ups and full reheats.
judge_comment: Simple single-button, two-gesture control with steam sensing is highly usable and buildable, though not very radical.

title: Transparent Dome Microwave
new_elements: Lift-off conductive-glass dome over base (A cloche-style cavity is lifted off and set down, replacing door, choke and lamp.)
rationale: Lifting a cover and setting it down is the simplest action imaginable, and the food stays fully visible.
judge_comment: A lift-off cloche cavity is a radical, intuitive interaction that replaces door, choke and lamp, but containing microwave leakage with a removable conductive-glass dome is a serious safety challenge.

title: Pictogram Food Dial
new_elements: Icon-detent food dial (Dial positions show a cup, soup bowl, plate, popcorn and frozen block, each cam-coded to a time and duty cycle.)
rationale: Users point at a picture of their food instead of translating it into minutes and watts.
judge_comment: Pictogram presets are intuitive and mechanically feasible with cam coding, but similar to existing preset buttons.

title: Defrost Lid Instead of Power Knob
new_elements: Partially shielding perforated-metal defrost cover (A dome with a calibrated metal pattern passes only about 30% of the field, giving gentle heating at full magnetron power.); Calibrated partial microwave shielding (Aperture density sets transmitted power.)
rationale: 'Cover it to cook gently' is a physical, obvious action that replaces an abstract power setting.
judge_comment: A physical shielding cover that replaces power settings is highly original and intuitive, but calibrating it and avoiding arcing or uneven heating is hard.

title: RFID Smart Plates
new_elements: RFID tag in ceramic plate rim and cavity reader (Each dish type, such as a mug, bowl or baby bottle, carries its own program.)
rationale: The container tells the oven what to do, so the user only chooses a dish.
judge_comment: A dish that tells the oven what to do is intuitive, but it needs special plates and an RFID reader in the cavity, and food-specific programs could be wrong for what is actually on the plate.

title: Packaging Barcode Cooking
new_elements: Door-mounted barcode scanner (Hold the ready-meal pack to the door and the oven loads the manufacturer's time and power.)
rationale: It removes the need to read small print on packaging and translate it into settings.
judge_comment: Scanning the pack automates the settings and is technically straightforward, but it only works for packaged meals and depends on manufacturer data.

title: Auto-Pop Door
new_elements: Solenoid door kicker (Pops the door ajar when the cycle ends, replacing both the bell and the release button.)
rationale: The open door means it is done, and the food is never forgotten or locked inside.
judge_comment: A solenoid door kicker is simple, plausible and needs no learning, since the open door itself signals completion, though it could startle users or cause spills.

title: Microwave Drawer
new_elements: Sliding drawer cavity on telescopic rails (Pull the handle out, place the food, and push it back; no hinges or swing clearance.)
rationale: Drawers are a universally understood motion and let users load from above.
judge_comment: Drawer microwaves already exist, so novelty is limited, but the drawer motion is intuitive and the rail mechanism is concrete.

title: Cloche Dome Microwave
new_elements: Lift-off mesh-glass cloche over choke-sealed base (Lift the dome off the plate and set it back to cook; this replaces the door, hinges and latch.); Circular quarter-wave choke seal (A rim choke prevents leakage at the dome base.)
rationale: Covering a plate with a dome is a centuries-old gesture with zero learning.
judge_comment: A cloche dome is radical and instantly understandable, but containing microwaves with a mesh-glass dome and a rim choke seal is very difficult, and it does not address controls.

title: Conveyor Tunnel, No Door
new_elements: Choke-tunnel belt conveyor (Plates placed on the left ride slowly through a shielded tunnel and come out hot on the right.); Open-ended choke tunnel shielding (Industrial tunnel-oven absorber chokes adapted to a small countertop unit.)
rationale: Put the food in and take it out the other end; there are no doors, buttons or settings at all.
judge_comment: Doorless conveyor with no settings is radical and zero-learning, but choke tunnels are large, leak-prone and hard to scale to a countertop unit, and heating cannot be adjusted per food.

title: Blind Door with Glow Ring
new_elements: Solid steel door with exterior status LED ring (Drops the window and lamp; the ring fills as time passes and turns green when done.)
rationale: A single filling ring communicates progress better than peering through mesh.
judge_comment: A filling LED ring is simple, cheap and intuitive, though losing the window removes useful visibility of the food.

title: Caregiver-Preset Single Button
new_elements: Hidden preset dials and one big START button (A family member sets time and power behind a cover; the user only sees START.)
rationale: It separates setup from use, so the elderly user faces exactly one choice.
judge_comment: Hiding the setup behind a cover leaves the user one START button, which is simple and practical, though it only suits fixed routines.

title: Fill-Line Cup Program
new_elements: Matched mug with fill lines and cavity recess (The mug fits a recess that triggers a fixed beverage cycle tuned to the fill line.)
rationale: Fill to the line, put it in and get a perfect hot drink, with no timing involved.
judge_comment: A matched mug in a recess that triggers a set cycle is a creative zero-input design, but it covers only beverages and needs the proprietary mug.

title: Weigh-and-Go Load Cell Floor
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (Existing mechanical timer from base_product meta); Load cell cavity floor (Weighs the food and computes heating time automatically); Auto-derive time from food mass (Time scales with grams loaded)
rationale: The user never has to guess a time; putting food in is the whole input.
judge_comment: Weighing the food to set the time means loading it is the only input, which is a strong fit. Mass is a weak proxy for heating time, though, and load cells in a microwave cavity add cost and complexity.

title: Steam Sensor Auto-Stop
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (Existing mechanical timer from base_product meta); Exhaust humidity sensor (Detects the steam burst that signals the food is hot); Stop when food is hot (Ends the cycle based on food state, not on a set time)
rationale: The oven decides when food is done, so the user needs no timing knowledge.
judge_comment: Steam-sensing auto-stop already exists in sensor-cook microwaves and works reasonably well. It removes the need to know timing, but it does not work well for dry or covered foods.

title: IR Thermometer Food-Done Stop
new_elements: 5-step power knob (Existing duty-cycle cam knob from base_product meta); Ceiling IR thermopile (Reads the food surface temperature and stops at about 70 °C); Heat to eating temperature (Targets a temperature instead of a power setting)
rationale: "Make it hot" replaces abstract power levels with something everyone already understands.
judge_comment: Heating to a target temperature matches how people think about hot food. A thermopile reads only the surface and can be fooled by uneven heating, and the retained power knob adds a control to learn.

title: Toaster-Style Push-Down Lever
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (Existing timer knob from base_product meta); Toaster lever (Push down to start; it pops up with a click when done); Familiar start/finish gesture (Borrows a mental model nearly everyone already has)
rationale: Everyone already knows how to use a toaster.
judge_comment: A familiar toaster lever gesture lowers the learning curve, and it is easy to build, though the timer knob is still needed and the idea is only moderately radical.

title: Fridge-Style Magnetic Pull Door
new_elements: Door push-release button (Existing door release from base_product meta); Magnetic gasket door with handle bar (Pull to open like a fridge; the RF choke seal is kept and interlocks are reed switches); Intuitive door opening (No hidden button to find)
rationale: A visible handle tells the user exactly how to open the door.
judge_comment: A visible pull handle is an intuitive and practical fix, but it is a modest change that some microwaves already use.

title: Auto-Open Door at Finish
new_elements: End-of-cycle bell (Existing bell from base_product meta); Solenoid door kicker (Pops the door ajar when the cycle ends); Physical done signal (Also vents steam and prevents food being forgotten inside)
rationale: An open door plainly means the food is ready to take.
judge_comment: A door that pops open gives an unmistakable done signal that needs no learning, but it substitutes a solenoid for the bell instead of replacing a part with something simpler.

title: Status-Color Interior Light
new_elements: Incandescent interior lamp (Existing lamp from base_product meta); RGB status LED (Amber while heating, green when done, red on a fault); Glanceable state display (Traffic-light colour logic)
rationale: Traffic-light colours are understood everywhere.
judge_comment: Traffic-light colour status is intuitive and easy to build, but it is a common and incremental approach.

title: Ice-Detecting Auto Defrost
new_elements: 5-step power knob (Existing knob whose low setting is used for defrost); Dielectric frozen-state sensor (Detects ice from reflected RF and switches to defrost pulses); Automatic defrost recognition (No defrost mode to choose)
rationale: The oven, not the user, knows the food is frozen.
judge_comment: Auto-detecting frozen food removes a decision entirely and is plausible, though RF-based ice sensing is imprecise.

title: Acoustic Popcorn Listener
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (Existing timer, which forces popcorn guesswork); Cavity microphone (Stops when the gap between pops exceeds 2 s); Sound-based doneness (Gives perfect popcorn with no setting)
rationale: This replaces the learned skill of listening for the pops to slow down.
judge_comment: Listening for gaps between pops is concrete and workable and removes guesswork, but it only covers popcorn.

title: Hourglass Mechanical Indicator
new_elements: Timer dial pointer (Existing small numeric dial); Rotating coloured disc window (Driven by the clockwork, a red sector shrinks to nothing; no electronics); Visual remaining-time cue (Low-cost mechanical display)
rationale: Shrinking colour reads like an egg timer, with nothing to interpret.
judge_comment: A mechanical shrinking-colour disc is a cheap, clever substitute for a numeric display, though it helps only with remaining-time feedback.

title: Reheat-to-Eat One Button
new_elements: 5-step power knob (Existing power knob from base_product meta); IR array + single Reheat button (A thermal map drives heating until the whole plate is evenly warm); Whole-plate even reheat (Ensures no cold centres)
rationale: The most common task becomes a single press.
judge_comment: A single Reheat button driven by an IR thermal map removes nearly all learning, but an IR array is costly and hard to make reliable for even heating.

title: Weight-Activated Auto Start
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (Existing manual start control); Door-closed + load-present logic (Starts only when food is present and the door is shut, then runs sensor cooking); Interface-free cycle (No buttons used at all)
rationale: The oven has no controls at all, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A controlless oven that starts on door close with food present removes all learning, though accidental starts and cooking accuracy are risks.

title: Reflected-Power Readiness Sensing
new_elements: Waveguide directional coupler (Replaces the timer cam: measures reflected microwave power, which shifts as water heats and evaporates.); RF load impedance sensing (Uses the magnetron's own signal as the sensor.); Self-terminating cycle (Stops the cycle when the load signature says the food is done.)
rationale: The microwave senses doneness itself with almost no extra parts, so the user has no decisions to make.
judge_comment: Using reflected power as a sensor is clever and radical, but the signal is hard to interpret reliably as doneness, and the coupler adds cost.

title: Snowflake Toggle
new_elements: Two-position defrost toggle (Replaces the 5-step power cam with a simple choice between a flame icon and a snowflake icon.); Binary mode selection (Offers only heat or thaw.)
rationale: Two universally understood icons are easier than five numbered power levels.
judge_comment: A heat/thaw toggle is simple and easy to build, but it is an incremental simplification that gives up control.

title: Colour-Coded Magnetic Containers
new_elements: Magnet-keyed bowls (Replaces the dials: red bowl means soup, blue means defrost, and Hall sensors under the floor read which bowl is inside.); Container sets program (The choice of dish is the choice of program.)
rationale: Choosing a dish is something everyone already knows how to do.
judge_comment: Magnet-keyed bowls with Hall sensors are cheap and intuitive, but they force users into proprietary containers and cover limited programs.

title: Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Sliding drawer cavity (Replaces the hinged door and release button: pull to open, push to close and start.); Drawer-style loading (Works like any kitchen drawer.)
rationale: Everyone knows how to use a drawer.
judge_comment: Drawer microwaves exist, and a close-to-start drawer is a very intuitive interaction, though it still leaves open how time and power are set, and spills are a risk.

title: Hidden Rotating Antenna
new_elements: Under-floor rotating antenna (Replaces the turntable motor and glass plate.); Fixed-floor uniform heating (Rotates the field instead of the food.)
rationale: It removes a fragile part that users often misplace or misseat.
judge_comment: Rotating stirrers or antennas under the floor are already used in production and remove a misseatable part, which helps ease of use a little.

title: Spoken Done Message
new_elements: Voice chip speaker (Replaces the bell with a spoken message such as "Done, careful, it's hot."); Explicit completion message (States the result and a safety warning in plain words.)
rationale: Words are clearer than a beep code.
judge_comment: A spoken message is clear and cheap but not radical, since talking appliances already exist.

title: Popcorn Listening Mic
new_elements: Acoustic pop detector (Replaces the timer for popcorn: stops when the gap between pops grows.); Sound-based stop (Ends the cycle before the popcorn burns.)
rationale: Nobody has to learn the popcorn timing trick.
judge_comment: Acoustic pop detection is concrete and plausible and removes the popcorn guesswork, though it covers one food only.

title: Zero-Standby Mechanical Interlock
new_elements: Door-driven master switch (Replaces the clock display and standby electronics: power flows only when the door closes on food.); Nothing to set, ever (There is no clock to reset after a power cut.)
rationale: It removes the infamous blinking 12:00 that nobody knows how to set.
judge_comment: A door-driven master switch removes the clock and its resetting, which is a clever simplification, but dropping the display and timer feedback may hurt usability and needs a clear way to set the cook time.

title: Close-the-Door-to-Start
new_elements: Door closure starts cycle (The interlock signal doubles as the start command, so there is no start button or knob.)
rationale: Shutting the door is the only action, and opening it stops cooking, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Very simple and plausible, but it needs a default time and risks accidental starts, so it is only a partial solution.

title: Bimetal Doneness Disc
new_elements: Exhaust-duct snap-disc cutoff (A cheap bimetal disc in the vent snaps open when hot steam arrives, killing power.)
rationale: This reuses the cheapest thermostat technology as a no-electronics auto-stop, so the user just presses go.
judge_comment: A cheap bimetal snap-disc substitute for the timer is clever and simple, but it is unreliable for dry foods and varying loads.

title: Package Barcode Reader
new_elements: Door-mounted barcode scanner (Scans the ready-meal package and loads the maker's heating profile.)
rationale: Waving the packet at the oven replaces reading the instructions and setting the knobs.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning is feasible and easy to use, but it only works for packaged meals and needs a profile database.

title: Smart-Lid Containers
new_elements: RFID-tagged microwave lid (The lid tells the oven what is inside, such as leftovers, soup or rice.)
rationale: The container carries the know-how, so the user carries none.
judge_comment: Zero-interaction operation is highly relevant and inventive, but it needs tagged lids, and RFID near microwave fields is a challenge.

title: Food-Recognition Camera
new_elements: Ceiling camera with food classifier (Identifies the dish and portion size, then sets the cycle.)
rationale: The oven looks and decides, so the user only closes the door.
judge_comment: A camera that identifies the food and sets the cycle removes all operation steps, but it is costly, accuracy is uncertain, and it doesn't fit the cheaper-or-simpler SUBSTITUTE aim.

title: Pull-Handle Door
new_elements: Simple grab-handle with roller catch (A roller catch with no push button, hooks or lever train.)
rationale: A handle affords pulling without explanation.
judge_comment: A pull handle is intuitive and cheaper than a push-button latch, but it is a common, incremental change.

title: Popcorn-Ear Acoustic Stop
new_elements: Cavity microphone with pop and boil detection (Listens for popping gaps or boiling and stops automatically.)
rationale: No more guessing popcorn time, because the oven hears when it is done.
judge_comment: Acoustic popcorn detection directly removes guessing and the learning curve, though it adds a microphone rather than substituting a simpler part, and detection inside a noisy microwave is tricky.

title: Spring Auto-Open Door
new_elements: End-of-cycle door kicker spring (The door pops ajar when done, replacing the bell and venting steam.)
rationale: 'Door open' unmistakably means done, and food isn't forgotten inside.
judge_comment: A spring-loaded door kicker is a cheap, simple substitute for the bell and makes 'done' obvious, although it does not help with setting the cook time.

title: Heat Pods
new_elements: Coded single-serve meal pods (Shaped pods key into the oven like coffee capsules and carry their own recipe.)
rationale: Insert the pod and you're done: the Nespresso model of zero learning.
judge_comment: Zero-decision operation, but it needs a pod ecosystem and microwave-safe packaging, and it is not really a cheaper substitution.

title: One-Push Electronic Timer
new_elements: Single +30 s push button with MCU timer (Each press adds 30 s and starts immediately.)
rationale: Count the presses; no dial calibration needed.
judge_comment: A +30 s button is simple and already used on many microwaves, so it is practical but not very novel.

title: Package-Reading Eye
new_elements: Interior barcode/label camera (Reads the ready-meal barcode or printed instructions and runs them exactly.); On-device OCR + barcode database (Low-cost vision chip with an offline product database.)
rationale: The machine reads the packet instructions for the user, which removes the need to set anything manually.
judge_comment: Reading package instructions automatically is a strong zero-learning idea, but it only works for labeled packaged food and needs a database and a camera inside a harsh cavity.

title: Infrared Target-Temperature Stop
new_elements: Ceiling IR thermopile (Measures the food surface temperature and stops at the warm, hot or boil target.); Heats to temperature, not time (Replaces the duration setting with a goal-state setting.)
rationale: Users choose how hot they want the food, which is intuitive, instead of a number of minutes, which is guesswork.
judge_comment: Choosing a target temperature is intuitive and a thermopile is cheap, but surface-only readings and unevenly heated food limit accuracy.

title: One Button: +30 Seconds
new_elements: Single +30 s pushbutton (Each press adds 30 s at full power, and the timing is electronic and precise.)
rationale: One button with one meaning can be understood instantly by anyone.
judge_comment: Very simple and highly learnable, but +30 s buttons already exist on many microwaves, and it replaces the keypad/dial only partially.

title: Pull-to-Open Magnetic Door
new_elements: Magnetic door catch with handle (Replaces the push-button lever latch with a plain pull.)
rationale: Everyone already knows how to pull a fridge door.
judge_comment: Simple, familiar interaction that removes a small learning step, though not very radical.

title: Progress-Color Cavity Light
new_elements: RGB LED progress lighting (The interior light shifts from red to green as the food heats, replacing the incandescent lamp and the timer dial.)
rationale: Green means ready, which anyone understands at a glance.
judge_comment: Color feedback is understandable at a glance, but estimating food doneness is unreliable and it does not replace setting a time.

title: Three Verb Buttons
new_elements: DEFROST / WARM / BOIL buttons (Each button runs a sensor-guided complete program.)
rationale: Users press the verb for what they want done, and the oven handles the rest.
judge_comment: Three goal-oriented verb buttons make operation nearly learning-free, though they rely on sensor reliability and the idea is not very radical.

title: RFID Meal Containers
new_elements: Passive RFID-tagged lids (Meal-prep containers carry their own reheat recipe.)
rationale: The container tells the oven what to do, so the user does nothing.
judge_comment: Passive RFID lids make operation zero-effort for tagged containers, but they require proprietary containers and an ecosystem, so it does not work for general use.

title: Knock-Knock Control
new_elements: Door accelerometer (Each knock on the door adds 30 s, replacing buttons.)
rationale: Knocking is a playful action that needs no explanation and leaves no greasy buttons.
judge_comment: Knock-to-add-time is playful and cheap to build with an accelerometer, but it is not self-explanatory and offers limited control beyond adding time.

title: E-Ink Pictogram Door
new_elements: E-ink door panel (Shows live step-by-step pictures such as 'stir now' and 'cover with lid'.)
rationale: The instructions appear where the user is looking, at the moment they are needed.
judge_comment: A door-mounted e-ink display with live pictorial prompts is intuitive, but a metal-mesh door and the sensing needed to time prompts make it harder than it looks.

title: Auto-Pop Door When Done
new_elements: Solenoid door kicker (Opens the door a few cm when finished, replacing the bell and the release button.)
rationale: An open door unmistakably means done, and the food stops overcooking in trapped steam.
judge_comment: A simple, clear done-signal that replaces the bell and release button, and it is easy to build.

title: Thermal-Camera Cold-Spot Hunter
new_elements: Low-res thermal camera (Maps cold spots and steers solid-state RF to them, replacing turntable rotation.)
rationale: The food comes out evenly hot without the user stirring, rotating or re-running the cycle.
judge_comment: Radical and removes manual stirring and rotating, but thermal sensing through steam plus solid-state RF is costly and hard.

title: Door-Is-The-Start-Button
new_elements: Door-closure start contact (Closing the door starts heating and opening it pauses, so there is no separate start action.); Starts and pauses cooking by door action (The door gesture everyone already knows becomes the only start/stop control.)
rationale: Using the door as the start/stop switch means there is nothing to learn: shut it to cook, open it to stop.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start is intuitive and cheap, but with no time set it needs a default or a way to end the cycle, and it risks accidental starts with an empty cavity.

title: One Big Button (+30 s)
new_elements: Single giant +30 s push pad (Each press adds 30 s at full power, replacing both knobs.)
rationale: One button that a child can understand on the first press replaces two abstract dials.
judge_comment: A single +30 s pad is very simple and feasible, but it is incremental and not radical, and many microwaves already have a similar quick-start button.

title: Food-Picture Dial
new_elements: Icon cam dial (A single knob shows pictures (mug, plate, frozen block, butter); each position sets both time and duty cycle on one cam.)
rationale: Users choose what they are heating, not minutes and watts, which removes any need to translate food into numbers.
judge_comment: A picture-based cam dial maps food type to settings with no numbers to learn, and it is mechanically simple, but it offers limited flexibility and is imprecise for portion size.

title: Solid-State RF Heart
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (A transistor source with continuous power control replaces the magnetron and its high-voltage chain.); Gallium-nitride RF power transistors (Low-voltage, frequency-agile microwave generation.)
rationale: Smooth power control lets the machine choose gentle heating itself, so the power knob can disappear.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is a real, plausible swap that could enable automatic power control and remove the knob, though it is currently costly and not simpler.

title: Self-Limiting Defrost Box
new_elements: Partially shielded defrost container (A perforated-metal lid lets through only about 30 % of the energy, giving passive low power at the full-power setting.); Passive power attenuation (Power level is set by the container rather than a knob.)
rationale: 'Frozen food goes in the silver box' is the entire instruction.
judge_comment: A passive attenuating container makes the instruction trivial and is a clever, cheap substitute for a power knob. Metal in a microwave raises safety concerns and uneven heating is likely.

title: Curie-Point Butter Dish
new_elements: Ferrite-lined melting dish (Ferrite absorbs microwaves until its Curie point (about 50 °C), then stops heating.); Curie-temperature self-regulating ferrite (Magnetic loss vanishes above a design temperature.)
rationale: Butter and chocolate cannot overheat in this dish, so users don't need any power-level skill.
judge_comment: Clever self-limiting ferrite is a true substitution of user skill with physics, but it only helps for melting tasks, so it only narrowly serves the simple-operation need.

title: Set Temperature, Not Time
new_elements: IR thermopile with Warm/Hot/Boiling dial (The cycle stops when the food surface reaches the chosen feel.); Heats to a target temperature (Outcome-based control.)
rationale: People think in 'warm' or 'hot', not seconds, so the control matches how they already think.
judge_comment: Outcome-based control with an intuitive dial matches how people think, though IR measures only the surface temperature and the idea is somewhat known.

title: Recipe Punch Cards
new_elements: Card slot with punched program cards (Printed cards ('Soup', 'Pizza slice') have notches that set the cam program mechanically.)
rationale: The user picks the card with the picture of their food and drops it in, with no electronics needed.
judge_comment: Mechanical cards with pictures need no learning and are feasible, but they limit flexibility and add a card library to manage.

title: Tactile Click Dial
new_elements: Detented raised-notch knob (Each click equals 30 s, and large raised marks can be felt as well as seen.)
rationale: Users can count clicks instead of aligning a pointer on a crowded scale.
judge_comment: Detented click dial is simple and easy to use, but it is close to existing mechanical microwave knobs.

title: The Door Is the Start Button
new_elements: Door-close start contact (Closing the door with a dish inside starts heating; opening the door stops it, so there is no separate start control.); Starts and stops cooking via door motion (The one action users already perform becomes the entire control.)
rationale: If shutting the door is the only step, there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Closing the door as the only action removes all learning, but it needs a duration default and raises safety and accidental-start concerns.

title: One 'How Hot?' Dial
new_elements: Single warm-hot-boiling dial (One knob that combines the power cam and the timer, labelled with outcomes rather than watts or minutes.)
rationale: Choosing the result you want is something anyone can do without instruction.
judge_comment: A single outcome-labelled dial is simple, cheap and feasible, though it is an incremental change that is not radical.

title: Steam Sniffer Auto-Stop
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor (Cuts heating when a burst of steam shows the food is done.); Ends cooking at doneness (Replaces the user's estimate of when food is ready.)
rationale: The microwave decides when to stop, so no timing skill is required.
judge_comment: Humidity-based auto-stop is proven in sensor-cook models and removes timing guesswork, though it is not especially novel.

title: RFID Smart Bowls
new_elements: RF-tagged ceramic bowl set (Each bowl, such as soup, pasta or mug, tells the oven what program to run.)
rationale: Picking the bowl is choosing the program.
judge_comment: Choosing the bowl as the program is an intuitive idea and technically feasible, but it forces users to buy proprietary bowls and RF tags in a microwave are tricky.

title: Pictogram Dial
new_elements: Food-icon selector (Icons for mug, plate, bowl, popcorn and frozen replace the numbers.)
rationale: Pictures are understood across languages and ages.
judge_comment: Icons in place of numbers directly lower the learning barrier and are easy to build, though similar interfaces already exist.

title: Door-Close-to-Start
new_elements: Door-actuated start ratchet (Each firm close adds 30 s to a spring timer and starts heating.)
rationale: The action the user already performs (shutting the door) becomes the whole interface.
judge_comment: Uses the door closing as the whole interface, which is clever and needs no learning, though accidental starts and an empty-run hazard are concerns.

title: Weighing Turntable Timer
new_elements: Spring-scale turntable cam (Food weight deflects a spring that sets cook time proportionally.); Sets time from food mass (Heavier load gets a longer cycle automatically.)
rationale: Put food in and the oven works out the time itself, with no setting required.
judge_comment: Placing food and getting the right time automatically is ideal for zero learning, but a mechanical spring-scale cam on a rotating turntable is hard, and weight does not reliably predict cook time.

title: Warm-Hot-Boiling Dial
new_elements: IR thermopile with analog comparator (The dial picks a target food temperature rather than a time.); Heats to target temperature (Closed-loop stop.)
rationale: People know they want 'hot', not '2 min 40'.
judge_comment: A temperature-target dial matches how people think about heating, though IR sensing of food through a cavity is tricky and it is not really a cheap substitution.

title: Two Big Buttons
new_elements: Short/Long paddle switches (One paddle gives 30 s, the other 2 min, each with a simple RC timer.)
rationale: Two choices cover most reheating jobs with no learning at all.
judge_comment: Very simple and cheap, but limited to two durations and a fairly obvious approach.

title: Defrost Mesh Basket
new_elements: Slotted metal defrost basket (A partially shielding basket gives gentle defrost at full magnetron power.)
rationale: Frozen food goes in the basket with no defrost settings needed.
judge_comment: A shielding basket that makes defrost automatic is clever and removes a confusing setting, but metal in a microwave makes it hard to make safe and effective.

title: Push-Depth Knob
new_elements: Plunger-style combined control (Rotate to set time; push in to choose gentle or full power.)
rationale: One knob replaces two and the second mode is a natural push.
judge_comment: A combined push-and-turn knob simplifies the controls and is mechanically plausible, though the push-for-power mapping is not fully self-evident.

title: Popcorn-Pop Acoustic Stop
new_elements: Piezo pop-rate cutoff (Heating stops when popping or bubbling sounds slow down.)
rationale: The oven listens to the food so the user doesn't have to.
judge_comment: Acoustic end-detection removes time guessing and is plausible for popcorn, though it works poorly for most other foods.

title: Fridge-Magnet Recipe Keys
new_elements: Magnetic program tiles (Sticking a 'soup' tile onto the front panel selects that program via Hall sensors.)
rationale: Choosing a tile is like choosing a picture card.
judge_comment: Magnetic tiles with Hall sensors are cheap and workable, and picture-based selection is intuitive, though tiles can get lost and it adds items.

title: Weight-Activated Start
new_elements: Load-sensing start interlock (Heating starts only if food is present and the door is closed; the default time comes from the weight.)
rationale: No start button and no empty-run mistakes.
judge_comment: Removing the start button and auto-setting time from weight directly removes learning, and load cells are cheap, though weight-to-time mapping for varied foods is imprecise.

title: Food Picture Push Buttons
new_elements: Three large mechanical buttons with food photos (Each button latches a preset time and power cam, like a vintage radio preset.)
rationale: Pressing the picture of what you are heating requires no reading or numeracy.
judge_comment: Large preset buttons with food photos are very easy to use and practical, but not very novel.

title: Steam Whistle Auto-Stop
new_elements: Bimetal steam vent switch (Hot steam in the exhaust duct snaps a bimetal disc that cuts the magnetron.); Stops cooking when food is hot (Closed-loop end point based on food state instead of time.)
rationale: The user never has to guess the time because the oven stops itself when the food steams.
judge_comment: Steam-triggered auto-stop removes time guessing, but covered or dry foods produce little steam and the bimetal needs careful tuning.

title: Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity with choke-seal front (Food sits in a drawer; there are no hinges, latch button or swinging door.); Telescopic slide rails (Cheap stamped steel drawer slides.)
rationale: Everyone knows how to open a drawer, and it is easier for elderly users to reach into.
judge_comment: A drawer is an instantly familiar interaction and easy to use, and drawer microwaves exist, though the choke seal and sliding mechanism are tricky.

title: Wind-Up Egg-Timer Core
new_elements: Spring clockwork escapement timer (A wind-up kitchen timer mechanism replaces the synchronous motor.); Clockwork timer switch (Works independently of mains frequency.)
rationale: It behaves exactly like the familiar egg timer users already understand, and one SKU works everywhere.
judge_comment: A familiar wind-up egg timer is a sound substitution for the motor and needs no learning, with a clear mechanism and independence from mains frequency.

title: One Power Only
new_elements: Single fixed power output (The power knob and duty-cycle cam are deleted entirely.)
rationale: Removing a control the user never understood leaves just one decision: how long.
judge_comment: Removing the power control is simple and effective for ease of use, though it limits cooking versatility and is not very radical.

title: Punched Recipe Cards
new_elements: Punched card reader driving cam pins (Ready-meal boxes carry tear-off punched cards that program time and power profiles.); Pianola-style punched-card mechanics (Pins drop through holes to set the cams.)
rationale: The food packaging programs the oven, so the user just inserts the card.
judge_comment: Packaging that programs the oven through a mechanical punched-card reader removes the need to learn settings and is very radical, but it needs ecosystem buy-in and is mechanically awkward.

title: Memory Detent Timer
new_elements: Timer with sliding memory stop (A movable stop remembers the last setting; turning the knob fully clockwise repeats it.)
rationale: The same daily coffee reheat becomes a single turn to the stop.
judge_comment: A mechanical memory stop makes repeat use a single turn and is plausible, though it's an incremental tweak to the timer knob.

title: Zoned Dial (Defrost Arc)
new_elements: Dual-arc timer dial with full and defrost sectors (Turning right gives full power and turning left gives defrost, using a single cam.)
rationale: Direction of turn is a simple binary choice that replaces a five-step power scale.
judge_comment: Turn direction as the power choice is clever and cheap, but users must still learn the left/right mapping.

title: Picture Power Knob
new_elements: Icon dial (cup, plate, ice cube, popcorn) (Each icon maps to a preset power and time cam profile.)
rationale: Users pick what the food is rather than translating that into watts and minutes.
judge_comment: Food-based icons remove the need to translate into time and power, and cam profiles are simple, but quantity variation is not handled.

title: Solid-State Beam Steering
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier array (Phase-steered RF spots replace the magnetron and moving turntable.); Heats evenly without rotation (Electronic field movement replaces the motor.)
rationale: No plate to seat or align, so food cooks evenly wherever it is placed.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is radical and removes the turntable, but its link to simpler operation is indirect and cost is still high.

title: Inverter Power Supply
new_elements: High-frequency inverter magnetron drive (Replaces the transformer, voltage doubler and duty-cycle cam with true variable power.)
rationale: Gentle continuous power means a single setting works for everything, with no power-level choice needed.
judge_comment: Inverter drives already exist, but they do remove the power-level decision, which helps simplicity.

title: Thermochromic Food Cover
new_elements: Colour-changing splatter dome (Turns from blue to red when the food beneath reaches about 70 °C.); Shows food doneness visually (Replaces checking and guessing.)
rationale: A colour change tells anyone the food is ready, without reading anything.
judge_comment: Visual doneness cue removes guessing and needs no reading, though it measures surface temperature and may not match the food's real state.

title: Auto-Pop Door Instead of Bell
new_elements: Spring-assisted door release at cycle end (The door pops ajar when cooking finishes.); Signals completion physically (Replaces the bell and prevents forgotten food.)
rationale: An open door means done, which is unambiguous even to first-time users.
judge_comment: A door that pops open gives a clear physical done signal, using a simple spring in place of a bell, and it suits first-time users.

title: Acoustic Arc Kill
new_elements: Microphone arc-crackle detector (Cuts the magnetron within milliseconds of detecting arcing sound.)
rationale: Mistakes become harmless, so learning is unnecessary.
judge_comment: Acoustic arc detection makes mistakes harmless, which is novel and relevant, but reliable sound-based triggering in a noisy oven is questionable.

title: Three-Word Interface
new_elements: Three keys: WARM, HOT, THAW (Each key runs a sensor-driven program.)
rationale: Three plain words cover nearly all single-person cooking.
judge_comment: Three plain-word keys directly eliminate the learning curve, though sensor-driven reheating programs already exist in some form and the substitution is of the keypad.

title: Whistling Steam Lid
new_elements: Microwave-safe cover with steam whistle (Whistles like a kettle when the food boils; a mic hears it and stops the oven.)
rationale: Borrows the kettle metaphor everyone already knows.
judge_comment: A kettle-style whistle that triggers auto-stop is an intuitive, creative substitution, though mic detection and consistent whistling are tricky.

title: Mug-Only Mini Microwave
new_elements: Cup-shaped single-serving cavity (Fits one mug, with built-in nucleation and a fixed 60 s cycle.)
rationale: One purpose and one action, with zero choices.
judge_comment: A single-purpose mug microwave with a fixed cycle removes choices, though it limits what the appliance can do.

title: Defrost-by-Shape Tray
new_elements: Magnet-coded accessory trays (Dropping in the 'frozen' tray auto-selects the defrost cycle.)
rationale: The chosen container sets the mode.
judge_comment: Magnet-coded trays that set the mode remove menu navigation and are plausible with simple sensors, though they add accessories and only cover some use cases.

title: Toaster Lever Start
new_elements: Spring-loaded push-down lever (Replaces the clockwork timer knob and start; lever depth sets heating time, like a toaster.); Set time and start in one motion (Pushing down both programs and starts the cycle.); Separate timer and start actions confuse users (Base product needs knob turning plus door logic.)
rationale: Everyone already knows how to use a toaster lever, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Familiar toaster metaphor removes learning, though lever depth as a time setting is imprecise and mechanically fiddly.

title: Weighing Turntable Auto-Time
new_elements: Load-cell weighing (A cheap strain gauge under the plate.); Scale-plate (Replaces the timer knob; weight drives the heating duration automatically.); Infer heating time from mass (Heavier food gets longer time.)
rationale: Users just put food in; the machine works out how long to heat it.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto-time removes input, though weight is a poor proxy for food type and needed heat.

title: Steam-Sniffer Stop
new_elements: Humidity sensing (A capacitive humidity sensor sits in the exhaust duct.); Exhaust steam sensor (Replaces the clockwork timer as the stop trigger.); Stop when food steams (Ends heating when steam release indicates the food is hot.)
rationale: No time guessing is needed: it stops when the food is hot.
judge_comment: Steam sensing for auto-stop exists in some microwaves, so it is plausible and removes timing, but it is less novel.

title: One Big Button
new_elements: Single giant front button (Replaces both knobs; each press adds 30 s at full power.); Single-gesture operation (Only one control exists.); Two knobs with unclear interplay (The power and timer relationship is opaque.)
rationale: With one button there is nothing to choose and nothing to get wrong.
judge_comment: Very simple and highly feasible, but incremental and lacks flexibility, so it is not radical.

title: Whole-Door Tap Pad
new_elements: Capacitive glass sensing (The ITO layer in the door glass doubles as a touch sensor.); Touch-sensitive door (Replaces the knobs; tap anywhere to add time.); Tap-anywhere control (Each tap equals +30 s.)
rationale: There is no control to locate: the whole door is the button.
judge_comment: Using the door glass as a tap-anywhere sensor is clever and intuitive, but the door's metal mesh and shielding make capacitive sensing tricky, and accidental touches are a risk.

title: Notched Mug Key
new_elements: Notched-base dishware (Notches in the dish base press microswitches in the floor that select a preset.); Dish selects program mechanically (Mug equals beverage, bowl equals soup, with no electronics needed.); Mechanical keying (Microswitch array read like a key.)
rationale: Choosing the dish is choosing the program, so nothing extra is learned.
judge_comment: Keyed dishware that selects a program is clever and needs no learning, but it requires proprietary dishes and the floor microswitches are exposed to spills and heat.

title: Microwave Cloche
new_elements: Shielded dome lid (Replaces the box, door and turntable access; a mesh-glass bell is lowered over the plate on a base.); Cover-to-heat (Lowering the dome closes the interlock and starts heating.); Dome-shaped RF shielding (Conductive mesh in borosilicate glass.)
rationale: Covering a plate is an intuitive, ancient gesture.
judge_comment: A cover-to-heat dome is a radical and intuitive interaction, but a safe mesh-glass shield with a reliable interlock is hard, and heating power and time are still undefined.

title: Frost Detector Defrost
new_elements: Ice-detecting RF sensor (Replaces the defrost power setting by detecting frozen load via reflected power.); Automatic defrost mode (Switches to gentle pulsing when ice is sensed.); Reflected-power sensing (A directional coupler measures the dielectric change of ice.)
rationale: Users never need to know the defrost setting exists.
judge_comment: Detecting ice via reflected power to trigger defrost automatically is concrete and clever, though reliability across loads is challenging.

title: Detent Presets Dial
new_elements: Clicking preset detents (The timer knob physically snaps to the 30 s, 1, 2 and 5 min common values.); Tactile guidance to common times (Snaps to sensible choices.); Fine dial imprecision (The 0-30 min range on a small dial is hard to set.)
rationale: The knob itself teaches good choices.
judge_comment: Practical detented knob guides users to common times, but it is an incremental tweak rather than a radical substitution.

title: Covered-Dish Steam Mode
new_elements: Lid-detecting height sensor (Replaces the power knob mode choice by detecting a covered dish and selecting steam-cook.); Mode by container state (Covered dish means gentle steam.); Optical beam-break sensing (An IR beam across the cavity.)
rationale: The setup users naturally do becomes the setting.
judge_comment: Auto-selecting the mode from the covered dish removes a decision, though reliable detection and the IR beam approach are uncertain.

title: Mug-Shaped Beverage Bay
new_elements: Cup-sized side pocket (Replaces dial setting for drinks; a dedicated mug alcove auto-runs a beverage program when occupied.); Shape-implied program (The location tells the oven what the item is.); Presence microswitch (Simple mechanical detection.)
rationale: If it fits there, it's a drink, so the affordance does the instructing.
judge_comment: A mug alcove with a presence switch is a clear, cheap affordance-based approach, though it covers only drinks.

title: Plate-Turn Timer
new_elements: Hand-turned turntable dial (Replaces the timer knob; rotating the plate itself before closing sets time via an encoder on the turntable shaft.); Set time by touching the food plate (Merges food placement with time setting.); Rotary shaft encoding (Reuses the turntable coupler.)
rationale: The control is where the food already is, so there is no panel to learn.
judge_comment: Setting time by turning the plate is intuitive and reuses existing parts, though discoverability and encoder integration with a rotating plate are questionable.

title: Weigh-to-Time Turntable
new_elements: Spring-scale turntable support (The roller ring sits on a spring whose deflection sets the timer cam; heavier food gets more time.); Sets cooking time from food weight (Time is chosen automatically from load mass.)
rationale: The user puts the food in and closes the door, and the food's own weight sets the time.
judge_comment: Weight-based automatic time is clever and removes input, but weight correlates poorly with the time needed, and the mechanism must be robust under heat and a rotating load.

title: Steam-Sense Auto Stop
new_elements: Bimetal steam sensor in exhaust duct (Snap disc in the vent air opens the circuit when hot humid exhaust shows that food is steaming.); Stops cooking when food is hot (Closed-loop end of cycle.)
rationale: The user just presses 'reheat' and never has to guess a duration.
judge_comment: Steam-based auto stop removes time guessing and is plausible, though bimetal snap discs are crude and food-dependent; humidity sensors already exist.

title: Big +30 s Button
new_elements: Ratchet +30 s push button (Each press winds the timer 30 s further and starts the oven.)
rationale: One large button that the user presses 'until enough' needs no instruction.
judge_comment: A single start button that adds time is simple and very feasible, but common on existing microwaves and not radical.

title: Temperature Dial, Not Time
new_elements: IR thermopile with warm/hot/boiling dial (The user picks a target feel; the IR sensor stops heating at that surface temperature.)
rationale: People think in 'warm' or 'hot', not seconds, so the dial uses their own words.
judge_comment: A dial of warm/hot/boiling matches how people think, but an IR thermopile only reads surface temperature through the cavity, and metal walls and steam cause problems.

title: Count-the-Cups Dial
new_elements: Cup-count detent dial (1-4 cups) (Dial with mug icons; each detent adds a calibrated beverage heating time.)
rationale: The user counts mugs instead of estimating seconds.
judge_comment: A mug-count detent dial is simple, cheap and easy to understand, though it only covers beverages and is not very radical.

title: Barcode Cook
new_elements: Front barcode scanner window (Wave the ready-meal pack; the oven loads the manufacturer's time and power.); Low-cost CMOS barcode decoding (Module costing under one dollar.)
rationale: The package instructions run themselves, so there is no reading or dialling.
judge_comment: Scanning a pack to load its instructions is cheap and realistic, but it only works for barcoded packaged meals.

title: Mug Port
new_elements: Dedicated shielded mug well (A cylindrical side port sized for one mug; inserting it closes the interlock and runs a fixed drink program.)
rationale: The most common task becomes 'put the mug in the hole', with zero settings.
judge_comment: A dedicated mug port with a fixed program gives true zero-setting operation for one common task, though it covers only a narrow use and needs shielding.

title: Close-Door-to-Start
new_elements: Door closure starts last-used cycle (The interlock closing triggers the last setting; opening pauses, reclosing resumes.)
rationale: Repeat users do nothing beyond shutting the door.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start removes every button press for repeat use, which is highly relevant, but it risks accidental starts and is unclear for first-time use.

title: Pulse-Haptic Knob
new_elements: Detented timer knob with tactile food-icon bumps (Raised braille-like icons and strong clicks at common times (30 s, 1, 2, 3 min).)
rationale: The right setting can be felt without looking or reading.
judge_comment: Tactile detents with icons are simple, cheap and easy to use without reading, but they are an incremental refinement rather than a radical idea.

title: Close-The-Door-To-Cook
new_elements: Door-closure start counter (Each door close starts or adds 30 s; opening the door stops and resets.)
rationale: The only action required is the one every user already performs: shutting the door.
judge_comment: Starting on door close is very intuitive and cheap, but accidental starts and unclear time control are issues.

title: Weigh-And-Go Turntable
new_elements: Spring-scale turntable timer (Turntable sits on a spring whose deflection winds the timer cam proportional to food weight.); Mechanical load-to-time transduction (Rack-and-pinion converts spring compression into timer setting.)
rationale: Putting food in sets the time automatically, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Auto-setting time by weight is radical and removes decisions, but weight alone poorly predicts cook time and the mechanism is awkward with a turntable.

title: Token Timer
new_elements: Gravity token slot (Drop chunky 30-second tokens into a slot; an escapement releases one token per 30 s and power stops when the last token falls.)
rationale: Counting physical tokens is as intuitive as feeding a parking meter, and the remaining time is visible.
judge_comment: Token-based time is intuitive and visible, though the tokens are fiddly and could get lost, and the escapement adds mechanical complexity.

title: Pull-Cord Timer
new_elements: Retracting pull-cord timer (Pull the cord out to a marked length; a governed spring slowly retracts it and power cuts at zero.)
rationale: The remaining cord length is a self-explanatory, glanceable progress bar.
judge_comment: A cord that retracts doubles as a timer and a progress bar, which is intuitive, but a governed spring over minutes needs good control and wears over time.

title: Magnet Latch Door
new_elements: Magnetic catch with pull handle (Fridge-style magnetic catch with a big handle; reed interlocks replace the lever latch.)
rationale: Just pull the door like a fridge: there is no hidden button to find.
judge_comment: A fridge-style magnetic catch and handle is simple and plausible, but it is an incremental change and magnetic latching alone needs redundant interlocks.

title: Quartz Knob Same-Feel
new_elements: Encoder knob with quartz countdown (Same rotary feel, but an RC/quartz chip gives precise short times and is mains-independent.)
rationale: It keeps the zero-learning knob while making 20-second jobs actually work.
judge_comment: A practical, familiar knob with a quartz timer fixes short-time accuracy, but it is an incremental change rather than a radical one.

title: Two-Handle Power Choice
new_elements: Dual start handles (gentle/strong) (Closing the door with the blue handle latches low duty; the red handle latches full power.)
rationale: Power selection is folded into closing the door with a colour-coded choice.
judge_comment: Choosing power by which handle you close the door with is clever and needs no learning, though it offers only two levels and the interlock design is tricky.

title: One Click = One Minute
new_elements: Heavy-detent minute knob (Each loud tactile click equals exactly one minute.)
rationale: Users count clicks instead of reading tiny scales.
judge_comment: Simple, intuitive mapping from clicks to minutes, with a mechanical detent that is easy to build, though similar mechanical timers already exist.

title: Whole-Door Bezel Dial
new_elements: Rotating window-frame ring timer (The round porthole frame itself is the timer knob, huge and impossible to miss.)
rationale: A giant single control is the face of the product: impossible to overlook and easy to grip.
judge_comment: A giant door-frame dial is bold and hard to miss, but it needs an integrated mechanism and sealing near the microwave door.

title: Close-the-Door-to-Start
new_elements: Door-actuated start switch (Closing the door starts a default 30 s heat; each extra close-open-close adds 30 s.)
rationale: The only action needed is closing the door, which every user already knows how to do.
judge_comment: Very simple, with no learning curve, but a default 30 s heat may be wrong for many foods and risks accidental starts, e.g. when the door is closed on an empty cavity.

title: Weigh-and-Go Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (A strain gauge under the tray weighs the food and sets the time automatically.); Strain-gauge load sensing (A resistive bridge measures weight.)
rationale: Putting the food in is the whole setup, so there are no settings to learn.
judge_comment: Weight alone does not determine heating time (food type, starting temperature), but load cells are cheap and the approach is concrete.

title: No-Tray Mode Stirrer
new_elements: Hidden metal mode-stirrer fan (A rotating reflector in the roof scrambles the standing waves.)
rationale: There is no tray to seat, lose or misalign; the user just puts the food down.
judge_comment: Removing the turntable by using a mode stirrer is real, proven tech that eliminates a setup step, but it is not a new idea.

title: Barcode Eye
new_elements: Front barcode scanner (Wave the packet past it to load the instructions.)
rationale: The supermarket-checkout gesture is already familiar to everyone.
judge_comment: A barcode scan uses a familiar gesture and is very feasible, but barcodes do not typically contain cooking instructions and the idea is fairly obvious.

title: Target-Temperature Dial
new_elements: IR thermopile food sensor (Stops heating when the food surface reaches the chosen Warm, Hot or Very Hot setting.)
rationale: Users pick an outcome rather than a duration.
judge_comment: Outcome-based dial removes time guessing, though IR sensing only reads the surface and is inaccurate through containers and steam.

title: Plus-30 Button Only
new_elements: Single +30 s pushbutton (Each press adds 30 s at full power and starts immediately.)
rationale: One button with one meaning gives zero learning curve.
judge_comment: This is trivially simple and buildable, but it is barely radical, and repeated presses are needed for longer times with no power control.

title: Just Say It
new_elements: Offline voice command chip (Recognises phrases such as 'warm my coffee' and 'defrost'.)
rationale: Natural speech replaces knob semantics.
judge_comment: Voice control has no learning curve and offline chips are plausible, but the idea is common and noisy kitchens affect reliability.

title: Knock to Heat
new_elements: Piezo knock sensor in door (Each knock adds 30 s and a fist-thump stops the oven.)
rationale: No controls to locate: just tap the box.
judge_comment: Knocking is a radical and discoverable input, but it is not self-explanatory, it risks accidental triggers, and a fist-thump stop is a bit crude.

title: Three Colour Buttons
new_elements: Blue/Orange/Red mode buttons (Blue for Defrost, Orange for Warm, Red for Hot.)
rationale: Colour meaning is culturally universal, unlike a numbered power scale.
judge_comment: Replaces the numeric power scale with three colored buttons, which is cheap and simple, though it gives little control over timing and is not radical.

title: Revolving Drum Oven
new_elements: Rotating cylinder cavity (Spinning the drum to the back closes the opening and starts heating; spinning it forward opens it.)
rationale: One turning gesture opens, closes and starts the oven.
judge_comment: A single rotating gesture that opens, closes and starts is radical and intuitive, but sealing microwave leakage in a rotating drum is very hard, and the design leaves out how time is set.

title: Warming Colour Light
new_elements: RGB cavity light driven by IR sensor (Shifts from blue to red as the food warms.)
rationale: The user sees progress intuitively without numbers.
judge_comment: Intuitive colour feedback on progress needs no numbers, though IR sensing of food temperature through the cavity is tricky and it does not simplify the controls themselves.

title: Food Pictogram Dial
new_elements: Icon dial (cup, plate, bowl, frozen) (Each icon position sets both time and power through the cam.)
rationale: The user points at a picture of their food instead of estimating minutes.
judge_comment: A pictogram dial is intuitive and easy to build, though it's an incremental and fairly familiar approach with coarse accuracy.

title: IR Thermometer Target Stop
new_elements: Ceiling IR thermopile (Stops heating when the food surface reaches 70 °C.)
rationale: The oven heats to a temperature, not a guessed duration.
judge_comment: Replacing the timer with a target temperature removes guesswork and the learning curve, though IR only reads surface temperature and sensing through steam or containers is difficult.

title: Revolving Hatch, No Door
new_elements: Rotating half-drum cavity (Rotate the drum to face you, load it, and rotate it back; the cavity is always shielded.)
rationale: A single rotate gesture loads the oven, and turning it back starts cooking.
judge_comment: A rotating shielded drum removes the door and makes loading and starting one intuitive gesture, but it is hard to seal and to keep food from spilling.

title: Kick-Open Drawer Oven
new_elements: Push-to-open drawer cavity (Push-latch drawer replaces the hinged door and release button.)
rationale: Opening it works like a familiar kitchen drawer.
judge_comment: A drawer is a familiar interaction and is feasible with RF choke seals, though it is only a modest departure from a door and liquids could spill.

title: Door-Close-to-Start
new_elements: Mechanical clockwork timer knob (Base-product component being substituted); Door-closure start switch with auto-sensing (Closing the door starts sensor-controlled heating; opening it stops heating); Start cooking without any explicit command (The only user action is to put the food in and shut the door)
rationale: Shutting a door is something everyone already knows how to do, so starting the oven requires no learning at all.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start is highly intuitive and feasible with a door switch plus sensing, though the safety of starting with no explicit command and the sensing logic are only loosely defined.

title: Weighing Floor Auto-Timer
new_elements: Mechanical clockwork timer knob (Base-product component being substituted); Load-cell cavity floor (Strain gauges under the floor weigh the food and set the cooking time); Derive cooking time from food mass (No minutes to guess)
rationale: Users no longer need to estimate minutes because the oven weighs the food and calculates the time itself.
judge_comment: A load-cell floor is concrete and plausible, but mass alone is a weak predictor of cooking time, and the user still has to start the oven.

title: IR Thermometer Done-Detection
new_elements: Mechanical clockwork timer knob (Base-product component being substituted); Thermopile array sensor (Low-cost infrared sensor in the cavity roof that reads the food's surface temperature); Non-contact infrared thermometry (Closed-loop heating control); Stop when food reaches eating temperature (Heating ends at about 70 °C)
rationale: The oven stops when the food is hot rather than after a guessed time, so there is no setting to learn.
judge_comment: A thermopile sensor with closed-loop stop is concrete and cheap, but it reads surface temperature only, and the user still has to start it.

title: Thermochromic Lid Readiness
new_elements: 20-25 W incandescent interior lamp (Base-product component being substituted); Thermochromic splatter cover (Microwave-safe cover that turns from blue to red when the food underneath is hot); Show doneness visually without a lamp (Colour-coded temperature)
rationale: A red-means-hot cue is universally understood and requires no interpretation.
judge_comment: A colour-changing cover gives an intuitive hot cue, but it only works with the cover, and it replaces the lamp's visibility function poorly.

title: Solid-State Phase-Steered Heating
new_elements: Glass turntable (Base-product component being substituted); GaN solid-state RF amplifiers (Multiple antennas with controllable phase); Phased RF emitter array (Steers energy toward cold spots electronically); Even heating with no user stirring (Removes the 'stir halfway' instruction)
rationale: Users never need to learn tricks such as stirring, rotating, or resting the food.
judge_comment: Solid-state phased RF is real and removes the need to stir, but it is costly and not simpler or cheaper, so it fits the substitute brief only loosely.

title: Food-Icon Dial
new_elements: 5-step power knob with duty-cycle cam (Base-product component being substituted); Pictogram dial (Icons for mug, plate, soup, frozen block and popcorn); Select by food type (Picture-based choice)
rationale: Pictures transcend language and literacy, so the dial is instantly usable by anyone.
judge_comment: Pictogram dial is easy to use and cheap, but it is a familiar concept and not radical.

title: Shape-Sensing Mug Dimple
new_elements: Glass turntable (Base-product component being substituted); Contoured floor with mug well and plate zone (Microswitches detect where the item was placed and choose the mode); Auto-select mode from placement (Where you put it decides what it does)
rationale: The physical layout itself is the interface, so users simply put things where they obviously fit.
judge_comment: The placement-as-interface idea is novel and zero-learning, but detecting food type from microswitches is unreliable and a contoured floor hinders even heating.

title: RFID Colour-Coded Containers
new_elements: 5-step power knob with duty-cycle cam (Base-product component being substituted); Shielded RFID tags in container lids (Blue lid for soup, red for rice; the oven reads the tag and runs the right cycle); Container dictates the program (Zero settings)
rationale: The intelligence lives in the container, so the user only has to put the food in.
judge_comment: Container-driven programs give zero settings and are creative, but they require proprietary containers, and RFID tags in a microwave raise safety and cost concerns.

title: Packaging Barcode Reader
new_elements: Mechanical clockwork timer knob (Base-product component being substituted); Door-edge barcode scanner (Wave a ready-meal box past it to load the manufacturer's heating instructions); Follow package instructions automatically (No reading the small print)
rationale: Users skip interpreting 'pierce film, 3 min, stir, 2 min' because the oven does it.
judge_comment: Scanning the package's own instructions removes reading and decisions, though it only works for barcoded ready meals and needs a database; the clockwork timer is mismatched with the rest.

title: Steam-Sensing Auto-Stop
new_elements: Mechanical clockwork timer knob (Base-product component being substituted); Exhaust humidity sensor (Detects the burst of steam released when food is heated through); End the cycle at the steam point (A cheap auto-cook method)
rationale: A cheap sensor replaces the user's guesswork about cooking time.
judge_comment: A humidity sensor replaces timing guesswork cheaply and plausibly, and sensor-cook already exists, though the user still has to start it.

title: Popcorn Ear
new_elements: Mechanical clockwork timer knob (Base-product component being substituted); MEMS microphone with pop counter (Stops heating when the interval between pops grows long); Perfect popcorn with no guessing (Acoustic doneness detection)
rationale: It removes the most notorious microwave learning task: knowing when popcorn is done.
judge_comment: Acoustic pop counting is clever and feasible and fixes a well-known pain point, but it is narrow in scope.

title: Hourglass Flip Microwave
new_elements: Mechanical clockwork timer knob (Base-product component being substituted); Flip-over tilt-switch timer block (Rotate the block to choose the number of illuminated sand-style segments); Tangible time metaphor (Shows how much time is left)
rationale: An hourglass is an ancient, universally understood timer.
judge_comment: Hourglass metaphor is intuitive and a tilt-switch timer is cheap and plausible, though the 'mechanical clockwork' and 'flip to choose segments' descriptions are somewhat muddled.

title: Repeat-Last Button
new_elements: Mechanical clockwork timer knob (Base-product component being substituted); Memory 'same again' button (Replays the previous successful cycle); Reuse a known-good setting (Habit-friendly)
rationale: Most people heat the same things daily, so one press repeats it.
judge_comment: A one-press repeat of the last cycle is highly practical and removes the learning curve for routine use, though it is a fairly familiar idea.

title: Pictogram-Molded Housing Replaces Manual
new_elements: Paper instruction manual (Base-product item being substituted); Embossed pictogram instructions on door frame (Three icons: put in, close, wait for the green light); Self-explaining device (Instructions live on the product)
rationale: Guidance sits exactly where it is needed, so nothing has to be learned in advance.
judge_comment: Embossed pictograms are cheap and practical, directly cut the learning need, but they are an incremental, not radical, change.

title: Traffic-Light Status Lamp
new_elements: 20-25 W incandescent interior lamp (Base-product component being substituted); RGB interior LED (Red while heating, amber when nearly done, green when ready); Illumination plus status in one (Merges the lamp and bell functions)
rationale: Traffic-light colours are understood worldwide.
judge_comment: An RGB LED status light is simple and intuitive, though it only aids feedback, not input, and is modest in novelty.

title: Kettle Rocker Switch
new_elements: Timer and power knobs (Base-product components being substituted); Single rocker switch with auto-cutoff (Flick on; it clicks off itself when the food is hot, like a kettle); Kettle-like operation (Familiar on/auto-off behaviour)
rationale: It borrows the most universally understood appliance interface.
