judge_comment: A kettle-style single switch with auto-cutoff is highly intuitive, but reliably sensing when food is hot is technically hard and risky.

title: Cordless Lunchbox Microwave
new_elements: Countertop box with mains cord (Base-product components being substituted); Shielded lunchbox with resonant base dock (Set the box on the dock and it heats automatically); Place-to-heat (Like charging a phone on a pad)
rationale: Setting an object down is the entire interaction.
judge_comment: Place-to-heat is the ultimate no-learning-curve interaction and radical, though resonant wireless microwave heating in a lunchbox is technically very challenging.

title: Three-Shelf Mode Selection
new_elements: 5-step power knob with duty-cycle cam (Base-product component being substituted); Height-labelled shelf rails (Top shelf for gentle warming, bottom shelf for full cooking; the oven senses which is used); Spatial mode selection (Placement equals intent)
rationale: Choosing a shelf is a natural kitchen action, unlike choosing a power percentage.
judge_comment: Using shelf position as intent is a clever, intuitive mapping, though sensing the shelf and the cooking physics are uncertain.

title: Pull-Cord Timer
new_elements: Retractable pull cord timer (Pulling the cord out sets the time by length; the cord slowly rewinds as it counts down, with seconds marked on the cord.)
rationale: Pulling longer for more heat is an intuitive physical metaphor that anyone grasps instantly.
judge_comment: The pull-cord timer is an intuitive, tactile metaphor and a mechanical substitute for the keypad, but the retractable mechanism and its precision are awkward.

title: Package Barcode Cooking
new_elements: Door-mounted barcode scanner (Reads ready-meal packaging and applies the manufacturer's time and power.)
rationale: It removes the need to read tiny instructions or translate them into settings.
judge_comment: Scanning the package removes any need to set times and is technically plausible, but it works only for packaged food and some barcodes lack cooking data.

title: Spring-Wound Kitchen Timer
new_elements: Motorless escapement wind-up timer (Egg-timer style clockwork; winding the knob stores the energy and the escapement runs it down.)
rationale: It works exactly like the egg timer every grandparent knows, and the cheaper parts help the low BOM target.
judge_comment: Mechanical wind-up timers already exist in older microwaves; very intuitive and cheap, but not very radical.

title: Package-Tag Autopilot
new_elements: NFC reader under floor (Reads a tag printed on ready-meal packaging.); Loads manufacturer heating profile (Applies the packaging's own time and power program.)
rationale: The meal tells the oven what to do, so the user reads no instructions.
judge_comment: An NFC tag on packaging is clever and effortless, but it needs industry adoption and fails for non-tagged food.

title: Arc-Sniffing Auto-Cut
new_elements: RF arc detector (Detects arcing signatures and kills power within milliseconds.)
rationale: A forgotten fork stops the oven instead of causing damage, so no rules need memorizing.
judge_comment: Arc detection removes a rule to memorize and is plausible, though it is more a safety feature than a simplification of operation, and it isn't really a substitution.

title: Glowing Door Done Signal
new_elements: Door-edge LED halo (Amber means working, green means ready, and red means hot inside.)
rationale: Traffic-light colors are universally understood.
judge_comment: A traffic-light LED halo is easy to understand and simple to build, but it is an obvious idea that substitutes little.

title: Picture Dial
new_elements: Pictogram food knob (Knob with cup, plate, popcorn and frozen-block icons instead of minute markings.); Select by food, not by number (Each icon position maps to a preset time and power cam.)
rationale: Pictures need no literacy, language or cooking knowledge.
judge_comment: A simple, very buildable pictogram knob that is intuitive, but it is an incremental change and presets are coarse.

title: Solid-State RF Heating
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifiers (Phase-steered emitters that adapt to the load.); Multi-antenna RF array (Heats evenly with no turntable and true variable power.); Even heating without user care (Removes the need to stir, rotate or position food.)
rationale: There are no techniques to learn for avoiding cold spots.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF removes the need to stir or rotate food and is a real technology, but it is costly and it replaces the magnetron rather than simplifying the controls.

title: Food Tokens
new_elements: Magnetic recipe tokens (Chunky tokens shaped like a cup, a pizza slice or a snowflake; drop one in the slot to choose.); Tangible program selection (Physical objects replace dial positions.)
rationale: Children and elderly users can operate it by matching shapes.
judge_comment: Physical tokens make program selection intuitive for children and the elderly, but they can be lost and the idea doesn't cover time or power.

title: Popcorn Ear
new_elements: Acoustic pop detector (A microphone counts pop intervals and stops when popping slows.); Sound-based doneness (Never burns popcorn.)
rationale: It removes the most common source of failure through trial and error.
judge_comment: Acoustic popcorn detection already exists in some ovens, but it removes a common guessing task and is clearly specified.

title: Lunchbox Microwave Pod
new_elements: Personal shielded heating pod (A lunchbox-sized RF cavity: snap the lid shut and it auto-heats the contents.); Single-purpose reheating (Replaces the whole countertop cavity with one fixed task.)
rationale: Snapping a lid shut is the only operation.
judge_comment: Closing the lid as the only action is extremely simple and a radical substitution of the cavity, though a safe, shielded and auto-sensing portable RF pod is technically challenging.

title: Door-Close-to-Start
new_elements: Door-actuated start switch with default 1-min cycle (Closing the door starts a 60 s heat; opening it stops. No start button.)
rationale: Putting food in and shutting the door becomes the whole operation, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Very simple interaction with no learning curve, but a fixed 60 s default and the risk of accidental starts or empty-cavity operation limit it.

title: One Picture Dial
new_elements: Single food-icon dial (One cam dial with icons (cup, plate, frozen, butter); each icon sets both time and duty cycle.)
rationale: One dial with pictures replaces two abstract numeric knobs.
judge_comment: Easy to build and intuitive, but icon dials are close to existing presets and not radical.

title: Magnetic Container Keys
new_elements: Coded-magnet container lids (Colored lids (mug, bowl, defrost box) carry magnet patterns read by Hall sensors under the tray.)
rationale: Choosing the right container is the only setting the user ever makes.
judge_comment: Container-coded presets remove menu learning, though magnets near a magnetron cavity and the need for specific lids raise practical issues.

title: RF-Powered Glow Bulb
new_elements: Wireless neon capsule excited by the microwave field (A sealed gas capsule glows only while RF is present, needing no wiring.)
rationale: The glow means 'heating now' in a way that is impossible to misread.
judge_comment: A neon capsule lit by the RF field is a plausible, simple, wireless indicator of heating, though it only modestly improves operation.

title: Pop-Open Door Ending
new_elements: Timer-triggered door kicker spring (The timer cam releases the latch at the end so the door swings ajar.)
rationale: An open door plainly says 'done' and hands the food back to the user.
judge_comment: A spring-kicked door at the end is simple, mechanical and unmistakable, and it removes the need to understand beeps.

title: Cloche Microwave
new_elements: Lift-off shielded dome over a base plate (A mesh-glass bell jar sits on a choke-sealed base; lifting it cuts power.)
rationale: Lifting a dome off a plate is the most intuitive access imaginable.
judge_comment: A lift-off dome is extremely intuitive and radical, but RF shielding with a mesh-glass bell and a safe interlock is difficult.

title: Countdown Light Ring
new_elements: LED ring around the door that empties as time runs (A visual progress ring replaces the numeric scale and the bell.)
rationale: Users see how much time is left without reading numbers.
judge_comment: An LED progress ring is easy to build and read, but it only shows status and does nothing to simplify setting the time.

title: Solid-State RF Heart
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Continuous, precise power from low voltage with no 4 kV supply.); Solid-state RF module (Replaces the magnetron and HV chain.)
rationale: Closed-loop power control lets the oven pick the right power, so the user does not set it.
judge_comment: A GaN solid-state RF source with closed-loop control could remove user settings entirely, but cost and maturity are barriers and the link to the need is indirect.

title: Popcorn Ear
new_elements: Acoustic pop-rate microphone (Stops the cycle when pops slow to fewer than one every 2 s.)
rationale: It removes the classic guesswork of how long popcorn should take.
judge_comment: Acoustic pop detection already exists in some microwaves, but it directly removes timing guesswork for popcorn, though it covers just one food.

title: Portion Lever
new_elements: Three-position portion lever (1, 2, 4 plates) (The lever position scales the cam timer range.)
rationale: Users think in plates, not minutes.
judge_comment: Plate-based lever matches users' mental model and is mechanically simple, though it is a modest departure and accuracy depends on food type.

title: Drink Pod Microwave
new_elements: Mug-sized microwave pod (A tiny cylindrical cavity for one mug, with one button.)
rationale: A single-purpose device can have zero settings.
judge_comment: A single-purpose mug pod removes settings entirely and is plausible, though it limits use cases.

title: Carry-Away Timer Puck
new_elements: Detachable magnetic timer puck (Twist the puck to set time; it docks on the door and can be carried, buzzing when done.)
rationale: It works like the familiar egg timer and keeps working away from the kitchen.
judge_comment: A twist egg-timer puck is familiar and intuitive and easily built, with the detachable buzzer a nice touch, though it only covers time, not power.

title: Self-Explaining Door Pictogram
new_elements: Printed 3-step pictogram on the door glass (Put in, close, turn: icons replace the manual.)
rationale: The user manual is replaced by the door itself.
judge_comment: It is cheap, directly cuts the learning curve and is easy to build, but it is a fairly obvious idea.

title: Weigh-and-Go Turntable
new_elements: Spring-scale turntable support (Roller ring sits on a calibrated spring; tray deflection sets cook time through a linkage); Mechanical load-to-time linkage (Deflection of the spring moves the timer cam's start position)
rationale: Putting the food in sets the time automatically, so there is no setting to get wrong.
judge_comment: Weight-to-time is clever and removes input, but weight poorly predicts the right cook time and the spring-scale tolerance is hard in a heavy turntable.

title: Smart Lids Set the Power
new_elements: Colour-coded magnet lids (Microwave-safe covers with embedded ferrite pellets in coded positions (red=reheat, blue=defrost, yellow=melt)); Reed-switch array in cavity roof (Reads the lid code through the roof and selects the duty cycle)
rationale: Choosing a coloured lid replaces the power setting entirely.
judge_comment: Coded lids are very novel and the choice is tangible, but they add accessories to lose and magnets/ferrite near a microwave cavity raise safety and reliability concerns.

title: Thermochromic Ready Dome
new_elements: Thermochromic splatter dome (Cover that turns from blue to red once the food underneath reaches about 70 °C); Leuco-dye thermochromic pigment (Reversible colour change at a set temperature)
rationale: Red means hot, so readiness is obvious without interpreting time.
judge_comment: A color-changing dome gives an intuitive readiness cue with cheap, known leuco-dye tech, though it doesn't address controls.

title: One Button, +30 Seconds
new_elements: Single big +30 s button (Each press adds 30 s at full power; a long press means defrost)
rationale: One control with one rule replaces two knobs and their scales.
judge_comment: One button with one rule gives a near-zero learning curve and is trivially buildable, but it is an incremental idea.

title: Talk to It
new_elements: Offline voice command module (Local keyword recognizer: 'warm my coffee', 'defrost', 'stop'); Edge keyword-spotting speech recognition (Low-cost microcontroller-based speech model with no cloud connection); Speech processing (Speech signal processing and recognition)
rationale: Speaking normally is the one interface everyone already knows.
judge_comment: Offline keyword spotting is feasible and intuitive, but it adds cost and may mishear in noisy kitchens, and it adds parts rather than substituting.

title: Packaging Tells the Oven
new_elements: Door-frame barcode/RFID reader (Reads the cooking code on a ready-meal package as it passes through the door); Auto-loads cooking program from food package (Sets time and power from the manufacturer's code)
rationale: The user never reads the instructions on the box, because the oven does.
judge_comment: Automatic programming from the package removes the need to operate anything, though it depends on manufacturers adopting a code standard and does not cover non-packaged food.

title: Glow-Ring Countdown
new_elements: Shrinking LED halo around door (A light ring that gets shorter as time runs out and flashes green at the end)
rationale: Time remaining is shown as a shrinking ring that can be read at a glance without numbers.
judge_comment: A clear glanceable countdown that is cheap to build, but it doesn't simplify input and is incremental.

title: Concentric Super-Knob
new_elements: Single knob with power zones on its sweep (First 120° is defrost, the next 120° melt/soften, the last 120° full reheat; the angle within each zone sets time)
rationale: One knob and one motion replace two-step programming.
judge_comment: A single knob with zones simplifies programming, though users still need to learn what the zones mean.

title: Door-Close Starts It
new_elements: Starts default reheat cycle on door close (Closing the door with a load inside triggers an auto cycle; reopening stops it)
rationale: Putting food in and shutting the door is the whole operation.
judge_comment: Starting on door close removes all operation steps, though it risks accidental starts and empty-cavity or unsuitable loads.

title: Punch-Card Recipes
new_elements: Recipe punch-card reader (Slide in a printed photo-card (e.g. 'Grandma's porridge') whose punched holes drive the power and time cams)
rationale: Choosing a picture card replaces all programming.
judge_comment: Picture cards with a mechanical reader remove programming, though card management adds some friction and cams are dated yet plausible.

title: Three-Mode Rocker
new_elements: Three-position rocker (Thaw / Soften / Heat) (Replaces the five-step knob with three plain-word modes)
rationale: Fewer choices, each named in everyday words, leave nothing to decode.
judge_comment: Three plain-word modes cut the choices sharply and are easy to build, but the idea is incremental rather than radical.

title: Mug Well
new_elements: Cup-shaped dimple with mug sensor (A mug placed in the dimple triggers a drink program with a superheat-safe pause)
rationale: The shape of the dimple shows where the cup goes and what will happen.
judge_comment: A shaped dimple that senses the mug and auto-runs a safe drink program is self-explanatory, though reliable sensing and the superheating logic add difficulty.

title: Weigh-and-Go Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (A strain gauge under the tray weighs the food and sets the heating time automatically.); Strain-gauge weighing (Low-cost load cell paired with a mass-to-time lookup table.)
rationale: The food's own weight chooses the time, so the user never has to guess how many minutes to set.
judge_comment: Auto-timing from weight is plausible and removes guesswork, but weight alone is a poor proxy for food type and heating need.

title: Picture Dial
new_elements: Pictogram selector dial (Positions show a mug, a plate, a snowflake and a butter block instead of minutes and watts.)
rationale: Users pick what they are heating rather than translating it into numbers, which works for any age and any language.
judge_comment: A pictogram dial is intuitive and language-free, though the food categories are coarse and it is not very radical.

title: Steam-Sniffer Auto Stop
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor (Detects the burst of steam when food gets hot and ends the cycle.); Ends cooking when food is hot (Closed-loop stop that needs no timer setting.)
rationale: The machine knows when food is done, so the user just presses go.
judge_comment: Sensor-based auto-stop makes operation press-go simple, and similar sensor cooking already exists, but reliability for varied foods is uncertain.

title: Mug Dock
new_elements: Mug-shaped mini cavity with drop-in slot (Drop a mug in and press the lever. The small cavity is evenly heated with no turntable.)
rationale: A device built for one job and one gesture has nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A one-gesture single-purpose device removes learning, though it limits versatility and the substitution of the cavity is a big change.

title: Shrinking Light Bar
new_elements: Mechanical progress-bar window (A coloured band driven by the timer shaft shrinks as time runs out, like a sand glass.)
rationale: Remaining time can be read at a glance without interpreting a dial scale.
judge_comment: Simple mechanical progress display is easy to read and cheap, but only addresses the time-remaining part of operation.

title: Smart Containers
new_elements: Shape-keyed or RFID container set (Each bowl carries a key or tag that tells the oven to defrost, reheat or melt.)
rationale: Choosing the container is the program selection, so there are no settings.
judge_comment: Container-keyed programs make the choice of container the selection, which is intuitive and feasible with RFID, though it needs a dedicated container set.

title: Defrost Sleeve
new_elements: Partially shielding defrost sleeve (A perforated foil-laminate cover passively cuts absorbed power to about 30%.)
rationale: Users cover the food and press start, with no duty-cycle concept to understand.
judge_comment: A passive shielding cover replaces the power setting with a simple physical action and is cheap and plausible, though foil laminate in a microwave raises safety concerns.

title: +30 Seconds Big Button
new_elements: Large incrementing push button (Each press adds 30 s and pressing it alone starts the oven.)
rationale: Pressing more for more is a self-explaining interaction.
judge_comment: A single incrementing button is simple and easily built, but it is close to existing quick-start features and not very radical.

title: Push-Anywhere Door
new_elements: Push-to-open magnetic door catch (Pressing anywhere on the door releases it, so there is no button to find.)
rationale: It removes the 'how do I open this?' moment.
judge_comment: It substitutes a simple push-to-open catch for a button or handle, which removes a point of confusion, and the mechanism is plausible.

title: Elbow Bump Opener
new_elements: Large lower bump-bar release (Can be opened with an elbow or hip while both hands hold a plate.)
rationale: The obvious body motion opens the door with no fiddly button.
judge_comment: A bump-bar release is intuitive and practical with full hands, and it replaces the button simply, though it doesn't cover the rest of the operation.

title: Coded Plates
new_elements: Plates with embedded ferrite ID dots (Underside markers read through the floor auto-select the program.)
rationale: Users use 'the soup bowl' and the oven knows what to do.
judge_comment: Auto-selecting a program from the plate is a truly zero-learning idea, but ferrite markers in a microwave raise safety and sensing problems and need dedicated plates.

title: Twist-the-Handle Timer
new_elements: Rotating door handle timer (Twisting the handle sets the time, and the handle unwinds as the food cooks.)
rationale: The one part the user always touches becomes the only control.
judge_comment: Using the handle as a twist timer is a clever, intuitive merge of functions, though the mechanism and door seal add engineering complexity.

title: One Power Only
new_elements: Fixed optimal 450 W output (One power level good for reheating and tolerable for defrosting, so the power knob is deleted.)
rationale: Deleting a control is the ultimate simplification, and it is also cheaper.
judge_comment: Removing the power control is simple and cheap and clearly cuts learning, but it compromises performance and is a fairly obvious move.

title: Fill-Line Cup Timer
new_elements: Supplied mug with coloured fill lines matching knob colours (Fill to the blue line and turn the knob to blue.)
rationale: Colour matching replaces any calculation of time against volume.
judge_comment: Matching colors between mug and knob makes timing easy for one use case, but it only covers liquids in the supplied mug.

title: Clicky Detent Dial
new_elements: Detented timer knob with a click every 15 s (Users count clicks instead of reading tiny markings.)
rationale: Haptic feedback makes setting short times foolproof.
judge_comment: A cheap, plausible tactile substitute for a digital keypad, though detented timer dials already exist, so it is not radical.

title: Wind-Up Turntable Timer
new_elements: Hand-wound turntable clock spring (User twists the glass plate to wind a spring; the plate unwinds while cooking and opens the switch at zero.)
rationale: The plate you touch is also the timer, so there is no separate control to find or learn.
judge_comment: A wind-up turntable timer is charming and has no separate control, but twisting a plate that holds food, and the wind-up spring mechanism, is awkward.

title: Food Token Coins
new_elements: Picture tokens with keyed edge profile (Dropping a 'soup', 'milk' or 'leftovers' coin into a slot lets its notches set both cam time and duty cycle.); Selects a complete cooking program in one action (Time and power are chosen together by picking a picture.)
rationale: Picking a picture of the food replaces understanding minutes and watts.
judge_comment: Picture tokens remove the need to understand time and power, but they add loose parts that can be lost and limit flexibility.

title: Door-Close Auto Start
new_elements: Door-actuated start cam with default 1-minute run (Shutting the door starts a 60 s cycle; opening it cancels the cycle.)
rationale: Closing the door is the only instruction the user needs.
judge_comment: Starting on door close is the simplest possible operation and easy to build, but a fixed 60 s run may cook wrongly and it is a safety concern.

title: Steam Snap-Off
new_elements: Bimetal steam-sensing snap switch in the exhaust vent (Hot steam leaving the vent trips a bimetal disc and ends cooking.); Bimetallic snap-disc thermostat (A cheap thermostat of the kind used in kettles.)
rationale: It works like a kettle and stops by itself when the food is hot.
judge_comment: Auto-stop on steam removes time entry entirely, though steam onset varies by food and covered or dry foods would not trigger it, so safety and reliability are concerns.

title: Sand Hourglass Interlock
new_elements: Flip hourglass cartridge with light-gate cutoff (User flips a 1, 2 or 3-minute hourglass; cooking stops when a photo-gate sees the top bulb is empty.)
rationale: Remaining time is shown as falling sand, which anyone can read at a glance.
judge_comment: An hourglass is an intuitive, readable timer, but flipping it plus a photo-gate is a gimmicky substitute for a simple timer knob and offers only fixed durations.

title: Defrost Shield Dome
new_elements: Perforated metal attenuation dome accessory (A dome placed over the food passes only part of the field, giving gentle heating with no power knob.); Partial-aperture microwave attenuation (Hole size and density set the transmitted fraction of power.)
rationale: Gentle mode means putting the cover on, a physical act that needs no setting.
judge_comment: A perforated dome that gives gentle heating just by being placed over the food is a clever physical substitute for a power setting, though the power attenuation and arcing risk need work.

title: Hot/Gentle Rocker
new_elements: Two-position Hot/Gentle rocker switch (Gentle mode inserts a half-wave diode for reduced power, replacing the 5-step cam.)
rationale: Two choices are simpler than five abstract steps.
judge_comment: A two-position rocker with a diode is cheap and proven, and clearly simpler than five steps, but it is not radical.

title: Tambour Roll-Top Door
new_elements: Sliding metal tambour door in a choke channel (Slides up like a breadbox, with no hinges or latch.)
rationale: Users slide it up to open and down to close, so it is obvious at first sight.
judge_comment: Slide-up door is intuitive and removes hinge and latch, but RF choke sealing on a sliding door is tricky, though doable.

title: Bell-Jar Mesh Dome
new_elements: Liftable metal-mesh dome over a base plate (The dome is lifted off and set back down; a weight switch acts as the interlock.)
rationale: Covering the food like a cake dome is a universally understood gesture.
judge_comment: The cake-dome gesture is universally understood, and the weight-switch interlock is clever, though mesh-to-base RF sealing and safety are concerns.

title: Reflected-Power Done Detector
new_elements: Waveguide diode detector for reflected power (A rise in reflected power as water boils off triggers shutoff.); RF load-impedance sensing (A cheap Schottky detector samples standing waves in the waveguide.)
rationale: The oven knows when to stop, so the user doesn't have to.
judge_comment: Sensing reflected power to detect doneness is radical and fully automatic, but the signal is unreliable across different foods and loads.

title: Popcorn Ear
new_elements: Piezo pop-counter that stops when popping slows (A contact microphone on the cavity wall listens to the popping.)
rationale: Popcorn comes out right without the user knowing a time.
judge_comment: An acoustic pop counter is clever and workable for popcorn, but it only covers one use case, which limits its effect on general simplicity.

title: Punch-Card Recipes
new_elements: Photo recipe cards with edge notches read by feeler pins (Insert the card showing the dish to set time and power.)
rationale: Users choose a photograph rather than a setting.
judge_comment: Photo cards make setting selection intuitive and are mechanically simple, but they add cards to manage and limit flexibility.

title: RC Single Button
new_elements: One big button: each press adds 30 s (RC/555 timer) (A cheap electronic timer replaces the clockwork motor.)
rationale: 'Press more for longer' is the simplest possible rule.
judge_comment: Very simple and workable, though similar to existing add-30-seconds buttons and not very radical.

title: Tilt-to-Start Body
new_elements: Rocking base where pressing down on the top starts a 1 min tilt-switch cycle (The whole appliance acts as the button.)
rationale: There is no control to find, because the whole body is the control.
judge_comment: Whole-body tilt-switch start is radical and removes controls, though a fixed 1-minute cycle limits flexibility and a rocking base is awkward with a heavy appliance.

title: Load-Cell Floor Auto-Timer
new_elements: Load-cell cavity floor (A weighing floor replaces the turntable and measures the food mass.); Mass-to-energy cooking table (Firmware converts the measured weight into a heating time.); Automatic time from weight (The oven chooses the duration, so the user never sets it.)
rationale: The user puts food in and the oven decides how long, so there is no number to guess.
judge_comment: Weight alone is a poor proxy for the heating time of different foods, and a load-cell floor is awkward to build, though it removes the time entry.

title: Portion Slider
new_elements: 1-2-3-4 portion slider (A slider with plate pictograms sets the energy dose.); Dose by portion count (Replaces the minutes scale.)
rationale: Counting plates is easier than estimating minutes.
judge_comment: Pictogram portion slider replaces the minutes dial with an intuitive input and is easy to build, though it ignores food type and is only moderately radical.

title: Reflected-Power Auto Defrost
new_elements: Reflected RF power sensing (Detects when ice turns to water because absorption changes.); Directional coupler sensor (Sits in the waveguide and measures reflected power.); Self-adjusting power (Lowers power as the food thaws.)
rationale: Defrosting no longer needs any power-level knowledge.
judge_comment: Reflected-power sensing is plausible and removes the need to know power levels, though it is not a radical idea.

title: Cup Nook
new_elements: Dedicated mug port (A side chamber sized for one cup that heats it to 65°C when a mug is inserted.); One-motion drink reheating (Needs no button press.)
rationale: The most common use becomes simply putting the cup in.
judge_comment: A single-purpose mug port needs no learning for the most common use and is feasible with a temperature sensor, though it covers a narrow range of tasks.

title: Solid-State RF Heater
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Phase-steered RF output with closed-loop control.); Multi-antenna RF array (Replaces the magnetron, duty-cycle cam and turntable.); Uniform automatic heating (Heats evenly with no stirring or power choice.)
rationale: Hardware that finds the food and heats it evenly removes every expert setting.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF with steering can plausibly automate heating and drop settings, though cost and maturity are hurdles and it is a substitution of the core part.

title: Wear-Count Big Dial
new_elements: Oversized single-ring dial (A palm-sized dial with only the 1, 2 and 3 minute marks.); Coarse sufficient timing (Covers 90% of reheating jobs.)
rationale: Fewer choices are faster to understand.
judge_comment: A simple oversized three-mark dial is highly usable and cheap, though it is an incremental rather than radical idea.

title: Close-the-Door-to-Cook
new_elements: Door push-release button + timer knob (Base controls being substituted.); Door-close start switch (Closing the door starts a 1-minute cycle; opening it stops the cycle.); Start and stop through the door alone (The door motion is the whole interface.)
rationale: Users already open and close the door, so that action becomes the full control set.
judge_comment: Door-close start is intuitive and eliminates controls, but it risks accidental starts, empty-run damage, and a fixed 1-minute duration limits usefulness.

title: Microwave Drawer
new_elements: Hinged door + release button (Base door system being substituted.); Push-to-start drawer (Pulling the drawer out opens it; pushing it shut starts heating.)
rationale: Works like any kitchen drawer, and closing it is the start action.
judge_comment: Drawer metaphor with close-to-start is intuitive, but microwave sealing and safety interlocks in a drawer are challenging.

title: Pop-Ajar Door Finish
new_elements: Bell + manual door release (Base alert and release being substituted.); Solenoid door kicker (Nudges the door open when the cycle ends.)
rationale: An open door means done; there is no signal to learn.
judge_comment: A door that pops open when the cycle ends is a simple, clear signal, but it only affects the end of the cycle and not how the user operates it.

title: Minute Tokens
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (Base timer being substituted.); Coin slot with silicone tokens (Each token dropped in adds one minute; tokens return at the end.)
rationale: Time becomes something users can count in their hand.
judge_comment: Tokens that each add a minute are a tangible and easy-to-grasp way to set time, but they can get lost and are clumsy for small time adjustments.

title: AI Food Camera
new_elements: Lamp + knobs (Base viewing and control parts being substituted.); Cavity camera with LED flash (Recognizes the food and picks power and time automatically.); Edge image classification (On-chip neural network trained on common foods.)
rationale: The oven sees what is inside and decides, so the user only shuts the door.
judge_comment: Camera recognition with automatic settings gives true zero-learning operation, though it is already being explored and can be error-prone and costly.

title: Shape-Keyed Dishes
new_elements: Power/time knobs (Base controls being substituted.); Keyed floor recesses (A square dish base triggers soup, a round base triggers plate, an oval base triggers defrost.)
rationale: Settings work like a shape-sorter toy that a child could use.
judge_comment: The shape-sorter approach removes controls entirely and is highly novel, but it forces users to buy proprietary dishes and the mapping is limited.

title: One Power Level Only
new_elements: 5-step power knob + duty cam (Base power control being substituted.); Fixed adaptive inverter (Automatically tapers power near the end of the cycle.)
rationale: Removes an entire decision from the user.
judge_comment: Removing power choice directly eliminates a decision and an adaptive inverter is plausible, but results may vary across foods.

title: Raised Tactile Icons
new_elements: Printed knob scales (Base markings being substituted.); Molded raised-icon dial (Icons can be felt by touch, so the dial is usable with low vision.)
rationale: Works by feel for everyone, including people who cannot read the labels.
judge_comment: Raised tactile icons are practical and inclusive, but they are an incremental, well-known approach.

title: Fridge-to-Hot Button
new_elements: Time/power combination (Base manual settings being substituted.); Labelled leftovers button (One button tuned for chilled leftovers, the most common use.)
rationale: Covers the 80% use case with a single labelled press.
judge_comment: A single labelled leftovers button directly removes the learning curve and is easy to build, but it is an obvious idea and varies with food type.

title: Weigh-to-Time Spring Turntable
new_elements: Spring-scale turntable support (The roller ring sits on springs; food weight deflects a lever that sets the timer cam's start position.); Sets cooking time from food weight automatically (A heavier load gets a longer time.)
rationale: Placing the food is the entire setting step, so the user never has to guess a time.
judge_comment: Weight-based automatic timing removes the setting step, but weight maps poorly to cook time across different foods and the spring mechanism adds some complexity.

title: Flat Floor Mode Stirrer
new_elements: Hidden ceiling mode-stirrer paddle (A rotating metal paddle above the mica cover scatters the field, replacing the tray, ring and motor.)
rationale: There is no tray to seat correctly or knock off its ring, and any dish fits.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in real microwaves, and removing the tray eliminates a setup step, so it serves the need with a proven approach.

title: Pull-Cord Timer
new_elements: Pull-string spring timer (Pulling the cord further gives more time, and it rewinds as the food cooks, like a toy music box.)
rationale: The cord length is a physical, intuitive measure of time that anyone grasps instantly.
judge_comment: A mechanical pull-cord timer is intuitive and a real substitution for the keypad, but it is imprecise and the cord is a slightly odd interface.

title: Door Pops Open When Done
new_elements: Cam-released auto-opening door latch (At zero the timer cam trips the latch and a spring nudges the door ajar.)
rationale: An open door unmistakably means 'take your food', and it also airs the food.
judge_comment: Auto-opening door is simple and feasible with a cam and spring, and gives a clear done cue, but it only addresses the end of operation.

title: Clicking Detent Knob
new_elements: 10-second click-detent timer knob (Each audible, tactile click equals 10 s, with a bigger notch every minute.)
rationale: Users count clicks instead of aligning a pointer to tiny marks.
judge_comment: Easy to build and tangibly simpler than a pointer dial, but it is an incremental and fairly familiar idea.

title: Hourglass Microwave
new_elements: Flip-over sand cartridge timer (Flowing sand interrupts an optical gate, and power runs until the top bulb is empty.)
rationale: Flipping an hourglass is centuries-old knowledge, and the remaining time is literally visible.
judge_comment: Flipping an hourglass to start is intuitive, with visible time remaining, and an optical gate controlling power is plausible, though time precision and flexibility are limited.

title: Instructions on the Glass
new_elements: Printed pictogram guide on door glass (A ceramic-fired icon strip on the door shows the common food times.)
rationale: It replaces the manual with a cheat sheet that is always in view.
judge_comment: A cheat sheet printed on the glass is simple and directly helps users, but it is hardly radical.

title: Open-Door Auto-Reset
new_elements: Returns timer to zero when door opens (The interlock lever releases the cam spring so leftover time is cleared.)
rationale: There is never a confusing leftover state, because every use starts fresh.
judge_comment: Clearing leftover time removes a confusing state, and the mechanical linkage is plausible and cheap.

title: Weigh-and-Go Scale Plate
new_elements: Load-cell turntable base (Weighs the food and sets heating time automatically.); Auto-sets cooking time from weight (Removes the need to choose a time.)
rationale: The user puts the food in and the scale decides the time, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto-timing removes time selection, but weight alone poorly predicts the right heating time for different foods, and load cells add cost.

title: Solid-State GaN RF Source
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Generates 2.45 GHz from low-voltage DC without a magnetron or HV doubler.); Low-voltage RF power module (Replaces the HV diode, capacitor and transformer.)
rationale: Precise electronic power control lets the oven offer simple goal-based buttons instead of a power-level knob.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is a real, radical substitution and enables precise control, but the link to a no-learning-curve interface is indirect and costs are high.

title: Mode-Stirrer Instead of Turntable
new_elements: Hidden ceiling mode-stirrer fan (A rotating metal paddle spreads the field evenly, so there is no turntable.)
rationale: There is no plate to seat, misalign or wash, and any dish size fits.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already common and remove the turntable hassle, so it is feasible but not radical.

title: Fridge-Style Magnetic Door
new_elements: Magnetic catch door with pull handle (Replaces the push-release button and lever latch.)
rationale: Pull to open and push to close, exactly like a fridge door.
judge_comment: The fridge-door metaphor is intuitive and the swap is cheaper and simpler, though it needs a choke seal that still works with a magnetic catch and a safety interlock.

title: Rice-Cooker Lid Microwave
new_elements: Hinged top-loading lid (Gravity holds the lid shut and the choke seal is in the rim.)
rationale: It uses the familiar pot-with-lid metaphor, so nobody needs to be taught how to load it.
judge_comment: The pot-with-lid metaphor is very intuitive and fairly novel for a microwave, but a top-loading lid choke seal and a cavity that can spill make it harder to build.

title: Revolving Drum Door
new_elements: Rotating half-shell drum (The user rotates the drum to load it; the opening faces inward during cooking, so the cavity is always shielded.)
rationale: Turning the drum is a single motion that loads, seals and starts the oven.
judge_comment: A radical rotating drum that loads, seals and starts in one motion is very novel and well described, but it is mechanically complex and its claim of intuitive use is uncertain.

title: Thermochromic Done-Dot Lid
new_elements: Colour-changing temperature lid (A dot goes from blue to red at serving temperature.)
rationale: A visual readiness cue replaces trial and error.
judge_comment: A thermochromic dot gives an intuitive readiness cue and is cheap to build, but it only helps at the end of cooking and not with operating the oven.

title: Reflected-Power Arc Guard
new_elements: Detects arcing and stops (Solid-state RF source monitors reflected power.)
rationale: Removes the 'no metal' rule users must memorise.
judge_comment: Arc detection removes the 'no metal' rule and is plausible with solid-state RF, though the substitution of the source is a big cost shift and arc safety is hard to guarantee.

title: Fading Window Countdown
new_elements: Electrochromic door window (Starts opaque and clears gradually; fully clear means done.)
rationale: The food literally appears when it is ready.
judge_comment: Intuitive visual progress indicator and clever, but it adds cost and doesn't remove the need to set time or power; the 'substitute' is weak.

title: Molded Pictogram Body
new_elements: Embossed universal pictograms (Replace printed text labels; readable by touch and in any language.)
rationale: Usable by anyone regardless of language or literacy.
judge_comment: Embossed pictograms help language and touch access and are easy to make, but they are an incremental change that only affects labeling.

title: Plus-30 Single Button
new_elements: Giant +30 s push button (Each press adds 30 s at full power; a low-cost RC/counter IC times it precisely.)
rationale: A single button that means 'a bit more' requires no instructions.
judge_comment: A single +30 s button is very easy to use and feasible, though it resembles existing quick-start buttons and is not wild.

title: Weigh-to-Time Turntable
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (Strain gauge under the turntable weighs the food and sets time proportional to mass.); Mass-proportional cook timing (Time = k × grams, using a fixed k per food class.)
rationale: Users put the food in and the oven decides how long, so there is nothing to set.
judge_comment: Weighing food to set time removes settings, but mass alone is a poor predictor of cook time and a load cell adds cost, so it is only partly a cheaper substitution.

title: Window-Ring Timer
new_elements: Rotating bezel ring around door window (A large ring turned like a clock face, with a sweep indicator unwinding around the food view.)
rationale: A big clock-like ring is easy to grip and mirrors a familiar clock face.
judge_comment: A clock-face bezel timer is intuitive and plausible, though it's a modest change and not truly a substitute for a cheaper part.

title: Pop-Open When Done
new_elements: Auto door release at end of cycle (The timer cam trips the latch so the door springs ajar.)
rationale: An open door is an unmistakable 'ready' signal that also prevents forgotten food.
judge_comment: Auto-opening at cycle end gives a clear ready signal and is easy to do with a solenoid or cam, but it is not very radical and may annoy some users.

title: Roll-Top Tambour Door
new_elements: Overlapping steel-slat roll-top door (Slides up into the housing like a breadbox; overlapping choke slats keep the seal.)
rationale: There is no swing to dodge, and it works the same way as a familiar breadbox.
judge_comment: A roll-top tambour door is radical and the breadbox analogy is familiar, but sealing against microwave leakage and keeping it clean are hard problems.

title: Light-Switch Rocker Control
new_elements: Wall-switch style rocker (Up adds 1 min, down stops; it is the familiar household switch form.)
rationale: It reuses a control everyone has used thousands of times.
judge_comment: A familiar rocker switch is easy and cheap to build, but it is a modest idea and limited in control scope.

title: Shrinking Light Bar
new_elements: LED countdown bar (A bar along the door edge shrinks as time elapses, in place of dial numbers.)
rationale: Users can see progress at a glance, without glasses.
judge_comment: An intuitive visual countdown replaces numeric dials, but it's an incremental idea that doesn't change how users set the time.

title: Whistling Steam Vessel
new_elements: Kettle-whistle lid container (The lid whistles when steam builds, and a tuned sensor hears it and shuts off the magnetron.)
rationale: It borrows the universally understood kettle whistle.
judge_comment: Using a kettle-style whistle with an acoustic sensor to shut off is intuitive and novel, but it only suits steam-producing foods and acoustic detection is unreliable.

title: One-Button Oven
new_elements: Single GO button with sensor auto-cook (One button; humidity and IR sensors decide power and stop point.)
rationale: With only one control, the learning curve is effectively zero.
judge_comment: Directly targets zero learning curve, though sensor-cook single-button designs already exist.

title: Food-Recognising Camera
new_elements: Cavity camera with food classifier (Identifies the dish and its volume, then sets the program automatically.)
rationale: Users just put the food in; the oven figures out what it is.
judge_comment: Removes all input, but a camera in a microwave cavity faces heat, steam and splatter, and food classification is error-prone.

title: Hand-Approach Auto Door
new_elements: Proximity-sensed motorised door (An IR proximity sensor opens the door when a hand or dish approaches.)
rationale: It opens like a supermarket door, with nothing to press while holding a plate.
judge_comment: Easy and intuitive door opening, but it only addresses door access, not the cooking settings, and risks accidental opening.

title: Three Verb Buttons
new_elements: Melt / Warm / Cook buttons (Three oversized buttons, each with a preset duty cycle and sensor stop.)
rationale: The buttons use the words people already think in.
judge_comment: Substituting numeric keypad with verb buttons directly removes learning, but similar presets already exist and it isn't very radical.

title: Door-Close-Starts
new_elements: Latch start switch (Closing the door starts cooking, so no separate start control is needed.); Implicit start (Treats closing the door as the intent to cook.)
rationale: Putting the food in and shutting the door is the whole operation.
judge_comment: Starting on door close is simple, but it risks accidental starts and it gives no control over time or power.

title: Food-Recognising Camera
new_elements: Cavity camera (Replaces the lamp-and-window viewing setup and also identifies the dish.); On-device food recognition (A small neural network maps the dish to a heating profile.); Auto program selection (Sets time and power from what it sees.)
rationale: The oven decides the settings, so the user makes no decisions.
judge_comment: A camera that recognises food removes every decision, but reliability, cost and heat/steam robustness are concerns.

title: Pictogram Dial
new_elements: Picture dial (Shows icons (cup, plate, frozen block, popcorn) instead of minutes and power steps.); Intent-based selection (The user picks what the food is, not how to cook it.)
rationale: Icons are understood instantly, with no numbers to interpret.
judge_comment: Intent-based icons cut the learning curve and are easy to build, but similar preset dials already exist on many microwaves.

title: Auto-Pop Door
new_elements: Solenoid door kicker (Opens the door a crack when the cycle finishes, replacing the push-release button for that moment.); Completion by action (An open door clearly signals that the food is done.)
rationale: It removes the button press and makes "done" unmistakable.
judge_comment: Practical and simple, but it addresses only the end-of-cycle moment and is a modest rather than radical change to operation.

title: Slot-Machine Pull Handle
new_elements: Side pull lever (Each pull adds 30 s, replacing the clockwork knob.); Count-based timing (Time is set by number of pulls: 2 pulls = 1 minute.)
rationale: Counting pulls is easier than reading a scale.
judge_comment: Playful and mechanically simple, but counting pulls still requires learning the 30 s mapping and gives no power control.

title: Acoustic Food Listening
new_elements: Cavity microphone (Listens for popcorn pops slowing or a liquid starting to boil.); Sound-based doneness (Ends the cycle based on the sounds the food makes.)
rationale: No popcorn button or timing guesswork is needed.
judge_comment: Sound-based doneness removes the timing guesswork and is novel, but a microphone in a noisy, shielded cavity and the wide variety of foods make it unreliable.

title: Traffic Light UI
new_elements: Three-colour lamp (Replaces the incandescent lamp and the bell with lights.); Universal status code (Green means ready, amber means cooking, red means hot and done.)
rationale: Traffic-light colours are understood worldwide.
judge_comment: Easy and cheap to build and universally understood, but it only changes status feedback and does nothing for setting the cook time.

title: Fixed Gentle Power
new_elements: Slightly longer cook time (A single 500 W-equivalent power level takes longer than full power.); One-level heating (Removes the 5-step power cam entirely.)
rationale: With one power level there is no power choice to learn.
judge_comment: Removing power choice is a simple and feasible way to cut complexity, but it is not very radical and can give uneven results for some foods.

title: Lunchbox RFID Programs
new_elements: Tagged lunchboxes (Family members' boxes carry their usual meal profile.); Personal auto-cook (Each user's box heats their meal the way they like it.)
rationale: Children just put their box in.
judge_comment: Tagged lunchboxes make operation zero-step for family members, though they need a compatible container ecosystem and a reader, and the idea only loosely fits 'substitute'.

title: Container-is-the-Oven
new_elements: Susceptor packaging (The packaging self-limits its temperature through Curie-point materials.); Self-regulating food packs (Overheating is physically impossible.)
rationale: Any time setting works, so there is nothing to get wrong.
judge_comment: Self-limiting susceptor packaging removes the risk of wrong settings, but susceptors don't truly prevent overheating of the food, and it depends on special packaging.

title: Phone-Free Projected Guide
new_elements: Pico projector (Projects "put food here" and "close door" arrows on the counter and inside the cavity.); In-context guidance (Shows the user the next step in place.)
rationale: The product teaches itself as it is used.
judge_comment: In-place projected guidance teaches use without a manual, though a projector inside a microwave cavity is hard to engineer and adds cost.

title: Glanceable Face Display
new_elements: Emoji status screen (Sleeping face = idle, working face = cooking, smiling face = done, worried face = problem.); Emotional status signalling (Shows the oven's state as expressions.)
rationale: Faces are read instantly by any age or language.
judge_comment: Emoji status is cheap and instantly readable, but it only communicates state and doesn't simplify the controls.

title: Close-the-Door-to-Cook
new_elements: Door-latch start switch (Closing the door starts an auto-sensed cycle, so there is no start control at all.); Zero-input cycle start (The natural act of closing the door becomes the command.)
rationale: No button, no knob: putting food in and shutting the door is the whole interface.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start is very simple and radical, but it risks accidental starts, and the auto-sensing is vague and unsafe if the microwave is empty.

title: Hotter/Colder Single Knob
new_elements: Merged warmth knob (One knob running from 'warm' to 'piping hot' that sets energy (time × power) as a single quantity.); Express desired outcome directly (Replaces both the timer and the power cam.)
rationale: Users ask for the result they want instead of the settings that produce it.
judge_comment: A single warmth knob is intuitive and simple to build, but it is a modest change and the result depends on food quantity.

title: Package Barcode Autopilot
new_elements: Door-frame barcode scanner (Reads the ready-meal barcode as the food is inserted.); Run manufacturer's exact heating profile (No need to read the instructions on the box.); Optical code recognition (Low-cost CMOS imager.)
rationale: The food tells the microwave how to cook it.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning removes the need to read instructions for packaged meals, but it depends on a database and covers only barcoded food.

title: AI Food-Recognition Camera
new_elements: Ceiling camera with vision chip (Identifies soup, pizza, rice and other foods, plus portion size.); Automatic program selection (Replaces all user settings.); Computer vision (Edge ML classification.)
rationale: The microwave sees what you put in and handles everything else.
judge_comment: Camera-based food recognition removes all settings, but it is an obvious AI approach, is unreliable on varied foods, and costs more rather than substituting something cheaper.

title: Thermal-Camera Done Detection
new_elements: IR thermopile array (Low-resolution thermal imager watching the food surface.); Stop at target serving temperature (Replaces the clockwork timer with closed-loop control.)
rationale: Food comes out at the right temperature with no guesswork.
judge_comment: A thermopile array enables closed-loop temperature control that removes timing guesswork, though it only measures surface temperature and the user still has to start the cook.

title: Tap-the-Top Timer
new_elements: Piezo knock sensor in casing (Each tap on the lid adds 30 s at full power.); Gesture time entry (Replaces the clockwork knob.)
rationale: Counting taps is the most primitive possible interface.
judge_comment: Tapping to add time is simple and cheap, but it has little discoverability, accidental taps are a risk, and it covers only time, not power or program.

title: Fixed Flat Floor Scale
new_elements: Flush ceramic floor with mode stirrer (A hidden metal fan stirrer replaces the turntable; the floor doubles as a scale.); Wipe-clean, place-anywhere cavity (Simpler cleaning and loading.)
rationale: Users just put food anywhere inside.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers and flat-bottom microwaves already exist, so this is practical but not radical, and the scale adds little to the stated need.

title: Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Slide-out drawer cavity (Replaces the hinged door, the latch and the turntable access.); Top-down loading (Drop food in from above, like a drawer.)
rationale: Everyone already knows how to open a drawer.
judge_comment: Drawer microwaves exist as products, and the familiar drawer interaction is intuitive, but it does not address how to set power or time.

title: Countertop Cloche
new_elements: Lift-off shielded dome (Place the plate on the base and lower the dome; no box and no door.); Cover-to-heat interaction (Covering the plate starts heating.)
rationale: Putting a lid on food is an action everyone understands.
judge_comment: A radical, intuitive lid-to-heat metaphor, but a door-less shielded dome that contains microwaves safely and detects when it is covered is technically challenging.

title: Coffee Mug Port
new_elements: Dedicated mug slot (A small side cavity sized for a single mug with a fixed reheat program.); Single-purpose instant reheat (Drop the mug in and it heats.)
rationale: The most common task needs zero decisions.
judge_comment: A single-purpose mug slot removes decisions and is plausible, but it is limited in scope and not very radical.

title: Two-Button Interface
new_elements: REHEAT and DEFROST buttons (Only two large buttons, backed by sensors.); Minimal choice set (Replaces both knobs.)
rationale: A choice between two options is instantly understood.
judge_comment: Highly feasible and simple, but an incremental button reduction rather than a wild idea.

title: Automatic Popcorn Pop-Count
new_elements: Acoustic pop microphone (Stops when the gaps between pops lengthen.); Sound-based done detection (Replaces guessing popcorn time.)
rationale: Users get perfect popcorn with no burnt bags and no trial and error.
judge_comment: Acoustic pop detection is concrete and works, but it only covers popcorn and so serves general simplicity narrowly.

title: Draining Light Bar Timer
new_elements: LED progress bar on door (A glowing bar shrinks as time runs out.); Glanceable remaining time (Replaces reading the knob scale.)
rationale: Remaining time can be judged from across the room without reading numbers.
judge_comment: A shrinking LED bar is simple and glanceable, but it is incremental and only covers the time display.

title: Door-Pressure Time Setting
new_elements: Force-sensing door hinge (A gentle close gives a short cycle; a held press gives a longer one.); Close-gesture parametrisation (Combines the door, start control and timer.)
rationale: One natural motion carries the whole command.
judge_comment: Encoding time in how the door is closed is radical and elegant, but it is hard to discover, imprecise, and awkward to make reliable.

title: E-Ink Door Coach
new_elements: E-ink door panel (Shows 'stir now' or 'let stand 1 min' at the right moment.); Just-in-time coaching (Replaces the user's need to know the procedure.)
rationale: Knowledge lives on the machine, not in the user.
judge_comment: Just-in-time prompts on an e-ink door reduce needed knowledge, though stir timing is preset rather than sensed and it adds cost rather than substituting a part.

title: Smart Plate Remote
new_elements: Plate with embedded button (The bundled plate's rim button starts the oven wirelessly when placed inside.); Object-as-controller (Replaces the control panel.)
rationale: The control sits in the user's hand, on the thing being heated.
judge_comment: A plate whose button starts the oven replaces the control panel with an intuitive object, though the wireless link and the plate being bundled add complexity and a lost-plate risk.

title: Wireless Power Lid Containers
new_elements: Sensor-lid containers (Lids harvest RF energy to report steam pressure and temperature to the oven.); In-food feedback loop (Replaces the timer with direct sensing.)
rationale: Users put the lid on and the system decides the rest.
judge_comment: Put the lid on and the oven senses the food, which removes settings entirely, but RF-harvesting sensor lids in a microwave cavity are technically very hard and costly, and not simpler or cheaper.

title: Picture-Dial Power Selector
new_elements: Pictogram food-type dial (One dial with icons (drink, reheat, defrost, popcorn) that sets both power level and duration internally.)
rationale: Users choose what the food is instead of a wattage, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Food-type icon dial is intuitive and easy to build, but similar presets already exist on many microwaves, so it is not radical.

title: Weight-Sensing Turntable
new_elements: Load cell under turntable (Weighs the food and computes the heating time automatically.)
rationale: The oven decides the time, so the user never has to estimate it.
judge_comment: A load cell for automatic timing is plausible and removes the need to estimate time, but weight alone is a poor proxy for food type and adds cost.

title: Flatbed Rotating Antenna
new_elements: Under-floor rotating antenna (A hidden spinning antenna below a flat ceramic floor replaces the glass turntable.)
rationale: A flat floor fits any dish and wipes clean, with no parts to reassemble.
judge_comment: Rotating-antenna designs with a flat floor already exist on the market, and the idea reduces fuss, but it is not about operation.

title: Arc-Watch Photodiode
new_elements: Arc-detecting photodiode (Senses arc flashes and cuts RF within milliseconds, then flashes a fork icon.)
rationale: Mistakes are caught by the machine rather than by memorised rules.
judge_comment: Arc detection is a clever safety net that removes a rule to memorize, but it only addresses one narrow mistake and is hard to implement reliably.

title: Susceptor Crisping Plate
new_elements: Susceptor-coated turntable plate (A thin metallised ceramic layer gets hot in the RF field and browns food from below.)
rationale: Food crisps automatically without a separate grill mode to learn.
judge_comment: Susceptor plates already exist and do reduce the need for a grill mode, but this is not radical and only partly serves the simplicity need.

title: Color Halo Status Ring
new_elements: Door-frame LED halo (Glows red while heating and green when done, replacing the bell.)
rationale: Traffic-light colors are understood instantly by anyone.
judge_comment: A color status ring is easy to understand and build, but it is a minor, incremental feedback change that leaves the controls unchanged.

title: Mug-Only Microwave
new_elements: Single-cup RF chamber (A cylinder that fits one mug or bowl, with a single heat button.)
rationale: Stripped to one use case, it has nothing to learn.
judge_comment: A single-button mug-only unit is very simple to use, but it is limited in function and resembles existing compact microwaves.

title: Continuous Inverter Power
new_elements: Switch-mode inverter magnetron drive (Truly variable power replaces the duty-cycle cam.)
rationale: Even heating at any setting means fewer surprises and less fiddling.
judge_comment: Inverter microwaves already exist and give more even heating, but the link to zero learning curve is indirect and the part is not cheaper.

title: Drink Button Pulse Mode
new_elements: Pulse-pause liquid heating (A dedicated cup icon heats in bursts with rests to avoid superheating.)
rationale: Safe drinks need no expert know-how.
judge_comment: A one-button drink mode directly lowers the learning curve and is easy to build, but it is more a feature addition than a substitution and is not very radical.

title: Food-Projected Timer
new_elements: Ceiling pico-projector (Projects remaining time and doneness icons onto the food itself, visible through the window.)
rationale: Information appears exactly where the user is looking.
judge_comment: Projecting the timer onto the food is a novel and concrete way to show status, but it only adds feedback and leaves the controls as complex as before; it also adds cost and can be hard to see on some foods.

title: Close-to-Cook Door
new_elements: Door-actuated start switch (Closing the door starts the last-used or preset cycle; opening it stops cooking instantly.)
rationale: Shutting the door is the only action needed, which everyone already knows how to do.
judge_comment: Door-close start removes all steps, but risks accidental starts on empty or unsuitable loads and needs a safe default cycle.

title: Magnet-Held Door
new_elements: Magnetic door catch with pull handle (Fridge-style magnets hold the door shut and a reed switch acts as the safety interlock.)
rationale: The door opens with a simple pull, as a fridge does, and no hidden release button is involved.
judge_comment: A magnetic catch with a reed switch is plausible and makes opening intuitive, though it only touches a small part of operation, and the safety interlock needs care.

title: Gravity Top-Loader
new_elements: Lift-up gravity-closing lid (A top-loading lid falls shut under its own weight, removing the need for a latch.)
rationale: Food drops in from above like a pot onto a stove, and the lid cannot be left ajar.
judge_comment: A self-closing top-loading lid is intuitive and removes the latch step, though it has spill, ergonomics and safety interlock issues.

title: Revolving Drum Cavity
new_elements: Rotating half-shell drum (Rotating the drum 180° turns its open side away from the user into a shielded housing; there is no door.)
rationale: A single spin both closes the oven and starts cooking.
judge_comment: Doorless rotating drum that closes and starts in one motion is wild and intuitive, but sealing microwaves and food spillage in a rotating cavity is hard.

title: Wind-Up Spring Timer
new_elements: Clockwork spring escapement timer (Replaces the synchronous motor, so the same part works on any mains frequency.)
rationale: The kitchen-timer twist is universally familiar and behaves identically in every region.
judge_comment: A wind-up mechanical timer is familiar and feasible, but it is a common old design and the mains-frequency rationale is only weakly tied to ease of use.

title: Wave-to-Open
new_elements: IR proximity door opener (A hand wave triggers a solenoid that releases the door.)
rationale: The door opens hands-free even when the user is carrying a plate.
judge_comment: A wave-to-open door is feasible and convenient, but a gesture is less discoverable than a button and it does not address the rest of the operation.

title: Shrinking Light Ring
new_elements: LED countdown ring around door (A ring of light shrinks as the remaining time decreases.)
rationale: Remaining time can be read from across the room without reading any numbers.
judge_comment: An intuitive shrinking light ring communicates time without numbers, which is easy to implement, though it adds a part rather than substituting a simpler one.

title: Talking Guide
new_elements: Voice prompt speaker (Announces 'two minutes, medium heat' as the dial turns and says 'ready' at the end.)
rationale: Spoken feedback confirms every action for low-vision or uncertain users.
judge_comment: Voice feedback reduces uncertainty and is very feasible, but it is a common, non-radical feature and adds a part rather than simplifying one.

title: Lift-Off Magnetic Lid
new_elements: Detachable magnetic door panel (The door has no hinges and magnetically self-aligns, sensed by a Hall-effect interlock.)
rationale: The door works like a pot lid that cannot be put on wrong.
judge_comment: A magnetic self-aligning lid with a Hall sensor simplifies door use and is feasible, but it is only an incremental change in operation and a loose lid could be a safety concern.

title: Tactile Minute Notches
new_elements: Detented knob with raised bumps (Each click is one minute and is felt rather than read.)
rationale: Users can count clicks, which works even with poor eyesight.
judge_comment: Easy to build and helps accessibility, but it is a modest tweak to a knob and does not remove the need to choose a time.

title: Dish-Coded Programs
new_elements: Coded cookware set (Mug, bowl and plate each carry magnets in their base that a reed array reads as a program.); Magnetic reed code sensing (Reed switches beneath the cavity floor read the magnet pattern.)
rationale: Choosing the dish is the whole interface: a mug heats like a drink and a bowl heats like soup.
judge_comment: Dish choice as the interface is clever, but it requires proprietary cookware, and magnets near the microwave field are problematic; users may also lose pieces.

title: Bimetal 'Cook-Till-Hot' Plate
new_elements: Under-tray snap-disc cutoff (A bimetallic disc touching the tray underside clicks the oven off when the dish reaches serving temperature, like a rice cooker.)
rationale: A single 'on' switch replaces time arithmetic, using a cheap part the oven already relies on.
judge_comment: A rice-cooker-style thermal cutoff is an appealing single-switch idea, but measuring food temperature through the tray underside is unreliable, and arcing and the varied dishes used with it are concerns.

title: LED Status Lamp
new_elements: Colour-state LED (One RGB LED lights the cavity: warm white while cooking, green when done.)
rationale: Light colour tells the user the oven's state without any reading or interpretation.
judge_comment: A colour-coded LED is cheap and easy to build and gives a simple state cue, but it is a fairly obvious idea.

title: Talk-to-Heat
new_elements: Offline voice chip (A fixed-vocabulary speech recognizer understands phrases like 'warm my coffee' or 'defrost'.); Keyword speech recognition (Low-cost on-device recognition that needs no cloud connection.)
rationale: Saying what you want requires no learning at all.
judge_comment: Offline keyword voice control removes the learning curve, though it is not especially cheap and the noise and accent handling are concerns.

title: Pictogram Buttons
new_elements: Three picture buttons (Three buttons marked Cup, Plate and Snowflake each trigger a preset program.)
rationale: Picture symbols replace two abstract knobs.
judge_comment: Simple and cheap, but pictogram presets are already common and not radical.

title: Hidden Mode Stirrer
new_elements: Roof mode-stirrer fan (A metal paddle in the roof scatters the field so the food stays still.)
rationale: There is no tray or ring to seat correctly or lose, and any dish fits.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in real microwaves and remove the turntable hassle, but they do little for the control interface.

title: Under-Floor Rotating Antenna
new_elements: Rotating floor antenna (A spinning radiator below a flat ceramic floor distributes the energy.)
rationale: The flat floor means nothing needs aligning, and the user just puts the food in.
judge_comment: Rotating antennas under a flat ceramic floor already ship in commercial ovens, so it is practical and clear but only modestly simplifies use.

title: Package Barcode Cooking
new_elements: Door-mounted barcode reader (Reads the ready-meal barcode and loads the manufacturer's cooking program.)
rationale: The user shows the packet to the oven and presses go, with no need to read instructions.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning removes reading instructions, but depends on a manufacturer program database and works only for packaged meals.

title: Twist-Handle Timer
new_elements: Rotating door handle timer (Twisting the door handle sets the time, and closing the door starts cooking.)
rationale: All operation happens at the one place the hand already goes.
judge_comment: Merging timer and door handle into one intuitive gesture is quite elegant, though the mechanical integration with the door latch and safety interlocks is challenging.

title: E-Ink Door Status
new_elements: E-ink door panel (Shows plain words, 'HEATING 1:20' or 'READY - HOT', and holds the message after power-off.)
rationale: Plain-language status needs no symbols to decode.
judge_comment: Plain-word e-ink status is clear and plausible, but it only helps with feedback and does not simplify input.

title: Close-Door Auto Start
new_elements: Starts on door close (Closing the door after loading starts a default 'warm' cycle with no button.)
rationale: Zero buttons means zero learning.
judge_comment: Starting on door close removes all controls and is radical, but it raises safety problems such as starting with an empty cavity or the wrong cook level.

title: Weighing Turntable Sets the Time
new_elements: Strain-gauge load cell (A low-cost scale built under the turntable hub.); Weighing turntable (Measures the food mass and sets the heating time automatically.); Auto-derive cook time from mass (Replaces the user's guess on the timer dial.); User must guess minutes (The 0-30 min dial gives no guidance on how long to heat.)
rationale: The oven decides how long to heat, so the user never has to estimate a time.
judge_comment: A load cell removes time guessing, but mass alone is a poor predictor of heating time for different foods and adds cost, so it may not truly substitute a timer.

title: Toaster Lever Microwave
new_elements: Push-down lever timer (Pressing the lever deeper sets a longer time; the lever pops up when the food is done.); Toaster-familiar time setting (Borrows a mental model nearly everyone already knows.); Two separate knobs confuse users (Having both a power knob and a timer knob splits one task into two decisions.)
rationale: Users already know how to operate a toaster lever, so there is zero learning curve.
judge_comment: The toaster-lever mental model is familiar and mechanically simple, but it is a fairly modest idea and it is unclear how power level is handled.

title: Steam-Sensing Auto Stop
new_elements: Humidity sensing (A capacitive humidity sensor placed in the exhaust vent.); Vent humidity sensor (Detects the rise in steam that signals the food is hot.); Stop when food is hot (Replaces the mechanical end-of-timer cut-off.); Over- or under-heating from wrong time (A fixed timer cannot adapt to how the food is actually heating.)
rationale: The machine knows when food is ready, so the user does nothing beyond pressing go.
judge_comment: Vent humidity sensing makes the oven self-terminating and removes time entry, but accuracy varies for dry or covered foods; sensor-cooking exists in premium models.

title: Auto-Pop Door
new_elements: Spring door kicker (The door unlatches and swings open a few centimetres when cooking ends.); Physical done signal (Replaces the bell and invites the user to remove the food.); Bell missed in another room (Food is forgotten and goes cold when the bell is not heard.)
rationale: An open door means 'done' without any explanation.
judge_comment: A spring-kicked door is a cheap and intuitive done signal, but it only helps at the end of cooking and does little to simplify operation.

title: Frost-Detecting Auto Defrost
new_elements: IR cold-spot detector (Detects frozen food and pulses power automatically.); Automatic defrost mode (Replaces the manual 'defrost' setting on the power knob.); Users forget to switch to defrost (Frozen food heated at full power cooks at the edges while the centre stays frozen.)
rationale: The oven sees that the food is frozen, so the user does not need to know about defrost mode.
judge_comment: Auto-detecting frozen food removes a real knowledge barrier, but IR sensing of internal frost is imperfect and adds cost.

title: Packaging Punch-Card Slot
new_elements: Card slot reader (A tear-off notched strip from the food packaging is inserted to set time and power mechanically.); Manufacturer-set program (The food maker encodes the correct settings on the strip.); Reading package instructions (Small print on packaging must be interpreted and transferred to the knobs.)
rationale: Inserting a card is as easy as posting a letter.
judge_comment: Mechanical card reading removes dial-setting but needs industry-wide packaging adoption, and the 'reading small print' element actually adds a step.

title: Weight-Loss Moisture Stop
new_elements: Precision hub scale (Tracks the mass lost as steam during heating.); Stop at target evaporation (Ends heating when the food is hot but not dried out.); Dried-out reheated food (Overshooting the time leaves food dry and rubbery.)
rationale: Good results come automatically without any skill from the user.
judge_comment: Weight-loss sensing is a real approach to automatic doneness, but a scale adds cost and is a poor fit for non-evaporating foods.

title: Spoken Done Announcement
new_elements: Voice chip speaker (Says 'Your food is ready, stir and enjoy' instead of ringing a bell.); Explicit guidance at completion (Tells the user what to do next.); Bell carries no instructions (A bell does not say whether the food should be stirred or rested.)
rationale: Instructions are delivered at exactly the moment they are needed.
judge_comment: A helpful, easily built voice prompt, but it only aids the end of the cycle and does little for operation itself.

title: Same-Again Memory
new_elements: Weight-keyed memory chip (Recognises a repeat item, such as the same mug weight, and reuses the last successful setting.); Learned personal presets (The machine learns instead of the user.); Re-entering settings daily (The same knob ritual is repeated every morning.)
rationale: The learning curve shifts from the human to the appliance.
judge_comment: Learned presets cut repeated input, but weight-based recognition is unreliable and the idea is not much of a cheap substitution.

title: Mug Slot Microwave
new_elements: Dedicated top mug well (A small shielded well on top heats a single drink when the mug is dropped in.); One-gesture drink warming (Handles the most common use case without the main door or knobs.); Full process for a tiny task (Reheating one coffee needs the same steps as a whole meal.)
rationale: Dropping a mug in is self-evident.
judge_comment: A drop-in mug well is intuitive and bold, though shielding, safety, and liquid detection are challenges and it covers only one use case.

title: One Giant +30s Button
new_elements: Single oversized +30 s push pad (Each press adds 30 s at full power; one interface element replaces both knobs.)
rationale: Counting presses is something anyone can do immediately.
judge_comment: Very easy to use and cheap, but already common on many microwaves and not radical.

title: Recipe Key Tokens
new_elements: Shaped plastic food tokens (Pictogram keys (cup, bowl, plate, frozen) whose notch profile mechanically sets the time and power cams.); Coded-key cam actuation (Key notches act directly on cam followers.)
rationale: Choosing a picture of a cup is easier than combining a time setting with a power setting.
judge_comment: A mechanical pictogram key replaces dials in an inventive way, but the user must still pick and handle tokens, which are easily lost and limited in coverage.

title: Talk-to-Heat Voice Control
new_elements: Offline voice command module (Recognises a small fixed vocabulary such as 'warm my coffee' or 'two minutes'.); Embedded keyword speech recognition (Low-cost microcontroller ASR with no cloud connection.)
rationale: Speaking a request needs no learning at all, including for elderly users.
judge_comment: Voice control fits zero-learning well and offline keyword ASR is cheap and feasible, though not very radical and the fixed vocabulary must be learned.

title: Push-to-Open Touch Latch
new_elements: Push-push cabinet touch latch (Pressing anywhere on the door pops it open; there is no separate button.)
rationale: The door opens with a push of an elbow, even with full hands and no button to find.
judge_comment: Simple and cheap mechanism that removes the button-finding step, but it only addresses opening the door, not operation.

title: Fridge-Style Magnetic Door
new_elements: Magnetic door seal with reed-switch interlock (Magnets hold the door shut; the user simply pulls it open.)
rationale: Everyone already knows how to open a fridge.
judge_comment: A fridge-style magnetic door is familiar and intuitive, but magnetic seals are weak against microwave leakage and safety interlock requirements, and it is not very radical.

title: Bell-Jar Dome Microwave
new_elements: Lift-off mesh dome over base plate (A cake-cover-like transparent shielded dome; its weight closes the interlock.)
rationale: Lift the dome, place the plate, lower the dome: there are no mechanisms to learn.
judge_comment: A lift-off dome is very simple to understand, but a large mesh dome has leakage, heat, and weight issues and may be unsafe when lifted.

title: Light-Not-Bell Finish
new_elements: Glowing door-frame status ring (An electroluminescent strip is red while cooking and green when done, replacing the bell as the main cue.)
rationale: Traffic-light colours are universally understood and visible across the room.
