judge_comment: Easy and intuitive status cue, though a simple LED ring is hardly radical and it doesn't address input operation.

title: Inverter Smooth Power
new_elements: Inverter magnetron supply with auto-power (Continuously variable power chosen automatically from load; no power knob.); High-frequency inverter power supply (Replaces the heavy transformer and on/off cycling.)
rationale: One fewer control, and the oven never needs a power decision from the user.
judge_comment: Inverter tech already exists; automatic power removes a decision, which modestly supports simplicity.

title: Slot-Machine Lever
new_elements: Side lever: up opens door, down sets time (One lever replaces both the release button and the timer knob.)
rationale: A single control with two obvious directions covers the whole interaction.
judge_comment: A single two-direction lever is intuitive and simplifies the controls, though setting the time by lever could be imprecise.

title: Twin-Chamber Gentle/Strong
new_elements: Two stacked cavities with fixed power (The top cavity is fixed for defrost/gentle heating and the bottom for full power, fed by a split waveguide.)
rationale: Choosing which door to use is the power choice.
judge_comment: Choosing a door instead of a power setting is intuitive and radical, but two cavities with a split waveguide add cost and complexity, which runs against the substitute operator.

title: Food-Recognition Camera
new_elements: Cavity camera with food recognition (Identifies the dish and its portion, then sets time and power automatically.); Edge AI image classification (Low-cost vision chip.)
rationale: The microwave figures out what the food is and how to heat it.
judge_comment: Fully automatic operation best removes the learning curve, but it is costly, not a cheaper or simpler substitution, and similar concepts already exist.

title: Power by Knob Removal
new_elements: Fixed full power plus a 'defrost' toggle snowflake (The 5-step cam becomes a single snowflake switch.)
rationale: Two states covering the jobs people actually do are simpler than five abstract levels.
judge_comment: A fixed full power setting with a defrost toggle is simple and cheap, but it is a modest simplification and not radical.

title: Audio Talking Knob
new_elements: Knob with spoken feedback (Announces 'one minute', 'two minutes' and so on as it turns, and 'ready' at the end.)
rationale: Spoken confirmation removes any need to read small markings.
judge_comment: Spoken feedback makes the knob easier for people with poor vision, but it adds a part instead of substituting a simpler one and is not very radical.

title: Hand-Hover Gesture
new_elements: IR proximity gesture sensor (A wave opens the door via a solenoid latch, and each further wave adds 30 s.)
rationale: Touch-free operation is as natural as an automatic tap.
judge_comment: Wave control is touch-free and concrete, but counting waves and relying on hidden gestures can be less intuitive than a simple button.

title: One Knob, Food Pictures
new_elements: Single pictogram dial (One knob with food icons (cup, plate, frozen meal, popcorn); each detent sets a coupled time and power cam profile.)
rationale: Users pick a picture of their food instead of translating it into minutes and power levels, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Pictogram dial is easy to understand and highly buildable, but similar auto-cook presets already exist and it is not very radical.

title: Toaster-Style Pop-Up Drawer
new_elements: Spring-loaded shielded drawer (Pushing the drawer in latches it and starts cooking; it pops out when time ends.)
rationale: It borrows the universally known toaster gesture: push in to start, and it pops out when done.
judge_comment: The toaster metaphor is very novel and intuitive, but shielding microwaves and handling liquids in a pop-out drawer is hard.

title: Time Tokens
new_elements: Token slot timer (Users drop a large, labelled, coin-like token whose diameter sets the cam timer (S, M, L).)
rationale: A tangible, label-free action suits elderly or cognitively impaired users.
judge_comment: A tangible token interface is simple for vulnerable users and cheap, but it adds loose parts that can get lost and offers coarse timing.

title: RC Chip Timer
new_elements: 555-based potentiometer timer (A cents-level timer IC with a pot knob replaces the clockwork, precise down to 5 s.)
rationale: It keeps the familiar single knob but makes short reheats predictable.
judge_comment: A 555 timer with a pot knob keeps the single-knob familiarity and is very feasible, but it is mundane and mainly improves precision.

title: Heat/Defrost Rocker
new_elements: Two-position rocker switch (A full/defrost toggle replaces the 5-step cam.)
rationale: Users understand two modes; five abstract power levels confuse them.
judge_comment: A two-mode rocker is simple and understandable but is a modest simplification that lacks radicalness.

title: Package Barcode Scanner
new_elements: Front barcode reader (Scanning a ready-meal pack loads the manufacturer's heating instructions.)
rationale: It eliminates reading tiny print and translating it into settings.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning removes manual setting for ready meals, but it only works for packaged foods and adds a component rather than substituting a simpler one.

title: Top-Loading Pot Lid
new_elements: Gravity-closed top lid (Food is lowered in from above; the lid's weight seals the choke and closes the interlock.)
rationale: It works like a saucepan lid, which everyone understands, with no latch or button.
judge_comment: A top-loading lid uses a familiar saucepan metaphor and removes the latch, but loading and placing food is awkward and the seal needs careful engineering.

title: Auto-Pop Door at Done
new_elements: Signals completion by opening the door (A spring kicker releases the latch at the end of the cycle.)
rationale: An open door means 'done' unmistakably, even for hard-of-hearing users.
judge_comment: A spring-kicker door pop is a feasible, intuitive done signal that replaces the bell, though it does little for setting up the cook.

title: Linear Gravity Slider
new_elements: Vertical damped slider timer (The user lifts a slider; it sinks slowly through viscous damping, and its height shows the time left.)
rationale: Higher means longer, a spatial mapping that needs no explanation.
judge_comment: A damped slider whose height shows remaining time is an intuitive spatial mapping, and the viscous damping is plausible, though accuracy and start/stop sensing need engineering.

title: Door-Handle Twist Timer
new_elements: Rotary door handle timer (Twisting the handle after closing the door sets the time; twisting back opens the door.)
rationale: Merging opening and timing into a single object halves the number of controls.
judge_comment: Merging the door handle with the timer cuts the number of controls and is intuitive, but twisting back to open may cancel or confuse the cook state.

title: Tactile Braille Dial
new_elements: Detented raised-icon dial (Strong clicks per minute plus raised shapes allow operation by touch.)
rationale: Counting clicks is easy for low-vision and elderly users.
judge_comment: A detented tactile dial makes operation intuitive by touch, but it is an incremental, fairly familiar improvement.

title: Just-Press-Start Microwave
new_elements: Single start button with combined sensing (One button plus steam and weight sensors handle all time and power decisions.)
rationale: One button is the absolute minimum interface, giving a true zero learning curve.
judge_comment: A single start button with sensors is the most direct route to zero learning curve and is quite feasible, but it's an established concept and so not very radical.

title: Steam-Stop Sensor
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor (Detects the burst of steam released by hot food and then cuts power.); Stops heating when food is hot (Closed-loop end point that replaces a guessed duration.)
rationale: The user never has to guess a time, because the oven stops when the food steams.
judge_comment: Steam-based auto-stop is closed-loop and needs no input, but it fails on foods that don't steam and on food that is only being warmed.

title: Push-to-Open Door
new_elements: Touch-latch door (A push-push latch, like a kitchen cabinet: press the door to pop it open, press again to close.)
rationale: There is no separate button to find, because the door itself is the control.
judge_comment: Push-push latches are common on appliances and cabinets, and the idea only simplifies door opening, not the whole operation.

title: Fixed Floor with Mode Stirrer
new_elements: Ceiling mode-stirrer fan (A rotating metal paddle scrambles the standing waves. The floor is a flat, fixed ceramic surface.)
rationale: With no tray to seat, wobble or lose, users simply put the plate down anywhere.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are a real, proven substitute for turntables and remove the tray, but they only marginally reduce the operating learning curve and aren't very radical.

title: Rotating Antenna Instead of Plate
new_elements: Under-floor rotating antenna (A slow-turning radiator below the ceramic floor sweeps the field pattern instead of turning the food.)
rationale: Large or oddly shaped dishes fit without jamming, so the user has nothing to think about.
judge_comment: Under-floor rotating antennas exist in commercial units; it removes the plate-fit issue but has little effect on controls simplicity.

title: Talk-to-Heat
new_elements: Offline voice command module (Understands phrases like 'warm my coffee' or 'defrost chicken' without any cloud connection.)
rationale: Speaking a natural request takes no training at all.
judge_comment: Offline voice control is natural and plausible, though noise, accents, and a limited phrase vocabulary can still frustrate users.

title: Auto-Pop Door at Done
new_elements: Solenoid door kicker (At the end of the cycle the door springs ajar slightly, signalling done and stopping overcooking.)
rationale: An open door means 'take your food', which is unmistakable and leaves nothing to remember.
judge_comment: A solenoid door pop is feasible and a clear done signal, but it only helps with end-of-cycle and doesn't address how to operate the oven.

title: Steam Whistle Alert
new_elements: Passive steam whistle in vent (Food steam passing through a tuned reed whistles like a kettle when the food is hot.)
rationale: It borrows the universally understood kettle signal, so 'whistle = hot' needs no explanation.
judge_comment: A passive whistle replaces an electronic beeper with a familiar cue, though it only works for steaming foods and doesn't simplify input.

title: Defrost Dome Instead of Power Knob
new_elements: Partial-shield defrost cover (A microwave-safe lid with a printed metal grid lets through about 30% of the power. Covering the food means defrost or melt.)
rationale: A physical 'gentle lid' replaces an abstract power scale that many users never understand.
judge_comment: A physical lid that attenuates power is a clever substitute for a power setting, but a printed metal grid in a microwave risks arcing and the user must still know when to use the lid.

title: Electronic Mains-Count Timer
new_elements: Mains-cycle counting timer chip (A cheap IC counts 50 or 60 Hz cycles for exact short durations, driven by the same single knob.)
rationale: Short heats give the same result every time, so users don't have to learn the dial's quirks.
judge_comment: A cheap mains-count IC replaces a mechanical timer, which fits the substitute operator, but users see little change in learning.

title: Defrost-by-Frost Sensing
new_elements: IR ice-detection camera (Detects surfaces below 0 °C and automatically runs gentle cycling until they are thawed.)
rationale: Frozen food is recognised automatically, so there is no defrost menu to learn.
judge_comment: Auto-detecting frozen food removes the defrost menu, though IR only sees surface temperature and adds cost.

title: No-Choice Fixed Power
new_elements: Food-adaptive fixed power cam (Removes the power knob. The first 20% of the cycle runs at low power, then switches to full power, which suits nearly all foods.)
rationale: Deleting a decision is the ultimate simplification, and the BOM also gets cheaper.
judge_comment: Removing power choice cuts decisions and cost, though one fixed profile may give poor results for some foods.

title: Close-the-Door-to-Cook
new_elements: Door-start interlock (Closing the door starts a default 1-minute cycle; opening it stops cooking.); Starts cooking on door closure (The door's own motion becomes the start command.)
rationale: Users already close the door, so starting the cook on closure removes the start step entirely.
judge_comment: Removes the start step, but accidental starts (including an empty microwave) are a safety issue and a default 1-minute cycle won't suit every food.

title: Picture-Dial Knob
new_elements: Pictogram food knob (Detents marked cup, plate, bowl, frozen block and butter instead of minutes.)
rationale: Pointing at a picture of what you are heating needs no knowledge of minutes or watts.
judge_comment: Intuitive and cheap mechanical substitute for time entry, but the fixed presets are imprecise and the idea is only moderately novel.

title: Thermochromic Ready Lid
new_elements: Thermochromic splatter cover (A microwave-safe lid that changes from blue to red at 65 °C.)
rationale: A colour change shows readiness at a glance instead of requiring the user to watch and judge the food.
judge_comment: A readiness cue is useful, but it does not simplify operating the controls and the lid is an add-on.

title: Push-to-Start Drawer
new_elements: Sliding drawer cavity (Drawer runners replace hinges, and pushing the drawer shut starts heating.)
rationale: 'Push the drawer in, food heats' is a single intuitive gesture.
judge_comment: Drawer with push-to-start is intuitive and radical, but start-without-time-setting and door seal/choke design are challenges.

title: Barcode-Reading Microwave
new_elements: Fascia barcode scanner (Hold a ready-meal package to the scanner and the time and power are set from a database.)
rationale: No one has to read the tiny instructions on the packet.
judge_comment: A barcode scanner removes reading the packet instructions, but it needs a database and only covers packaged foods, so it adds a step for other food.

title: Front Reset Breaker
new_elements: Front-panel resettable thermal breaker (Replaces the buried ceramic fuse with a pop-out reset button.)
rationale: A fault becomes 'press the red button' instead of calling a technician.
judge_comment: A front reset button is simple and feasible, but it is only an incremental change and addresses rare fault events rather than everyday operation.

title: Portion Chips
new_elements: Insertable portion chips (Small, medium and large coloured chips slot in to set the power level.)
rationale: Power becomes 'how much food' in plain physical terms.
judge_comment: Physical chips that map power to portion size are intuitive and easy to build, though small chips could be lost and the setup is still a step.

title: Traffic-Light Ring
new_elements: RGB status light ring (Red means heating, green means ready, blinking means stir.)
rationale: Traffic-light colours are universally understood.
judge_comment: A status light ring is simple and easy to understand, but it is an obvious feedback add-on that does not simplify input.

title: Hand-Wave Start
new_elements: IR proximity gesture sensor (Each wave over the top adds 30 s.)
rationale: It works with messy hands and no targeting, which is natural for elderly users.
judge_comment: Wave-to-add-time is no-learning and hands-free friendly, but the lack of feedback or precision may cause confusion.

title: Solid-State GaN RF Engine
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Generates 2.45 GHz at about 50 V, so no kV doubler is needed.)
rationale: Fine, continuous power control makes one-touch automatic programs possible and removes the lethal stored charge.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is a real and radical substitution, but it serves simplicity only indirectly and is costly today.

title: Three Pictogram Buttons
new_elements: Defrost / Reheat / Cook icon buttons (Three large picture buttons replace the 5-step power knob.)
rationale: Users choose an intention from a picture instead of decoding wattage steps.
judge_comment: Intent-based picture buttons clearly simplify operation and substitute the power knob, but this is a fairly incremental and common approach.

title: Glowing Door Status
new_elements: Edge-lit door frame LED (Shows red while heating, green when done and amber for 'stir me'.)
rationale: Its traffic-light colours can be read from across the room without any learning.
judge_comment: A traffic-light door frame is intuitive and concrete, but it is mostly a status indicator and does not make operation itself simpler.

title: Microwave Drawer
new_elements: Slide-out cavity drawer (Pushing the drawer closed seals it and starts the cycle.)
rationale: A drawer is the most familiar household motion, and there is no latch button to find.
judge_comment: A drawer that starts on closing is a familiar, button-free action, but sealing against microwave leakage and auto-start safety are engineering challenges.

title: Push-to-Open Magnetic Door
new_elements: Magnetic push-latch (Pressing anywhere on the door releases it, replacing the lever button.)
rationale: The whole door is the button, so there is nothing to locate.
judge_comment: Push-latch doors are proven and make opening intuitive, though it is an incremental substitution rather than a radical one.

title: Resonant Inverter Supply
new_elements: Resonant inverter HV supply (A lightweight switched-mode supply replaces the transformer and doubler.)
rationale: True low-power heating replaces on/off cycling, so a 'gentle' setting simply works.
judge_comment: Inverter microwaves already exist (e.g., Panasonic); it makes low-power settings work properly, which modestly helps intuitive use.

title: Gravity Flap Door
new_elements: Top-hinged gravity flap (Lifts up and falls shut by its own weight, with no latch.)
rationale: The door cannot be left half-closed and needs no button.
judge_comment: A latchless gravity door removes a step, but microwave safety interlocks and leakage standards make it hard to certify, and the substitution is wild yet clear.

title: Top-Loading Lid Seal
new_elements: Top lid with conductive gasket (Seals like a rice-cooker lid instead of using a quarter-wave choke door.)
rationale: It uses a familiar pot-lid gesture and lets the user drop food in from above.
judge_comment: A familiar rice-cooker lid gesture is intuitive, but top-loading and gasket sealing raise leakage and spill concerns.

title: AI Camera Chef
new_elements: Cavity camera with food recognition (Recognises the dish and sets the program.)
rationale: The machine sees the food and needs no input.
judge_comment: Camera-based food recognition fully removes user input and fits the need well, but it is already known and has reliability and cost challenges.

title: Knee-Bump Door Release
new_elements: Low front bump bar (A hip or knee bump opens the door when the user's hands are full.)
rationale: It opens with a natural body gesture while carrying a plate.
judge_comment: Easy, intuitive door opening for full hands, though it addresses only one step and risks accidental opening.

title: Close-Door-To-Start
new_elements: Door-actuated start switch (Closing the door starts a preset 'reheat' cycle; opening it stops heating instantly.); Starts cooking on door closure (Merges access and start into one action.)
rationale: The whole operation becomes 'put food in, shut door', with zero controls to read.
judge_comment: Zero-control operation is very simple, but it risks accidental starts, empty operation and a fixed one-size cycle.

title: Same-As-Last-Time Memory Knob
new_elements: Non-returning setpoint knob with follower cam (The knob stays where it was set while a separate follower counts down, so closing the door repeats the last cook.)
rationale: Elderly users who reheat the same thing daily set the knob once and never touch it again.
judge_comment: A non-returning knob with a follower cam makes repeat cooks effortless, though the mechanism is somewhat complex and the knob's setting no longer shows the remaining time.

title: Pull-Cord Timer
new_elements: Retracting pull-cord timer (Pulling a cord out further gives a longer time; the cord slowly retracts as it counts down, showing the remaining time.)
rationale: Remaining time is shown physically by cord length, so the user does not need to read a scale.
judge_comment: A pull-cord timer is wildly novel and shows remaining time physically, but it is awkward on a microwave, wears out, and gives little precision.

title: Linear Big-Print Slider
new_elements: Wide linear time slider with large numerals (A 15 cm slider with tactile 30 s notches returns slowly to zero during cooking.)
rationale: A ruler-like control with huge numbers is readable and obvious, even for users with poor eyesight.
judge_comment: A ruler-like slider with large numerals is clear and readable, but a slider that returns to zero is mechanically fiddly and only moderately novel.

title: Tactile Click-Count Knob
new_elements: Detented knob with one click per 30 s and raised dots (Users count clicks or feel dots; no printed scale is needed.)
rationale: Counting clicks is intuitive and works for visually impaired elderly users.
judge_comment: A detented knob with raised dots is easy to build and accessible, but it is close to existing mechanical timer knobs.

title: Wind-Up Crank Timer
new_elements: Spring-escapement clockwork (no motor) (A kitchen-egg-timer mechanism wound by the knob itself.); Spring-wound escapement timer (Replaces the synchronous motor, so timing is independent of mains frequency.)
rationale: It works exactly like the familiar egg timer and is cheaper, with one world-wide variant.
judge_comment: A mechanical egg-timer style wind-up is familiar and intuitive and was a real historical approach, but it is not very radical.

title: Fixed Power, No Power Knob
new_elements: Single fixed power level (The oven always runs at full power, and defrosting is done by time alone.)
rationale: Removing an entire control removes a whole category of user decisions.
judge_comment: Removing the power control simplifies operation, though time-only defrosting works poorly and the idea is not very inventive.

title: Three Colour Power Buttons
new_elements: Blue/orange/red rocker power selector (Three coloured positions (defrost, warm, hot) replace the five unclear steps.)
rationale: Colour-coded temperature words are understood instantly, whereas five numbered steps are not.
judge_comment: Colour-coded three-position power selection is easy to understand and easy to build, but it is an incremental UI change.

title: Inverter Gentle Power
new_elements: Continuous inverter magnetron drive (Supplies true continuous low power instead of on/off cycling.); Inverter power board (A lighter, single-board supply that also accepts both mains variants.)
rationale: Even, continuous heating means a single default setting works for everything, so there are no power choices to learn.
judge_comment: Inverter microwaves already exist, and a single default setting only partly removes the need to learn controls, though the idea is plausible and concrete.

title: Shelf-Height Power Selection
new_elements: Two-level rack at different field-strength heights (The lower rack sits in a weaker standing-wave region, so low-rack placement means gentle heating.)
rationale: Where you put the food decides how hot it gets, which is as intuitive as the shelves in an oven.
judge_comment: Using rack height as an intuitive power control is clever, but standing-wave fields are uneven and hard to control reliably, so the heating would be inconsistent.

title: Steam-Sensing Auto Stop
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor (Detects the steam burst from hot food and ends the cycle.)
rationale: The oven stops when the food is hot, so the user never has to guess a duration.
judge_comment: Humidity-sensor auto-stop already exists in sensor-cook microwaves, so it is practical but not novel, and it works only for foods that steam.

title: Spoken Ready Announcement
new_elements: Voice chip end-of-cycle announcer (Replaces the bell with 'Your food is ready, careful, it's hot'.)
rationale: A plain-language message is unambiguous for hard-of-hearing or confused elderly users.
judge_comment: A voice chip is cheap and easy and clearly helps users, but it is already common and only affects the end-of-cycle message.

title: Magnetic Pull Handle
new_elements: Magnetic catch and reed-switch interlocks (A fridge-style pull handle replaces the push button and lever latch.)
rationale: A fridge door needs no instruction, and a magnet takes less force than a stiff button.
judge_comment: A fridge-style magnetic pull handle is familiar and easy to use, but it only simplifies opening the door, and safety interlocks need careful design.

title: Twist-Drum Cavity
new_elements: Rotating cylindrical cavity shutter (Twist the drum to close the opening; twisting further winds the cook time.)
rationale: One twist closes the oven and sets the time, so operating it takes a single gesture.
judge_comment: Single-gesture close-and-set is very simple to use, but a rotating drum cavity with microwave sealing is mechanically hard and the cook time is imprecise.

title: Thermal Image Window
new_elements: Door-integrated IR thermal display (A low-res thermopile array shows the food in cold-blue to hot-red colours on the door.)
rationale: Users immediately see cold spots and know whether to keep going, with no expertise needed.
judge_comment: A thermopile heat map is concrete and helps users judge doneness, but it adds cost and complexity and does not simplify controls.

title: Sand-Glass Progress Window
new_elements: Visible hourglass-style progress gauge (A coloured bead column on the front drains as the cam turns, showing remaining time.)
rationale: Remaining time is shown by analogy to an hourglass, which needs no numbers.
judge_comment: An analog hourglass-style gauge needs no numbers and fits cam timers, making it intuitive and buildable.

title: One-Tap +30s Button
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (Existing 0-30 min mechanical timer from base_product meta, not yet a graph node); Single +30s push button (Each press adds 30 s at full power; the only control on the oven); Set heating duration in one gesture (Duration is set by counting presses)
rationale: Pressing one button more times for more heat needs no explanation.
judge_comment: A single +30s button is very simple to use and easy to build, but it is already common on real microwaves and it is not very radical. It also lists a clockwork knob that seems redundant next to the button.

title: Package Barcode Autoprogram
new_elements: 5-step power knob (Existing power knob from base_product meta); Door-edge barcode reader (Reads the barcode on a ready-meal pack and loads the maker's program); Auto-load packaged food program (No need to read the instructions on the box)
rationale: Showing the box to the oven replaces reading and translating cooking instructions.
judge_comment: Scanning a barcode removes the need to read instructions, but it only works for packaged food and needs a program database (some existing ovens already do this).

title: RFID Smart Containers
new_elements: 5-step power knob (Existing power knob from base_product meta); RFID-tagged microwave containers (Each container tells the oven its content type); Container-driven program (The bowl configures the oven)
rationale: Choosing the soup bowl is the only decision the user makes.
judge_comment: The container configures the oven, which is novel and nearly effortless, but it requires proprietary tagged containers and adds cost and lock-in, and the oven fails with ordinary dishes.

title: Spoken Ready Announcement
new_elements: End-of-cycle bell (Existing timer bell from base_product meta); Voice chip speaker (Says "Your food is ready, careful, it's hot"); Explicit completion message (Unambiguous meaning, unlike a beep)
rationale: Words carry meaning that tones have to be learned for.
judge_comment: Easy to build and clear, but it only improves the end-of-cycle signal and not the operation itself, and talking appliances are not new.

title: Sensor-Modulated Single Power
new_elements: 5-step power knob (Existing duty-cycle cam from base_product meta); Closed-loop inverter controller (Adjusts power automatically from sensor feedback); Automatic power selection (Removes the power choice entirely)
rationale: One less decision for the user means one less thing to learn.
judge_comment: Removing the power decision directly cuts what the user has to learn, though reliable sensor-based control is hard and the idea is not very radical.

title: Solid-State RF Antenna Array
new_elements: Glass turntable (Existing turntable from base_product meta); GaN solid-state RF (Phase-steered RF amplifiers); Steerable antenna array (Aims energy at cold spots automatically); Self-targeting heating (Food heats evenly whatever it is and wherever it sits)
rationale: Users never need tricks like stirring or repositioning food.
judge_comment: Solid-state steerable RF is real technology and removes the need for tricks like stirring, but it mainly addresses even heating rather than the operation interface, and the cost is high.

title: Mug Slot Personal Heater
new_elements: Glass turntable (Existing 20 L cavity and tray from base_product meta); Cylindrical mug-sized cavity (Drop in a cup and it heats to drinking temperature); Single-purpose drink warming (One job with zero settings)
rationale: An appliance with one job cannot be misused.
judge_comment: A single-purpose mug heater with zero settings is very easy to use but narrow in scope, and the cylindrical cavity limits what it can heat.

title: Printed Door Instructions
new_elements: Paper user manual (Implied accessory of the base product); Etched door glass guide (Three-step pictogram printed permanently on the door); Always-present instructions (The guide cannot be lost)
rationale: The instructions are exactly where the user is looking.
judge_comment: Substituting an etched door guide for the manual is cheap and simple but incremental, not radical.

title: No-Clock Design
new_elements: Clock-setting chore (Typical digital microwaves flash 12:00 after every power cut); Clockless progress-only indicator (Shows only remaining heating, never the time of day); Zero setup at plug-in (Ready to use out of the box)
rationale: This keeps the base product's no-clock advantage as it gains electronics, so there is never a setup step.
judge_comment: Removing the clock eliminates a setup step and is trivially feasible, but it is more a removal than a radical idea.

title: Dishwasher-Safe Removable Liner
new_elements: Painted fixed cavity (Existing cavity that is hard to scrub); Snap-out microwave-transparent liner (PP/PTFE shell that goes in the dishwasher); Effortless cleaning (No special cleaning technique needed)
rationale: Cleaning becomes an action everyone already knows: put it in the dishwasher.
judge_comment: A dishwasher-safe snap-out liner makes cleaning familiar and plausible, but it addresses upkeep rather than operation.

title: VOC Burn Sniffer
new_elements: Overcooking risk (Wrong settings burn food); Metal-oxide gas sensor (Smells scorching and cuts power); Burn prevention (Recovers from user mistakes)
rationale: Mistakes are caught by the machine, so novices can't fail.
judge_comment: A gas sensor that cuts power on scorching is plausible and protects novices, but it is reactive and does not simplify operation.

title: Door Progress Light Bar
new_elements: Timer dial pointer (Existing tiny dial readout of remaining time); Door-wide LED fill bar (Fills left to right as cooking progresses); Readable-from-afar progress (Shows progress without reading numbers)
rationale: A filling bar is understood intuitively, like a loading bar.
judge_comment: An LED progress bar is easy to read and feasible, but it only aids feedback, not operation, and an LED strip behind the door is a minor change.

title: Kettle-Style Rocker Switch
new_elements: Clockwork timer knob (Existing timer and power knob pair); Single rocker switch with sensor auto-off (Flip on and it clicks off itself when the food is hot, like a kettle); Binary on/auto-off operation (Simplest possible control)
rationale: Everyone already knows how to use a kettle switch.
judge_comment: A kettle-style single switch with auto-off is very intuitive and plausible, though reliably sensing doneness for varied foods is hard.

title: Weight-Sensing Auto Plate
new_elements: Load-cell floor plate (Replaces the clockwork timer knob: weighs the food and sets the time automatically.); Strain-gauge weighing (Cheap kitchen-scale sensor.); Auto-set cooking time from mass (Heavier food gets a longer cycle.)
rationale: The user never has to guess a time.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto-timing removes time guessing and is plausible, but mass alone is a poor predictor of the time needed for different foods, and a load cell in a microwave is a challenge.

title: Fixed Inverter Power
new_elements: Self-modulating inverter supply (Replaces the 5-step duty-cycle power knob by tuning power to the load automatically.); Automatic power level (The user never chooses a wattage.)
rationale: Removing a whole control removes half of the possible confusion.
judge_comment: Removing the power control cuts complexity, and inverters exist, but the automatic load sensing is vague and not a cheaper substitute.

title: QR Packaging Reader
new_elements: Door-face barcode scanner (Replaces both knobs for ready meals: scanning the pack sets time and power.); Program from packaging (Uses the manufacturer's own heating instructions.)
rationale: The user only has to show the box to the microwave.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning of packaging is simple and practical, but it is already known and only covers ready meals.

title: Bell-Jar Dome
new_elements: Shielded transparent dome (Replaces the box, door and lamp: lower the dome over the plate and heating starts.); Cover-and-heat (Covering the food is the only action.)
rationale: Lowering the cover is the entire operation.
judge_comment: Lowering a cover as the only action is radical and extremely simple, but a transparent dome that blocks microwaves is hard to make safely.

title: Flatbed Mode Stirrer
new_elements: Ceiling mode-stirrer fan (Replaces the glass turntable: a metal paddle scatters the microwaves evenly.); Even heating without rotation (Leaves a flat floor that is easy to wipe.)
rationale: There is no plate to seat correctly and no wobbly dishes.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in many microwaves, and removing the turntable avoids placement errors and is easy to implement.

title: Solid-State Beam Steering
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifiers (Phase-controlled antennas that can aim energy.); Multi-antenna RF array (Replaces the magnetron and turntable by steering energy to cold zones.); Targeted uniform heating (Directs heat where it is needed.)
rationale: Food comes out evenly hot without any stirring tips or tricks to learn.
judge_comment: Solid-state beam steering is real and gives even heating, but it is costly and not simpler, and it addresses operation only indirectly.

title: Pictogram Buttons
new_elements: Cup, plate and bowl icon keys (Replaces the numeric dials with three picture buttons.); Pick what you are heating (The user selects the object, not a time.)
rationale: Pictures work across languages and ages.
judge_comment: Cup, plate and bowl keys let users choose by object rather than time, which is intuitive, but the resulting heating logic is vague.

title: Food-Picture Slider
new_elements: Linear slider with food images (Replaces the rotary timer: slide to the coffee, soup or frozen-meal picture.); Visual program choice (Each picture maps to a preset.)
rationale: Users match pictures instead of translating food into minutes.
judge_comment: Matching food pictures to presets on a slider avoids converting food to minutes, though the range of foods covered is limited.

title: Haptic Detent Dial
new_elements: Detented food-type dial (Replaces the smooth timer: the dial clicks into a few food positions.); Feel-based selection (Positions can be found by touch.)
rationale: It works by touch alone, including for visually impaired users.
judge_comment: A tactile detented food dial is simple and accessible, but it's a modest, fairly obvious variation on existing dials.

title: Giant Start Button
new_elements: Palm-sized illuminated START (Replaces the knob cluster: green means go, red means running, and a press runs an auto-sensed cycle.); Single-action operation (One press does everything.)
rationale: The design follows the "Easy button" philosophy of one obvious action.
judge_comment: One-press operation directly removes the learning curve, but it isn't radical, and auto-sensing cycles are only loosely specified.

title: NFC Smart Plate
new_elements: NFC-tagged plate (Replaces the knobs: a caregiver pre-loads meal settings onto the plate.); Pre-programmed meals (The plate carries its own heating instructions.)
rationale: Elderly users just put the plate in.
judge_comment: An NFC plate that carries its heating program is a creative substitution for the controls, but it needs caregiver setup and special plates.

title: Mug-Only Microwave
new_elements: Cup-shaped mini cavity (Replaces the full box and controls for drinks: drop a mug in and it heats to drinking temperature.); Single-purpose reheating (Does one job with no settings.)
rationale: A single-purpose device can be completely obvious to use.
judge_comment: A single-purpose mug heater is very simple to use and plausible, but it only covers drinks and a few similar products already exist.

title: Tray Slides Out When Done
new_elements: Motorised serving tray (Replaces the bell and turntable: the tray glides out toward the user when the food is ready.); Food presentation on completion (Delivers the food instead of signalling.)
rationale: The food is literally handed to the user.
judge_comment: A motorised tray that presents the food is a clear mechanism and a fun one, but it adds complexity and does nothing to simplify the controls.

title: Projected Guide on Countertop
new_elements: Mini projector under microwave (Replaces printed knob labels by projecting arrows showing the next step.); In-context guidance (Shows the next step where the user is looking.)
rationale: The appliance teaches itself, so no manual is needed.
judge_comment: Projected step-by-step guidance directly removes the learning curve, though projecting onto a countertop or the appliance near steam and glare is awkward and it adds cost rather than substituting something cheaper.

title: Solid-State GaN Heart
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Low-voltage transistors generate 2.45 GHz with exact power control and no magnetron.)
rationale: Precise automatic power control removes the power knob from the user's world entirely.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is radical and enables precise automatic control, but it is costly today and only helps simplicity if the interface is also redesigned.

title: Timer-Spring Turntable
new_elements: Clockwork-driven turntable gear (The wound timer spring also turns the plate, which removes the motor.)
rationale: The single knob twist both times and rotates, keeping the product simpler and cheaper.
judge_comment: A clockwork timer that also drives the turntable is clever and simple, but spring power is limited and it is awkward for long cook times.

title: Food Token Pucks
new_elements: Picture-coded RFID tokens (The user drops a 'soup', 'pizza' or 'milk' token onto a slot on top to set the program.)
rationale: Choosing a picture is understood instantly by children, seniors and non-native speakers.
judge_comment: Picture tokens make program selection intuitive, though they add loose parts and the idea only loosely fits 'substitute'.

title: Metal Detector Auto-Stop
new_elements: Reflected-power arc sensor (Detects the reflected power and arc signature of metal, stops, and lights a 'metal' icon.)
rationale: Users need not memorise what is microwave-safe because the oven protects them.
judge_comment: Arc and reflected-power sensing is plausible and removes the need to know what's microwave-safe, but it doesn't substitute a part cheaply and similar protections already exist.

title: Push-to-Cook Drawer
new_elements: Microwave drawer with gravity seal (Pulling the drawer out stops cooking and pushing it in starts it.)
rationale: One push-pull motion is the whole interface.
judge_comment: Pull-to-stop and push-to-start is a very simple interface, but it needs a time or power setting and a drawer with a reliable microwave seal is difficult.

title: Frozen-Food Auto Defrost
new_elements: Detects ice and auto-defrosts (RF reflection reveals frozen water and switches to a gentle duty cycle.)
rationale: The user never has to know that defrosting needs low power.
judge_comment: Automatic frozen-food detection hides the complexity of power levels, though RF sensing is hard to make reliable.

title: Container-Is-the-Oven
new_elements: Shielded meal-box cavity (A metal-lidded lunchbox docks onto an RF base and becomes the cooking cavity.)
rationale: Snapping the box on and eating from it requires no transfer, door or settings.
judge_comment: A radical rethink with no door or settings, but a docked shielded lunchbox cavity is hard to make safe and effective.

title: Auto-Pause Stir Prompt
new_elements: Built-in rest and stir interval (The oven automatically pauses heating mid-cycle and flashes a spoon icon.)
rationale: Standing-time expertise is built in, so users don't need to know it.
judge_comment: A built-in pause and stir prompt is easy to implement and encodes expertise, but it is a mild idea and may annoy users.

title: Pack Reads Itself
new_elements: Packaging code reader (Camera or RFID reader in the cavity ceiling reads a code on the food pack.); Auto-selects time and power from packaging (The manufacturer's heating profile loads automatically.)
rationale: The user puts the food in and closes the door; nothing has to be read, set or learned.
judge_comment: Removes all settings for packaged food, but it depends on manufacturers adopting codes and does nothing for non-packaged food.

title: Talk to Heat
new_elements: Offline voice command module (Understands phrases like 'warm my coffee' or 'two minutes'.)
rationale: Natural speech is an interface no one needs to learn.
judge_comment: Natural speech directly removes the learning curve, but voice control in appliances is not new and offline recognition in a noisy kitchen is tricky.

title: Fixed Ceramic Floor
new_elements: Flat glazed ceramic cavity floor (Replaces the removable glass turntable plate.)
rationale: Nothing to seat, break or reassemble after washing.
judge_comment: Fixed ceramic floor removes a part to seat and handle, but loses turntable rotation unless solved, and mostly eases cleaning rather than operation.

title: Shape-Memory Latch
new_elements: Nitinol wire door latch (A silent electric pulse retracts the latch; there is no lever train.)
rationale: A light touch anywhere opens the door, with no stiff button.
judge_comment: Nitinol latch is a clever part substitution, but it only fixes door opening and a light touch still needs a trigger; benefit to no-learning-curve is modest.

title: Elbow-Bump Opening
new_elements: Proximity / knock door sensor (A wave or bump with full hands opens the door.)
rationale: Opening works intuitively even while holding a plate.
judge_comment: Hands-free opening is intuitive and plausible, though accidental triggers are a risk and it addresses only opening.

title: The One-Button Microwave
new_elements: Single 'HEAT' button sensor microwave (Steam, weight and IR sensing hidden behind one button.)
rationale: One button for everything is the ultimate no-learning-curve device.
judge_comment: One button with hidden sensing removes the learning curve entirely, but reliable automatic cooking across foods is hard and similar sensor features already exist.

title: Mug-Warmer Mini Cavity
new_elements: Single-mug cylindrical microwave (A tiny cavity tuned to one mug; drop it in and it heats to 65 °C.)
rationale: A single-purpose device removes every choice.
judge_comment: A single-purpose mug-sized cavity with a fixed heat target removes nearly all choices and is directly zero-learning, though cavity tuning for varying loads is challenging.

title: Weigh-and-Go Scale Floor
new_elements: Load-cell cavity floor (Strain-gauge floor weighs the food and sets time and power automatically.); Auto-sets cook time from food mass (Mass-to-energy lookup removes the need for timer and power knobs.)
rationale: The user puts food in and closes the door, and the oven works out time and power from the weight, so there are no settings to learn.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto settings remove the controls, but mass alone is a poor proxy for the energy a food needs, so results will vary.

title: Steam-Sniffer Auto Stop
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor (Detects the steam burst that signals food is hot and ends the cycle.)
rationale: The food itself signals when it is done, so the user never has to guess a time.
judge_comment: Humidity-based auto stop is proven in sensor-cook microwaves and removes the timing guesswork, but it fits only some foods and still needs a start action.

title: Food-Icon Power Dial
new_elements: Pictogram dial (ice cube, soup, mug, plate) (Replaces the abstract 5-step power scale with pictures of food.)
rationale: Pictures of food need no reading and no understanding of wattage.
judge_comment: Pictograms are intuitive and easy to build, though the idea is incremental and still requires choosing a time.

title: Solid-State RF Heart
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier (Low-voltage 2.45 GHz power amplifier that replaces the magnetron and HV doubler.); Solid-state RF module (Runs on about 50 V DC, so there is no lethal capacitor and no HV diode.)
rationale: Precise, controllable power makes fully automatic modes possible, so the user only needs to press start.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is a real substitution of the magnetron and enables automation, but the link to no-learning-curve operation is indirect and cost and power are still hurdles.

title: USB-C Mug Microwave
new_elements: USB-C PD 3.1 240 W input (A mug-sized solid-state microwave powered by a laptop charger.)
rationale: A desk gadget with one cable and one button, using a charger the student already owns.
judge_comment: A one-cable, one-button desk microwave is appealing and fresh, but 240 W solid-state heating is slow and limited in capability.

title: Flat Ceramic Floor, Hidden Stirrer
new_elements: Under-floor rotating mode stirrer (A fan-like metal stirrer under a fixed ceramic floor replaces the glass plate.)
rationale: Square dishes fit, there are no loose parts, and cleaning is a single wipe.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers under a ceramic floor already exist in commercial products; it is practical and removes loose parts, though it does little for operation.

title: Door-Wound Spring Turntable
new_elements: Clockwork turntable spring wound by door closing (The motion of closing the door stores enough energy for a 5-minute rotation.)
rationale: Removing the motor costs nothing in usability, because rotation happens automatically when the door is closed.
judge_comment: A radical idea that is automatic for the user, but a door-wound spring is unlikely to store enough energy for 5 minutes and it lacks control over rotation time.

title: Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Slide-out cavity drawer (The food drops in from above and the drawer is pushed shut.)
rationale: Loading becomes one intuitive push-pull motion with no hinged door swing.
judge_comment: Intuitive loading motion and fairly novel, but spills, sealing and the drawer mechanism are challenges.

title: Talking Ready Announcement
new_elements: Voice chip replacing bell (Says 'Ready — stir and let it rest 1 minute'.)
rationale: The appliance tells the user the next step in plain words instead of an ambiguous ding.
judge_comment: A voice chip in place of the bell is cheap, easy and gives clear guidance, but it is an incremental idea and not radical.

title: Smart NTC Overheat Guard
new_elements: NTC thermistor on MCU (Replaces the bimetal snap-disc and also detects an empty-cavity run.); Detects empty or near-empty cavity (Stops automatically if nothing absorbs energy.)
rationale: The oven protects itself from user mistakes, so there is nothing to learn about misuse.
judge_comment: An NTC sensor with empty-run detection is plausible and protects against misuse, though it is mostly invisible to the user and only indirectly serves ease of use.

title: Arc-Sensing Self-Stop
new_elements: Reflected-power + spark optical sensor (Detects metal or arcing, stops, and shows a 'remove metal' icon.)
rationale: Users do not need to memorize the 'no metal' rule, because the oven catches the mistake.
judge_comment: Catching the metal mistake removes a rule users must remember, though it only addresses one error and arc detection is partly already known.

title: Glanceable Hourglass Bar
new_elements: LED hourglass progress bar (A draining light bar replaces the clockwork dial reading.)
rationale: A draining bar shows time left without the user reading numbers.
judge_comment: An LED draining bar is simple and glanceable, but it is a modest, fairly obvious replacement for a numeric display.

title: Photo Buttons of Real Foods
new_elements: Printed food-photo membrane keys (Keys show photos of pizza slice, rice bowl, milk and popcorn.)
rationale: The user matches the food in hand to a photo, with no reading or language needed.
judge_comment: Photo keys remove reading and language barriers, but food presets already exist in some form and need accurate power/time mapping.

title: Door Pops Open When Done
new_elements: Spring kick-open latch release (At the end of the cycle the timer cam releases the latch and the door swings ajar.); Presents finished food (A physical, visible end-of-cycle signal.)
rationale: An open door means 'ready' to anyone, like a toaster popping up.
judge_comment: A toaster-like pop-open door is an intuitive end signal and mechanically simple, but it does not help with setting up a cook.

title: Stirrer Instead of Turntable
new_elements: Metal mode-stirrer fan in ceiling (Air-driven rotating reflector scrambles the field, so a flat floor replaces the turntable.)
rationale: With no tray to seat, no roller ring to lose and no jamming dishes, the user simply puts food on a flat floor.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers already exist in commercial microwaves. A flat floor does remove a small friction point, but the idea is not radical.

title: Inverter Power Supply
new_elements: Switch-mode HV inverter board (A light board accepting 100-240 V that provides truly variable power.)
rationale: Real low power means defrost just works without users learning on/off cycling tricks.
judge_comment: Inverter microwaves are already on the market. They improve defrost, but the user still has to choose settings.

title: Camera Eye Chef
new_elements: Interior camera with food recognition (Identifies the food, sets the program and streams a view to the user's phone.); Embedded image classification (Low-cost vision system-on-chip.)
rationale: The microwave recognises the food and decides how to heat it, so the user decides nothing.
judge_comment: Zero-input operation fits the need perfectly, but food recognition is error-prone, costly, and not very radical now.

title: Milk-Mug Pod
new_elements: Mug-sized single-purpose cavity (A tiny cavity that fits only a mug and has one 'heat drink' button.); Heats one drink perfectly (A fixed program tuned to about 250 ml.)
rationale: A device that does one thing with one button cannot be misused.
judge_comment: A one-button mug heater is simple and very feasible, but it is narrow in use and not very radical.

title: Listening Microwave
new_elements: Acoustic boil and pop sensor (A microphone hears simmering or popping and stops heating at the right moment.); Acoustic event detection (Spectral detection of bubbling and popping sounds.)
rationale: The microwave 'hears' when food is done, just as an experienced cook would, so the user needs no timing skill.
judge_comment: Acoustic detection of boiling and popping is plausible and removes the need to set a time, but it only works for some foods and the user still starts it.

title: Handle-Twist Control
new_elements: Rotating door handle timer (Twisting the door handle sets the time, and closing the door starts cooking.)
rationale: Combining the controls into the part the user already holds removes the control panel entirely.
judge_comment: Merging time setting into the door handle is a clever substitution, though the twist-to-set mechanism and accidental starts need care.

title: Brightness-Fade Progress Lamp
new_elements: Dimming warm-to-white cavity LED (The interior light shifts from warm orange to bright white as cooking nears completion.)
rationale: The light the user is already looking at doubles as the progress indicator, so no display needs reading.
judge_comment: Using the cavity light as a progress cue is neat and cheap, but it only conveys status and does not simplify setting the time.

title: Elbow-Bump Door
new_elements: Push-to-open full-face door (Pressing anywhere on the door with an elbow or knee pops it open, which helps when both hands hold plates.)
rationale: There is no specific spot to find, because the whole door is the button.
judge_comment: A push-anywhere door is simple and practical and substitutes for the handle, but it covers only door opening, not the cooking operation.

title: Phone-Is-The-Panel
new_elements: NFC tap-to-cook tag (Tapping a phone shows a familiar app with photos and starts the cooking program.)
rationale: The phone interface the user already knows replaces an appliance-specific panel.
judge_comment: Phone tap-to-cook is feasible and uses a familiar interface, but it requires a phone and app, so it is not truly zero-learning and is a fairly common idea.

title: Weighing Turntable Sets the Time
new_elements: Load-cell turntable hub (A strain gauge under the turntable coupler weighs the food and derives the cook time.); Auto-sets duration from food mass (Replaces the guesswork of the clockwork knob.)
rationale: The user puts food in and the machine works out the time itself.
judge_comment: Weight-based auto time is helpful, but mass alone poorly predicts cook time, and the load cell adds cost rather than substituting something cheaper.

title: Spoon-Proof Reflected-Power Guard
new_elements: Reflected-power arc detector (Senses the field changes caused by metal or arcing and pauses heating with a clear 'remove metal' icon.)
rationale: Users don't need to remember the 'no metal' rule; the machine forgives the mistake.
judge_comment: Forgiving metal detection removes a rule users must remember and is plausible, though reliable detection is hard and it is not a substitution of a cheaper part.

title: Hourglass Flip Microwave
new_elements: Tilt-switch flip handle (Flipping the top handle starts a heating cycle shown by a visible sand-like LED fall.); Visualises remaining time (Replaces the clockwork dial.)
rationale: Borrows the hourglass metaphor everyone already knows.
judge_comment: The hourglass flip is an intuitive, wild metaphor for starting and showing time, though fixed durations and flexibility are unclear.

title: One-Word Voice Control
new_elements: Offline keyword listener (Recognises only 'warm', 'hot', 'defrost' and 'stop'.)
rationale: Saying what you want requires no interface literacy.
judge_comment: A four-word offline listener is plausible and needs no learning, but noisy kitchens and accents hurt reliability, and it doesn't clearly replace a part cheaply.

title: Barcode-Reading Door
new_elements: Door-edge barcode scanner (Reads the food package and loads the maker's heating instructions.)
rationale: No need to read the instructions on the box.
judge_comment: Scanning a package barcode could remove all input, but it needs a database of heating instructions that barcodes don't carry, so it would need a lot of infrastructure.

title: Inverter True-Power Control
new_elements: PWM inverter supply (Delivers continuous variable power instead of on/off duty cycling.)
rationale: Even heating at any setting means fewer failed attempts and less to learn.
judge_comment: Inverter microwaves already exist and give even heating, but the link to zero learning curve is indirect.

title: Mono-Mug Microwave
new_elements: Single-mug cylinder cavity (A tiny cylinder cavity with one fixed program for one mug or bowl.)
rationale: One size and one setting, so there is literally nothing to choose.
judge_comment: A single-mug, one-program microwave removes choice and is radical and clearly on-need, but it is limited in use and has uncertain heating uniformity.

title: Weight-Triggered Start
new_elements: Tray presence switch (Heating runs only while there is a load on the tray and the door is closed.)
rationale: Putting food in and closing the door is the whole operation.
judge_comment: Removing the start step makes operation nearly zero-learning, but it needs a default power/time and could heat unintended loads; it is plausible with a load sensor.

title: Snap-Disc as Done Clicker
new_elements: Audible bimetal doneness clicker (A bimetal disc in the exhaust snaps audibly and cuts power when the vapour is hot.)
rationale: Cheap, sensor-free automatic stopping.
judge_comment: A mechanical bimetal vapour-triggered auto-stop is cheap and needs no user settings, though accuracy across different foods is questionable.

title: Pull-Out Drawer Cavity
new_elements: Choke-sealed sliding drawer (Cavity slides out on rails with a handle; no button and no hinges.)
rationale: Pull and push is the most intuitive opening motion there is, and it suits frail hands.
judge_comment: A drawer is an intuitive pull-and-push motion, but choke-sealing a sliding cavity is hard, and it only simplifies opening, not time or power operation.

title: Magnetic Pull Handle
new_elements: Magnetic door catch with grab handle (A fridge-style magnet holds the door; the interlock is a reed switch.)
rationale: There is no hidden button to find; users just pull like a fridge.
judge_comment: A magnetic catch with a reed-switch interlock is very feasible and removes the hidden button, but it is incremental and leaves the controls unchanged.

title: Auto-Pop Door at End
new_elements: Cam-tripped door kick spring (The timer cam releases the latch at zero so the door swings ajar.)
rationale: An open door shows that the food is done without anyone needing to hear a bell.
judge_comment: A mechanical auto-pop door is simple and clear, but it only signals completion and does not simplify setting up a cook.

title: Shrinking Bar Slider
new_elements: Linear slider with receding coloured bar (The slider creeps back home, visibly showing remaining time.)
rationale: Remaining time reads at a glance, like a fuel gauge.
judge_comment: A receding slider makes remaining time easy to read and set, but it is a modest variation on existing timers.

title: ITO Glass Door
new_elements: Transparent conductive oxide coating (A clear ITO film on the glass provides the Faraday shielding.); Clear coated glass door (Replaces the perforated mesh window.)
rationale: A clear view of the food means users simply watch it and stop when it looks right.
judge_comment: An ITO door gives a clear view of the food, but it is only tangentially tied to operation, and shielding at microwave frequencies and durability are uncertain.

title: Turntable-Motor Timer
new_elements: Peg-on-turntable revolution counter (A peg dropped into a rim hole trips the cutoff after N revolutions.)
rationale: This reuses the existing motor, and placing a peg near or far is self-explanatory.
judge_comment: Clever reuse of the turntable motor, but placing a peg to count revolutions is not intuitive and the turntable speed makes timing coarse, so it needs some learning.

title: Wind-Up Spring Timer
new_elements: Escapement clockwork timer (Spring-driven with no synchronous motor; identical for every mains region.)
rationale: It behaves exactly like a familiar egg timer.
judge_comment: A familiar egg-timer interface with proven mechanical clockwork, though mechanical timers already exist in basic microwaves, so it is not very novel.

title: +30 Second Slap Button
new_elements: Single ratchet palm button (Each slap adds 30 s to a mechanical store.)
rationale: One button with one meaning: more.
judge_comment: A single-meaning button is easy to grasp, but the mechanical ratchet store is vague and it gives no easy way to decrease the time.

title: Handle-Twist Timer
new_elements: Rotating door handle timer (Twisting the handle after closing sets the time; twisting back opens the door.)
rationale: One control does everything, so the hand is always in the right place.
judge_comment: Merging door and timer into one twisting handle is intuitive and unusual, though twisting to open conflicts with setting time and the mechanism needs care.

title: Wax Melt Timer Cartridge
new_elements: Wax-pellet thermal actuator (A wax pellet near the food expands at about 70 °C and trips the switch.)
rationale: Cooking stops when the food is done, without the user doing anything.
judge_comment: Auto-stop at food temperature removes all settings, but a wax actuator near the food is unreliable, since it only senses one spot and it sits in a microwave field.

title: Sand Hourglass Window
new_elements: Flipping hourglass timer in the door (Flipping the glass starts heating; it stops when the sand runs out.)
rationale: An hourglass has been understood for centuries.
judge_comment: The hourglass is a universally understood timer, but a fixed duration is inflexible and the glass must be mechanically linked to the heating switch.

title: Pictogram-Only Fascia
new_elements: Language-free icon panel (Snowflake, cup, plate and pot icons replace text and numbers.)
rationale: It is understood regardless of literacy or language.
judge_comment: Easy to build and clearly cuts the learning curve, but icon panels already exist and are not radical.

title: Phone-Camera Barcode Scan
new_elements: Built-in optical package reader (Holding the package to the window sets time and power automatically.)
rationale: Show the box to the oven and you are done.
judge_comment: Scanning the package removes all input and is highly relevant, but it depends on a barcode-to-instruction database and isn't quite a cheaper substitution.

title: Microwave Kettle Pod
new_elements: Single-mug sealed pod oven (A mug-sized shielded pod with a press-lid that heats until it boils.)
rationale: It works like a kettle: put the mug in, press, done.
judge_comment: A kettle-like single-purpose pod is intuitive, but it is limited to liquids and boiling a sealed mug raises safety and shielding concerns.

title: Close the Door = Start
new_elements: Door-actuated start cam (Closing the door winds a spring cam that gives a default 1-minute heat; opening the door stops it.); Starts heating by the natural act of closing the door (No separate start action is needed.)
rationale: The only operation is something everyone already does, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Closing the door to start is intuitive and cheap, but a fixed 1-minute default is limiting and accidental starts are a risk.

title: Weigh-to-Time Turntable
new_elements: Spring-scale turntable linked to timer cam (Food weight deflects a spring that pre-sets the timer cam's position.); Automatically sets duration from food mass (Heavier food gets proportionally more time.)
rationale: The user puts food in and the machine decides the time, so no setting is required.
judge_comment: Setting time from weight removes the setting step, but weight is a poor proxy for heating time, and a spring scale inside a microwave is hard to build.

title: Revolving Drum Cavity
new_elements: Rotating cylindrical cavity with single opening (Turning the drum toward the user exposes the food; turning it away seals it and starts heating.); Combines access, sealing and start in one motion (Rotation replaces both the door and the start control.)
rationale: A single, obvious twist both closes the oven and starts it.
judge_comment: A single twist that closes and starts the oven is radically simple, but a rotating cavity is hard to seal against microwave leakage and to build.

title: Door Pops Open When Done
new_elements: Timer cam trip linked to latch lever (At zero the cam releases the latch and a spring nudges the door ajar.); Signals completion by opening the door (Replaces the bell and stops steam build-up.)
rationale: An open door is an unmistakable 'done' signal, even for users with hearing loss.
judge_comment: Clear done signal replacing the bell, but it addresses only the end of the operation, not the setup learning curve.

title: Twist-the-Handle Timer
new_elements: Rotating door handle that sets time (Twisting the handle while closing the door winds the timer.)
rationale: The hand that closes the door also sets the time, in one fluid gesture.
judge_comment: Merging door closing and time setting into one gesture is intuitive and mechanically plausible.

title: Slot-Machine Lever
new_elements: Large side lever, one pull equals one minute (A big ratcheting lever is easy to grip for arthritic hands.)
rationale: A big, chunky, countable action replaces fine dial positioning.
judge_comment: Countable lever pulls are easy to grasp and accessible, though they are slow for longer cook times.

title: Hold-to-Heat Button
new_elements: Momentary press-and-hold heat button (Heats only while held, for quick 5-20 s top-ups.)
rationale: 'Hold until warm' is as intuitive as holding a tap open.
judge_comment: Very intuitive and trivially feasible, but it requires the user to stand and hold, and it is not very radical.

title: Popcorn-Pop Acoustic Stop
new_elements: Piezo pop-gap detector (Stops heating when the gap between pops exceeds 2 s.)
rationale: It removes the guesswork from the trickiest everyday food.
judge_comment: Acoustic popcorn detection is plausible and concrete, but it only addresses one food and is not a broad simplification of operation.

title: Toaster-Lever Microwave
new_elements: Slide-down lever lowering food into cavity (Pushing the lever down seals the cavity and starts heating; the food pops up when done.)
rationale: It copies the toaster, the most universally understood kitchen gesture.
judge_comment: The toaster gesture needs no learning, but sealing the cavity, lowering food safely and handling liquids and containers are hard problems.

title: Steam-Sensing Auto Stop
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor (Detects the steam burst released when food is hot and cuts power.); Ends cooking when food is hot (Replaces time estimation.)
rationale: Users never guess a time because the oven stops itself when the food is done.
judge_comment: Sensor-cooking exists in premium models, though using a humidity sensor as a cheap substitute for timers is a sound approach; reliability varies with food types.

title: Sand Hourglass Timer
new_elements: Flip-over hourglass switch module (Flipping a 1-, 2- or 3-minute hourglass on top tilts a switch that runs the oven until the sand empties.)
rationale: Remaining time is visible and set by an instinctive flip, with no dial to calibrate.
judge_comment: Playful and visual, with a clear mechanism, but fixed durations limit flexibility and the tilt switch is a bit gimmicky.

title: Built-in Susceptor Floor
new_elements: Ferrite-coated crisping plate (Absorbs microwaves and heats to about 200 °C to brown food bottoms.)
rationale: Crisp results come with the same single button, with no separate grill mode.
judge_comment: Susceptor plates are already common and feasible, and they remove the need for a separate mode, but they have only a weak link to learning-free operation.

title: Airflow Mode Stirrer
new_elements: Fan-driven metal mode stirrer (Spun by the existing cooling-air stream, replacing the turntable motor.)
rationale: A flat floor fits any dish shape, with no turntable to seat or jam.
judge_comment: An airflow-driven stirrer removes the turntable and its fit issues, though uniform heating and cost are uncertain and operation itself is barely simplified.

title: Talking Microwave
new_elements: Voice prompt chip (Says 'ready, careful, hot' instead of ringing a bell.)
rationale: Plain-language feedback removes ambiguity.
judge_comment: Voice prompts are easy and clear, though talking appliances are not new and it only replaces the bell, not the operating complexity.

title: Food-Recognizing Camera
new_elements: On-device image classification (A low-cost vision chip runs a food classifier.); Cavity camera (Replaces the knobs and lamp-window inspection; identifies food and sets the program.); Auto-program by sight (Chooses time and power from the food it sees.)
rationale: The user's only job is to close the door.
judge_comment: Closing the door as the only step is ideal, but a camera that classifies food in a steamy, high-RF cavity is hard and unreliable, and it is not a cheap substitution.

title: Package Barcode Autopilot
new_elements: Door-edge barcode reader (Replaces manual timer setting by reading the cook code on the food pack.); Cook per manufacturer spec (Applies the exact time and power printed on the package.); Translating pack instructions to knobs (Pack watts often differ from oven watts.)
rationale: No reading or converting is needed: users wave the pack and go.
judge_comment: Scanning the pack removes all time and power entry, though it depends on barcode data availability and on the cook codes being standardized, and it only partly matches the SUBSTITUTE operator.

title: Magnetic Pull Door
new_elements: Magnetic catch door (Replaces the push-release button with a fridge-style magnetic seal and a grab edge.); Open by pulling (Uses the same gesture as a fridge door.); Permanent-magnet latching (Ferrite strip with a redundant interlock switch.)
rationale: There is no hidden button to find: users simply pull.
judge_comment: A fridge-style pull door is simple and highly feasible, but it is incremental and addresses only the door-opening step.

title: Phase-Steered Solid State Heating
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF (Multiple phase-controlled RF amplifiers.); RF emitter array (Replaces the magnetron plus turntable; steers energy to cold spots.); Targeted energy placement (Heats evenly without user stirring.)
rationale: It removes the 'stir halfway' tribal knowledge users would otherwise need.
judge_comment: Solid-state phase-steered RF is real and removes the need to stir, but it is costly and does little for the operating interface.

title: Glow-Lid Doneness Cover
new_elements: Colour-changing splatter cover (The included cover turns from blue to red at eating temperature, standing in for timer guesswork.); Doneness indicator (Shows the food is ready, visible through the window.); Users can't judge doneness (The bell signals time elapsed, not food readiness.)
rationale: Users wait for red and need no expertise.
judge_comment: A cover that changes color at eating temperature is simple and plausible and removes the need to judge doneness, but the description is inconsistent about what it signals and it does not replace any controls.

title: Portion Slider
new_elements: Portion-size slider (Replaces the timer knob with small, medium and large plate images.); Select amount, not time (Converts portion to time internally.); Time is an indirect proxy (Users think in amounts of food.)
rationale: It matches how people actually think about their food.
judge_comment: Selecting by portion matches how people think, but it needs food-type assumptions and is less radical.

title: Door Twist Timer
new_elements: Rotating door handle (Replaces the timer knob; twisting the handle while closing sets time.); Close and set in one grip (Merges two actions into one.); Controls far from the hand (Users must move to a separate panel.)
rationale: Control sits exactly where the hand already is.
judge_comment: Merging closing and time-setting into one gesture is intuitive, though the handle mechanism and its precision are challenging.

title: Punch-Tab Packaging
new_elements: Cardboard tab slot (Replaces knob setting; a tear-off tab from food packaging inserted in a slot encodes the cook program via punched holes.); Mechanical program card (No electronics needed.); Punch-card reading (Spring pins read the holes.)
rationale: Users insert the tab and it's done, like posting a letter.
judge_comment: A radical punch-tab approach is easy to use but depends on packaging standardization, and the mechanical power programming is implausible.

title: Carry-Away Timer Puck
new_elements: Detachable magnetic timer puck (The timer knob pops off and vibrates in your pocket when done.); Portable completion alert (Alerts the user wherever they are.); BLE beacon (Coin-cell radio puck.)
rationale: The control you set is literally the thing that tells you it's done.
judge_comment: A detachable timer puck with an alert is feasible and neat, but it adds a part to manage and does little to cut the learning curve.

title: Mains-Hum Sound Cue
new_elements: Spoken status chip (Replaces the bell with a short voice line: 'Your food is ready.'); Explicit spoken feedback (No signal decoding needed.); Voice playback IC (Cents-cost greeting-card chip.)
rationale: Plain words beat a ding for first-time users.
judge_comment: A voice chip is cheap and clear, but talking appliances are common, and the title 'Mains-Hum Sound Cue' doesn't match the content.

title: Smart Single-Serve Pods
new_elements: Tag-reading floor coil (Replaces knobs with a reader for a microwave-safe passive tag in meal containers.); Container-driven cooking (The pod carries its own program.); Microwave-tolerant passive tags (Printed carbon resonator.)
rationale: It works like a coffee-pod machine: drop the pod in and it's done.
judge_comment: Pod-driven cooking removes nearly all operation, but printed carbon tags that survive microwaves and a container ecosystem are hard to deliver.

title: Pop-Open Door Alert
new_elements: Cam-triggered door kicker spring (At end of cycle the timer cam releases the latch and a spring nudges the door ajar.)
rationale: An open door means the food is done, so there is no signal to learn and no button to press.
judge_comment: A door that pops ajar at the end is an intuitive signal and easy to build, but it only addresses the end-of-cycle cue, not operation overall.

title: Push-to-Open Door
new_elements: Push-push touch latch door (Pressing anywhere on the door releases it; pushing it shut locks it.)
rationale: Users don't have to find a release button; any push on the door opens it.
judge_comment: Push-push latches are proven and simple, but they are an incremental usability gain that is already common in other products.

title: Flat Floor with Stirrer
new_elements: Hidden mode-stirrer paddle (Metal fan blade under the ceiling scatters the field; the cavity floor is flat and fixed.)
rationale: There is no tray to seat, no wobbling, and no stuck dishes, so users put food in anywhere.
judge_comment: Stirrer-based flat-floor microwaves already exist and the benefit is easier loading, only indirectly tied to operation.

title: Microwave Drawer
new_elements: Pull-out shielded drawer (Drawer with a choke rim slides on runners, replacing the hinged door and latch.)
rationale: Users pull it open and drop food in from above, like any kitchen drawer.
judge_comment: A drawer is familiar to use, but it changes only the door and not the operation, and it makes RF choke sealing harder.

title: Ice-Sensing Defrost
new_elements: Detects ice-to-water transition via reflected RF (Ice absorbs poorly; a rising absorption signal marks the thaw and switches to rest pulses.)
rationale: Defrosting becomes a single 'frozen' press with no weight tables.
judge_comment: Auto-detecting thaw cuts weight tables and simplifies defrosting, but it doesn't clearly substitute a part and the RF sensing is hard to do reliably (ice actually absorbs weakly, so the signal is plausible but noisy).

title: Self-Weighing Power
new_elements: Load-cell floor selecting duty cycle (Small loads get lower power automatically to avoid exploding or drying out.)
rationale: The oven matches power to the portion without the user knowing what watts mean.
judge_comment: Auto power from weight is plausible and removes a decision, but it only partly substitutes for the controls.

title: Manual Molded Into the Cavity
new_elements: Embossed pictogram cavity walls (Enamel-printed icons inside show 'no metal', 'cover', 'stir', replacing the paper manual.)
rationale: The instructions are right where the user's eyes are, at the moment they are needed.
judge_comment: Enamel pictograms inside the cavity replace the paper manual cheaply and are contextual, though they only help with safety guidance and not with operating the controls.

title: Door Defrost Toggle
new_elements: Snowflake slider on door edge (Slide to snowflake to engage a fixed defrost pulse pattern; slide back for normal heating.)
rationale: Defrost is an obvious binary choice instead of a power-level percentage.
judge_comment: A binary defrost slider replaces power-level percentages with something simpler and easy to build, though it is only an incremental change.

title: Voice Command Chip
new_elements: Offline 10-word voice recognizer (Recognizes 'heat', 'more', 'stop', 'defrost' locally with no app or Wi-Fi.)
rationale: Users just say what they want in ordinary words.
judge_comment: Offline voice commands require no learning, and the chips are cheap and proven, though noisy kitchens and unclear quantities ('more' of what?) limit reliability.

title: Glow Progress Cavity
new_elements: Colour-shifting interior LED (Interior light fades from cool blue to warm amber as cooking progresses, then flashes when done.)
rationale: The light itself shows progress intuitively, merging two indicators into one.
judge_comment: A single colour-shifting LED merges the light and the progress indicator cheaply and is intuitive, but it does not help with setting the cook time.

title: Giant Linear Slider
new_elements: Full-height time slider (Vertical slider spanning the control panel with huge printed minutes; motor-driven back to zero.)
rationale: A large linear scale reads like a ruler and is easier to see and grip than a small knob.
judge_comment: A big slider is clear and easy to build, but it is an incremental change to a dial.

title: Top-Loading Lid
new_elements: Gravity-closing top lid (Lift-up lid like a chest freezer; its own weight presses the interlocks.)
rationale: Lifting a lid is obvious, and gravity closes and latches it with no button.
judge_comment: A chest-freezer-style lid is intuitive and a real departure from side doors, but spill risk, ergonomics, and gravity-only interlock safety are concerns.

title: Ballast Cup Defrost
