new_elements: Water ballast cup (A clip-in water reservoir absorbs part of the microwave energy, giving gentle heating at fixed full power.)
rationale: Removing the power knob leaves only time to set, and gentle mode is a visible physical object.
judge_comment: A water ballast cup is a wild, physical way to get gentle heating and leave only a time setting, though it is inefficient and its control is imprecise.

title: Package Code Reader
new_elements: Barcode scan-to-cook window (Hold the ready-meal box to the window; the time and power printed in its code are applied.)
rationale: The manufacturer's instructions are applied automatically, with no reading of fine print.
judge_comment: Scan-to-cook removes reading instructions, but it depends on packaging standards and only covers ready meals.

title: Pop-Open Finish
new_elements: Timer-tripped door kicker (The end-of-cycle cam releases the latch so the door springs ajar, replacing the bell.)
rationale: An open door unmistakably means done, and food is never forgotten inside.
judge_comment: A spring-open door is a simple, cheap substitute for the bell and an obvious done signal, though it addresses only the end of the cycle and might startle users.

title: Tactile Shape Knob
new_elements: Raised-pictogram power knob (Embossed snowflake, flame and double-flame shapes at each detent, readable by touch.)
rationale: Low-vision users identify settings by feel, with no numbers to decode.
judge_comment: Easily built and helps accessibility, but it is a modest relabeling of a knob, not radical, and the power-level choices still need understanding.

title: Recipe Punch Cards
new_elements: Punched program card slot (Insert a card, printed on packaging or hung on a keyring; its notches set the time and duty cams.)
rationale: A carer can prepare cards so the elderly user just inserts 'Soup'.
judge_comment: Punch cards let a carer preset the program so the user only inserts 'Soup', which is simple for the user, but card handling and the cam mechanism are somewhat clunky.

title: Fill-Line Mugs
new_elements: Height-gauged mug and fixed cycle (The supplied mug's fill line matches the microwave's single fixed 90 s cycle.)
rationale: Measuring the food replaces setting the machine.
judge_comment: A single fixed cycle paired with a fill-line mug removes settings entirely, but it only suits a narrow range of foods and depends on the supplied mug.

title: Talking Bell
new_elements: Voice playback 'Your food is ready' (A sound chip replaces the mechanical bell and announces 'ten seconds left' and 'ready'.)
rationale: Spoken words need no interpretation of beeps or bells.
judge_comment: A voice chip is cheap and easy and removes the need to interpret beeps, but it is a fairly common idea.

title: Carer Remote Preset Cap
new_elements: Lockable preset knob cap (The carer sets a typical time and power under a cap; the user just presses one big START plate.)
rationale: The complexity is hidden from the user and handled once by someone else.
judge_comment: A lockable preset with one start plate is very feasible and easy to use, but it depends on a carer and is similar to existing one-touch presets.

title: One Energy Dial
new_elements: Single energy-dose knob (One knob marked in 'portions'; firmware or cam derives time and power together.)
rationale: Two abstract controls become one intuitive 'how much food' choice.
judge_comment: Practical simplification to one control, but it is incremental and the 'portions' mapping is somewhat ambiguous.

title: Pictogram Timer Scale
new_elements: Pictogram dial face (Mug, plate, bowl and frozen-block icons replace minute numbers.)
rationale: Users point the dial at a picture of their food instead of guessing minutes.
judge_comment: Easy and intuitive to use, but it only swaps the labels and is not radical.

title: Steam-Sniffer Auto Stop
new_elements: Exhaust humidity sensor (Detects the steam burst from heated food and ends the cycle.)
rationale: The oven decides when food is done, so the user never has to estimate a time.
judge_comment: Auto-stop removes the need to estimate time, and humidity sensing already exists in sensor-cook ovens, but it is less reliable for non-steaming foods and the user still has to start it.

title: Fixed Gentle Power
new_elements: Single-level inverter supply (Continuous medium power suits defrosting, melting and reheating alike.)
rationale: Removing the power choice entirely removes a decision the user would otherwise have to learn.
judge_comment: Removing the power choice cuts complexity and is easy to build, but one setting gives poor results for many foods.

title: Pull-Anywhere Door
new_elements: Full-edge grip handle (Pulling anywhere on the door edge releases it; there is no button to find.)
rationale: The door opens the way people expect a door to open.
judge_comment: Intuitive door opening removes one hurdle, but a pull handle is already common and the idea is not radical.

title: Pop-Open Finish
new_elements: Spring door kicker (At end of cycle the timer cam releases the latch and the door swings ajar.)
rationale: An open door means 'done' universally, and the food is already accessible.
judge_comment: A spring door that pops open at the end is an intuitive 'done' signal and a mechanical substitute for the beep, though it may startle users or let food cool.

title: Solid-State Beam Steering
new_elements: Phased multi-antenna GaN RF (Phase-shifted antennas move hot spots electronically.)
rationale: Food heats evenly without the user stirring or repositioning it.
judge_comment: Electronic beam steering is radical and removes the need to stir, but it is costly and not simpler, so it fits the SUBSTITUTE operator poorly.

title: Twist-the-Window Timer
new_elements: Rotating door bezel timer (Twisting the window frame like a giant egg timer sets the time.)
rationale: A huge, obvious control borrows the egg-timer mental model.
judge_comment: The egg-timer mental model is intuitive, but a rotating door bezel raises sealing and mechanical challenges around the door.

title: Breakaway Magnetic Cord
new_elements: Magnetic breakaway power connector (Snaps on in any orientation and releases if the cord is yanked.)
rationale: Plugging in needs no alignment and does no harm if the cord is snagged.
judge_comment: Orientation-free magnetic breakaway plug is practical and safe, but plugging in is a one-time action and not a real learning-curve issue; also fairly common on other appliances.

title: It Sees the Food
new_elements: Cavity camera with food classifier (Identifies the dish and sets time and power.)
rationale: No input is needed, just the door and a start.
judge_comment: Removes nearly all input, which serves zero learning curve well, but food recognition accuracy and safety are open concerns and the idea is fairly familiar.

title: Close-the-Door-to-Cook
new_elements: Door closure starts the cycle (Firmly shutting the door starts an auto-cook cycle, so no start control is needed.)
rationale: Shutting the door is the only action required, so there is nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Starting on door close removes the start control, but it risks accidental starts, empty-oven operation, and unclear cook parameters.

title: Mode-Stirrer Fan Replaces Turntable
new_elements: Rotating metal mode stirrer in ceiling (Scatters microwaves evenly, so the floor can be flat and fixed.)
rationale: There is no turntable to seat, clean or lose, and any dish shape fits.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers are already used in many microwaves; it removes turntable handling but does little for operation simplicity.

title: Solid-State RF Amplifier
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF source (Low-voltage transistor amplifier replaces the magnetron, HV diode and HV capacitor.)
rationale: Precise electronic power control makes one-button auto-cook reliable.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF is real and enables precise control, but cost and power levels are hurdles, and the link to simple operation is indirect.

title: Arc Detector Auto-Stop
new_elements: Optical/RF arc sensor (Detects arcing flashes and stops heating within milliseconds.)
rationale: Users no longer need to memorise a no-metal rule because mistakes are caught for them.
judge_comment: Arc detection directly removes a rule users must learn and is feasible, though it adds a sensor rather than substituting a part.

title: Say 'Warm It'
new_elements: Offline voice keyword module (Understands phrases such as 'warm it', 'defrost' and 'stop'.)
rationale: Natural speech replaces knobs entirely.
judge_comment: Offline voice keywords replace the controls with natural speech, which cuts the learning curve, though voice-controlled appliances already exist.

title: Spoken 'Done' Instead of Bell
new_elements: Voice-chip end notifier (Says 'Your food is ready, careful, it's hot'.)
rationale: A spoken message tells the user what happened and what to do next.
judge_comment: A cheap voice chip gives clear end-of-cycle guidance, but it only covers the end of use and is not radical.

title: Energy Dial (One Knob)
new_elements: Single 'how much food' dial (One knob sets total energy; the oven picks the power and time itself.)
rationale: Two confusing knobs become one intuitive question about quantity.
judge_comment: A single quantity dial is simple and feasible, but it still requires some estimation and is only moderately novel.

title: Three-Button Mug/Plate/Bowl
new_elements: Three pictogram push buttons (Mug, plate and bowl presets.)
rationale: These cover about 90% of single-household use with zero thought.
judge_comment: Preset pictogram buttons are easy to build and use, but they are a common, incremental approach and not radical.

title: Shrinking Light Bar Countdown
new_elements: LED progress strip on door (Shrinks as cooking progresses.)
rationale: Remaining time is understood at a glance, with no numbers to read.
judge_comment: Easy to read at a glance, but it only displays remaining time and does not simplify setting up a cook, and it adds a part rather than substituting one.

title: Tap-the-Package NFC
new_elements: NFC reader in door (Reads instructions embedded in food packaging.)
rationale: Ready meals program the oven themselves.
judge_comment: It removes programming for packaged meals, but it needs packaging-industry adoption and does not help with non-packaged food.

title: Traffic-Light Interface
new_elements: Red/amber/green status ring (Green means ready to load, amber means heating, red means hot inside.)
rationale: Universal colours need no language or reading.
judge_comment: A status ring that needs no reading is simple and easy to build, but it is a common, incremental idea and does not replace a part.

title: One Dial: Warm / Hot / Very Hot
new_elements: 5-step power knob with duty-cycle cam (Base-product component being substituted); Three-position outcome dial (A single dial labelled by the result wanted rather than wattage or minutes); Specify the desired result instead of the process (Outcome-based control)
rationale: People already know how hot they want their food, whereas they do not know what wattage or duty cycle means.
judge_comment: A simple outcome-based dial is easy to build and to understand, but it is an incremental change and gives vague results without duration control.

title: Camera Food Recognition
new_elements: Mechanical clockwork timer knob (Base-product component being substituted); Edge AI image classification (On-device recognition model); Shielded cavity camera (Identifies the food and its portion size); Choose the cycle by sight (Fully automatic)
rationale: The oven recognises the food, so the user makes no decisions.
judge_comment: Fully automatic and zero-learning, but cameras in a microwave cavity are costly and recognition of portion and doneness is unreliable; it is not a cheaper substitution.

title: Defrost by Sensing, Not Setting
new_elements: Low step on power knob (Base-product component being substituted); Frozen-state RF impedance sensor (Ice absorbs microwaves differently, so the oven auto-detects frozen food); Auto-detect and gently defrost frozen food (No defrost mode to choose)
rationale: Users do not need to know that defrosting requires a different mode.
judge_comment: Automatic frozen-food detection removes the need for a defrost mode, but impedance sensing of food state is unproven and hard to make reliable.

title: Mug-Is-the-Oven
new_elements: 20 L cavity (Base-product component being substituted); Personal shielded mug cavity (A mug-sized resonant chamber; dropping a mug in starts heating); Single-purpose beverage heating (Ultra-focused use)
rationale: A device that does one thing has no options to learn.
judge_comment: A mug-only chamber with drop-in start is very simple but narrow, and shielding plus detection in a small cavity is challenging.

title: Reheat-Only No-Control Box
new_elements: Timer and power knobs (Base-product components being substituted); Sensor fusion controller (Combines weight, IR and humidity sensing to fully automate reheating); Zero-control reheating (No user interface at all)
rationale: Removing every control eliminates the learning curve by definition.
judge_comment: Fully automatic reheating eliminates the interface, but it's a known concept and sensor reliability across foods is uncertain, and it's not really a cheap substitution.

title: Spring-Pop Door on Finish
new_elements: End-of-cycle bell (Base-product component being substituted); Solenoid-released door latch (The door gently swings ajar when the food is done); Open-door ready signal (Unmissable and also lets steam escape)
rationale: An open door plainly means 'take your food out'.
judge_comment: A solenoid-released door gives a clear done signal and is easy to build, but it only addresses the end of the cycle and could pop open at awkward moments.

title: Steam-Sensing Auto Stop
new_elements: Low-cost humidity sensor cutoff (Stops heating when the exhaust humidity spike shows the food is steaming hot.)
rationale: The user presses 'heat' and the oven stops itself when the food is done, with no time guessing.
judge_comment: Humidity sensing gives true one-touch operation, but it already exists in sensor-cook models and fails for dry foods or covered dishes.

title: Bimetal Food Probe
new_elements: Shielded bimetal thermostat probe (Cheap snap-disc probe pushed into the food opens the circuit at the target temperature.)
rationale: The oven cooks until the food is hot rather than until a guessed time runs out.
judge_comment: A bimetal probe that cooks to temperature removes time guessing, though metal in a microwave needs shielding and one probe won't suit every food.

title: Buttonless Magnetic Door
new_elements: Magnetic catch with full-width grab handle (Ferrite magnet holds the door shut; the interlock is a reed switch; a simple pull opens it.)
rationale: It opens like a fridge, so users no longer have to find and press a stiff button.
judge_comment: A magnetic door with a reed-switch interlock is very feasible and easier to open, but it is a modest change that is not radical.

title: Talk-to-Heat
new_elements: Offline keyword voice module (A cheap chip recognises phrases like 'warm my tea' or 'defrost'.)
rationale: Speaking a natural request is something every user can already do.
judge_comment: Voice control needs no learning and offline chips are available, but noisy kitchens and accents cause errors, and it is a fairly expected idea.

title: Solid-State 555 Timer
new_elements: RC/555 electronic timer behind the same knob (A potentiometer knob drives an IC timer that is precise at 10 s and independent of mains frequency.)
rationale: The familiar knob stays, but short times finally work as the user expects.
judge_comment: A cheap 555 timer behind the familiar knob is very feasible and fixes accuracy at short times, but it is incremental and barely changes how simple the oven is to use.

title: Hourglass Cartridge Timer
new_elements: Flip-in sand hourglass with optical cutoff (The user flips a 1, 2 or 3 min hourglass into a front socket; heating stops when the light beam is unblocked.)
rationale: Remaining time is visible as physical sand, making the countdown self-explanatory.
judge_comment: A visible hourglass is charming and self-explanatory, but fixed durations and optical cutoff make it clumsy and limiting.

title: Pass-Through Conveyor
new_elements: Slow conveyor tunnel with choke curtains (Food enters one side and exits the other hot; belt speed replaces the timer.)
rationale: Users put the food in and take it out the other side, with nothing to set.
judge_comment: Truly removes timer setting, but belt speed cannot adapt to different foods, and the device is bulky and has leakage challenges.

title: Two-Position Gentle Switch
new_elements: Rocker switch: Normal / Gentle (Replaces the 5-step cam with a 2-state duty cycle.)
rationale: Fewer, clearly named options lower confusion and also cost less.
judge_comment: Reducing power levels to two simple options is clear and cheap, but it is an incremental and fairly obvious simplification.

title: Self-Tapering Power
new_elements: Time-coupled power cam (Long settings automatically ramp the power down to prevent boil-over and hot spots.)
rationale: Users never need to think about power because the oven chooses it.
judge_comment: Automatic power tapering removes a decision and is plausible with a cam or timer, though the mechanism is only loosely defined.

title: Token Drop Timer
new_elements: Reusable token slot timer (Each token dropped in gives 30 s; tokens fall into the tray as time runs.)
rationale: Counting physical tokens is concrete and tactile, which suits dementia-friendly design.
judge_comment: Tactile token counting is intuitive with no learning curve, but handling tokens is clumsy and they can get lost.

title: Weight-Triggered Auto Start
new_elements: Load cell + door switch auto reheat (Food detected plus door closed starts a reheat scaled to the food's weight.)
rationale: Zero interaction is needed beyond putting the food in.
judge_comment: Zero interaction fully removes the learning curve, but weight alone is a poor guide to heating needs and auto-start raises safety concerns.

title: Countdown Shadow Clock
new_elements: Shrinking colored disc on the window (An analog shutter disc closes as time passes, like a pie being eaten.)
rationale: The remaining time is shown as an intuitive shrinking pie rather than numbers.
judge_comment: An analog shrinking-disc timer is intuitive and a cheap substitution for a digital display, but it only addresses time display rather than the full operation.

title: Weigh-and-Go Floor
new_elements: Load-cell cavity floor (Strain-gauge floor weighs the food and sets heating time automatically.); Auto-sets time from mass (Replaces the clockwork timer knob with mass-based time calculation.)
rationale: The user puts the food in and presses one button, with no dial to learn.
judge_comment: Weight-based timing is plausible and removes the dial, but mass alone poorly predicts heating needs for varied foods, and a load cell in a microwave cavity is hard to build.

title: Mode-Stirrer Instead of Turntable
new_elements: Ceiling mode-stirrer fan (A rotating metal blade scatters microwaves evenly, so no turntable is needed.)
rationale: There is no glass plate to seat, remove, or break, and any dish shape fits.
judge_comment: Mode stirrers already exist in many microwaves, so it is feasible and removes the plate to seat, but it is only loosely tied to operation simplicity and is not radical.

title: Solid-State Beam Steering
new_elements: GaN phased-array RF sources (Multiple solid-state emitters steer energy electronically toward the food.); Electronically uniform heating (Removes cold spots without moving parts.)
rationale: Food heats evenly without stirring or flipping, so the user has no tricks to learn.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF steering is real and gives even heating with no tricks, but it is costly and not a cheaper substitute, and it only indirectly reduces the learning curve.

title: Cloche Dome Microwave
new_elements: Shielded drop-over dome (The user lowers a metal-mesh dome over the plate on a base, and its weight seals the RF.)
rationale: Covering food with a dome is an obvious gesture that needs no door, latch, or button.
judge_comment: Radical and intuitive gesture, but a mesh dome that seals RF by weight and is safe is difficult, and it still needs a start mechanism.

title: IR Thermal Eye Shutoff
new_elements: Thermopile IR sensor (Reads the food surface temperature and stops at a safe serving temperature.); Stops at target food temperature (Prevents scorching and dried-out food, complementing the bimetal disc.)
rationale: Food cannot be overcooked, so users never need to estimate time.
judge_comment: Target-temperature stop removes the need to guess time, though IR on varying food surfaces is imperfect and it adds cost rather than substituting something simpler.

title: Draining Light Bar Timer
new_elements: LED hourglass bar (A bar of light drains as the time runs out, replacing clockwork numerals.)
rationale: Remaining time is understood at a glance, like an hourglass.
judge_comment: Intuitive time display that's cheap and simple, but it's mild and doesn't resolve how the time is set.

title: Thermal-Image Door Display
new_elements: E-ink door showing heat map (Shows food colored blue-to-red by temperature instead of a lit window.)
rationale: Users see when food is hot all the way through, with no guessing.
judge_comment: A heat-map door display is intuitive and removes guesswork, but accurate thermal imaging of internal food temperature is difficult inside a microwave cavity.

title: Ultrasonic Anti-Superheat
new_elements: Floor ultrasonic nucleator (Gentle ultrasound seeds bubbles in liquids to prevent superheating.)
rationale: The user no longer needs to know the 'put a spoon in the cup' rule.
judge_comment: Removes a hidden safety rule, which is clever, but it's tangential to everyday operation and ultrasonic nucleation in a microwave cavity is hard to engineer.

title: Hungry Dial
new_elements: Warm/Hot/Very-hot dial (One dial maps desired outcome to a time and power combination.)
rationale: Users express the result they want rather than technical parameters.
judge_comment: Outcome-based dial directly replaces time and power entry with something intuitive, though similar presets already exist.

title: Delete the Power Knob
new_elements: Automatic duty-cycling from food temperature (Firmware pulses power based on sensed temperature, so there is no user power setting.)
rationale: Half the controls disappear entirely.
judge_comment: Eliminating the power setting by auto-modulating from sensed temperature strongly cuts complexity, but reliable temperature sensing of food inside a microwave is challenging.

title: Mug Slot Microwave
new_elements: Vertical drop-in cup chamber (A cup-sized cylindrical cavity whose lid seals by gravity.)
rationale: Drop the mug in and it heats, as obvious as a toaster.
judge_comment: A toaster-like drop-in cup slot is intuitive and radical, though limited to mugs and has safety/sealing concerns.

title: Turntable-Is-the-Timer
new_elements: Time set in plate rotations (The user sets laps, for example 2 laps for coffee, shown by a marker on the plate.)
rationale: Users watch progress as visible motion instead of reading a dial.
judge_comment: Setting time in laps is an intuitive, visible way to time heating, though lap counts only loosely map to heating time and need a sensor.

title: Linear Inverter Power
new_elements: Switch-mode inverter HV supply (Continuous power instead of on/off cycling, so one setting suits all foods.)
rationale: Gentle default heating removes the need to choose defrost or low.
judge_comment: Inverter microwaves already exist, and a single gentle default setting really does remove the power-level choice, but it is not very novel.

title: Zoned Field Floor
new_elements: Fixed-intensity floor zones (A shaped cavity gives hot, medium, and gentle zones marked with mug, plate, and bread icons.)
rationale: Where you place the food sets the power.
judge_comment: Placement-as-power is intuitive and radical, but fixed power zones inside a microwave cavity are hard to achieve reliably and may heat unevenly.

title: Power-Level Lids
new_elements: Mesh-graded microwave covers (Engineered perforated shields cut energy by 25, 50, or 75%, with no arcing edges.)
rationale: The defrost setting becomes a physical lid you simply put on.
judge_comment: Physical lids that attenuate power are a clever substitute for settings, but the user has to manage several lids and the attenuation is unpredictable.

title: One Big Go Button
new_elements: Single +30s push button (One large button; each press adds 30 s at full power and starts heating immediately.); Set time and start in one action (Merges time selection, power selection and start into a single repeated gesture.)
rationale: Pressing one button repeatedly needs no explanation.
judge_comment: Very simple and workable, but similar to the existing +30s button on many microwaves, so it isn't radical.

title: Weighing Turntable Auto-Timer
new_elements: Load-cell turntable (Strain-gauge platform weighs the food and computes the heating time.); Mass-to-energy heating model (Estimates the energy needed from mass, assuming the food is mostly water.); Automatic duration setting (Removes manual timing decisions.)
rationale: The user puts the food in and closes the door; the oven works out the time itself.
judge_comment: Removes timing decisions, but mass-only estimation ignores food type and starting temperature, so results would be unreliable.

title: Close Door to Start
new_elements: Door-latch start switch (Closing the door starts the auto cycle; opening it pauses.); Implicit start/stop (Uses an action the user already performs as the control.)
rationale: Closing a door is already second nature to everyone.
judge_comment: Starting on door close is simple and intuitive, but it risks accidental starts and the cycle parameters are undefined.

title: Traffic-Light Status Glow
new_elements: RGB status light ring (Red while heating, green when done, pulsing white when food is left inside.); Universal status signal (Replaces the bell with a colour everyone understands.)
rationale: Traffic-light colours are understood instantly, including by deaf users.
judge_comment: A simple color status ring is easy to build and understand, but it only helps with feedback, not with operating the oven, and it is a modest substitute for a bell.

title: Push-Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Sliding drawer cavity (Push the drawer shut to start auto-heating; it slides open when done.); Load and go (Combines door, start and end signal in one motion.)
rationale: Opening and closing a drawer is something everyone already knows how to do.
judge_comment: A drawer that starts on closing merges several steps into one familiar motion, though auto-heating without any input needs a sensing system and a drawer must still contain RF.

title: AI Food Recognition Camera
new_elements: Cavity camera with on-device vision AI (Identifies the food type and portion size.); Embedded image classification (Small neural network running on a microcontroller.); Zero-input programming (The oven decides everything.)
rationale: No operation is needed beyond inserting the food.
judge_comment: It would deliver true zero-input operation, but reliable recognition of food and portion on a microcontroller is hard, and similar ovens already exist.

title: Thermochromic Lid
new_elements: Thermochromic splatter cover (Changes from blue to red when the food beneath is hot enough.); Readiness made visible (Replaces judging doneness by eye under the lamp.)
rationale: A colour change tells users the food is done with no skill required.
judge_comment: A thermochromic cover is a cheap and simple way to show doneness, but it only signals readiness and does not help with operating the oven; surface color may not match core temperature.

title: Three-Way Rocker
new_elements: Warm/Cook/Defrost rocker switch (Replaces five abstract power levels with three verbs.); Intent-based power selection (Selects by goal rather than by wattage.)
rationale: Three plain words are easier than five numbered levels.
judge_comment: Practical and easy to understand, but it is an incremental simplification rather than a radical substitution.

title: Spring-Pop Door at End
new_elements: Timer-triggered door kicker (The clockwork releases the latch and the door swings ajar when done.); Physical completion signal (Replaces the bell and prevents forgotten food.)
rationale: An open door unambiguously means the food is ready.
judge_comment: A clockwork door-pop is a simple, feasible physical signal, but it doesn't reduce the learning needed to operate the controls.

title: Smart-Label Packaging
new_elements: Printed resonator food label (Chipless RF tag that the oven reads to obtain the program.); Package-encoded instructions (No barcode alignment needed.)
rationale: Put any tagged meal in, in any orientation, and it is handled.
judge_comment: Zero-input cooking via a chipless RF label is compelling but depends on an ecosystem of tagged packaging and unproven oven-side reading.

title: Door Handle Is the Timer
new_elements: Rotary door handle timer (Twist the handle to close, latch and set time in one motion.); Merged closing and timing (Removes the separate knob and release button.)
rationale: Users interact with one control, in the one place they already touch.
judge_comment: Merging close, latch and time-set into one twist is intuitive and replaces parts, though the door-latch and timer mechanism and the precision of setting the time are tricky.

title: Portion Slider
new_elements: Bowl-size slider (Slider marked with small, medium and large bowl silhouettes.); Visual quantity input (Replaces mental time calculation.)
rationale: Users match the picture to their bowl instead of converting grams to minutes.
judge_comment: A picture-based portion slider removes time calculation and is easy to build, but accuracy depends on food type and it is a fairly modest substitution.

title: Colour-Zone Single Knob
new_elements: Unified colour-zone knob (Blue zone for defrost, yellow for warm, red for cook; turning further adds time.); One-knob mode and time (Merges both knobs.)
rationale: Halving the controls halves the confusion.
judge_comment: A single knob combining mode and time cuts the controls, but the color zones are only mildly novel and the time-setting step is still there.

title: Drink Spot
new_elements: Marked cup spot with IR sensor (Any cup placed on the spot is heated to drinking temperature.); One-step drink warming (Handles the most common use case with no settings.)
rationale: Users put the cup on the circle and close the door.
judge_comment: A drink spot with IR sensing gives one-step operation for a common use case, though it covers only one narrow use.

title: Label-Your-Own Favourites
new_elements: Writable big-key favourites (Three large keys that carers can label, for example "Mum's soup".); Personalised one-touch presets (Set up once by a helper.)
rationale: Users with dementia or limited dexterity press a button with their meal's name on it.
judge_comment: Practical and highly usable with a labelled one-touch key, but it is a modest and fairly obvious tweak that requires a helper to set up and does little for first-time users.

title: Talking Bell
new_elements: Voice prompt speaker (Says "Ready, careful it's hot" or "Stir and close the door".); Spoken guidance (Replaces the ambiguous bell.)
rationale: The appliance tells users what to do next.
judge_comment: Spoken prompts clearly reduce ambiguity and are easy to build, but they are common in appliances and do not radically rethink the microwave.

title: Weighing Turntable Sets Time
new_elements: Load-cell roller ring (Strain-gauge coupler weighs the food and sets cook time automatically.); Strain-gauge weighing (Low-cost load cell embedded under the turntable.)
rationale: The food's weight sets the time, so the user never has to estimate it.
judge_comment: Weight-based time is helpful, but weight alone poorly predicts heating time and a load cell under a rotating turntable is awkward.

title: Kettle-Logic Microwave
new_elements: Steam-bimetal auto-off rocker (Kettle-style rocker switch; a bimetal disc in the steam duct flips it off when food steams.)
rationale: It borrows the kettle interaction everyone already knows: flick it on and it switches itself off.
judge_comment: The kettle metaphor is a clever and familiar interaction, but a passive bimetal disc is unlikely to detect food steam reliably across different foods.

title: Hourglass Tilt Timer
new_elements: Flip-over sand-glass timer with tilt switch (Flipping a visible hourglass module starts heating; the cycle ends when the sand runs out (optical gate).)
rationale: Remaining time is shown physically by the sand, so there are no numbers to read.
judge_comment: A physical hourglass is a charming, number-free timer, but a fixed sand duration limits flexibility and adds mechanical and optical complexity.

title: Talk-To-Heat
new_elements: Offline keyword voice chip (Cheap on-device recognizer for phrases like 'warm my coffee' or 'defrost'.)
rationale: The user simply says what they want in plain language.
judge_comment: Offline voice keywords remove the interface entirely, but there is some learning of phrases, noise issues and ambiguity about quantities.

title: Packaging Tells the Oven
new_elements: In-cavity RFID/NFC reader (Reads a tag on ready-meal packaging and sets time and power automatically.)
rationale: The food programs the oven, so the user does nothing beyond putting it in.
judge_comment: Package-driven programming means zero user input for ready meals, but it needs industry-wide tags and an RFID reader that works inside a metal cavity, and it fails for non-tagged food.

title: Microwave Drawer
new_elements: Slide-out drawer cavity (Telescopic rails replace the hinged door; the food is loaded from above.)
rationale: Users drop food in from above and slide it shut, a self-explanatory motion.
judge_comment: A drawer is a clear and intuitive motion, and microwave drawers exist, but the rails, choke seal and spill handling add complexity.

title: Top-Loading Bowl Cooker
new_elements: Rice-cooker style top-lid cylinder cavity (A lid with choke seal and a single lever, like a rice cooker.)
rationale: It copies a familiar one-lever appliance, so it needs no instructions.
judge_comment: Borrowing the rice-cooker form gives instant familiarity, but a cylindrical cavity heats unevenly and fits few dish shapes.

title: Stirrer Instead of Turntable
new_elements: Air-driven mode stirrer fan (A metal blade in the waveguide outlet, spun by cooling airflow, scatters the field.)
rationale: There is no tray to seat or roller ring to lose; food goes in anywhere.
judge_comment: Stirrer fans are real, proven tech, and they remove the tray, but the link to ease of operation is indirect.

title: Metal Alarm
new_elements: Arc-detection photodiode with voice warning (Senses arc flashes, cuts power and says 'remove metal'.)
rationale: Users do not need to memorize the 'no metal' rule.
judge_comment: Arc detection with a voice warning removes the need to remember the rule, and it is plausible though it needs reliable sensing.

title: One Button Heat
new_elements: Sensor-fusion single HEAT button (Weight, IR and humidity sensors decide power and time.)
rationale: The entire user interface is one labeled button.
judge_comment: Single-button operation is the ideal for zero learning curve, but reliable sensor fusion is costly and it is not truly a cheaper substitute.

title: Rocking Cradle Tray
new_elements: Eccentric rocking tray (The motor rocks the tray in a figure-eight, moving food through the field and agitating liquids.)
rationale: It removes the 'stop and stir halfway' instruction users forget.
judge_comment: A rocking tray removes the stirring step, but it addresses only part of operation and has mechanical challenges with spills.

title: Barcode Scan Fascia
new_elements: Front barcode scanner (Swiping the package past the scanner loads the maker's cooking instructions.)
rationale: No small-print instructions to read off the box.
judge_comment: Scanning removes reading instructions and is plausible, but depends on a database and barcode coverage, and similar concepts already exist.

title: Elbow Bump Door
new_elements: Large lower-edge bump bar release (A full-width bar that can be pushed with an elbow or wrist.)
rationale: It opens with full hands, with no need to find a small button.
judge_comment: A simple, feasible mechanical swap that eases opening, but it addresses only one small part of operation and is not very radical.

title: Wind-Up Spring Power
new_elements: Clockwork spring timer driving the turntable (Winding the knob stores spring energy that both times the cycle and turns the tray.)
rationale: One familiar wind-up gesture, with fewer parts to fail.
judge_comment: A wind-up knob is very familiar and simple, but a spring can't power the magnetron, so it only replaces the timer and turntable.

title: Hold-to-Heat Dead-Man
new_elements: Press-and-hold heat pad (Heats only while held; for 10-20 s touch-ups of drinks.)
rationale: Short reheats need no setting at all: let go when it is enough.
judge_comment: Hold-to-heat needs no settings and is intuitive, though it only suits short reheats and it is not a real substitution of a part.

title: Push-the-Door Opening
new_elements: Push-to-open door latch (Press anywhere on the door to release it, as with touch-latch cabinets); Heart-cam touch latch (Push-push latch mechanism)
rationale: There is no button to find; the user pushes the door they can already see.
judge_comment: Push-to-open is simple and feasible, but it only removes the door-open step and isn't very radical.

title: Drop-Anywhere Magnetic Tray
new_elements: Magnetic-coupled self-centering tray (The tray self-aligns on a conical seat and is driven through the floor by magnets)
rationale: The tray cannot be fitted wrongly; it just drops into place.
judge_comment: A magnetic self-centering tray makes fitting foolproof and is a clever substitution, though the benefit is minor and the added cost is notable.

title: Only a START Button
new_elements: Single illuminated START/STOP button (Sole control, backed by humidity and weight sensing)
rationale: With one button, there is literally nothing to learn.
judge_comment: One button is maximally simple and sensors make it workable, but the concept is fairly obvious and sensor-only cooking is imperfect.

title: Twist-Handle Control
new_elements: Rotary door handle timer (Pull the handle to open; once the door is closed, turn the same handle to set time)
rationale: The hand is already on the handle, so the control is where the user expects it.
judge_comment: Combining the handle and timer is intuitive and mechanically simple, though a dual-function handle could cause some confusion.

title: Door Pops Open When Done
new_elements: End-of-cycle door kicker (The timer cam releases a spring that cracks the door open at the end of the cycle)
rationale: A visibly open door means done, and there is no extra step to open it.
judge_comment: A door kicker is easy to build and gives a clear done signal, but it only addresses the end of the cycle rather than operation as a whole.

title: Shielded Food Pods
new_elements: Self-shielding cooking pod (A metal-mesh lidded container is the cavity; dock it onto an RF base); Cooks inside the serving container (Cook, carry and serve in one vessel)
rationale: It works like a kettle on a base: place the pod and press.
judge_comment: A kettle-like pod on an RF base is radical and very simple to use, but shielding and safety of a mesh-lidded pod are hard to achieve.

title: Glowing Photo Fascia
new_elements: Edge-lit photo fascia (A food photo lights up beside the knob position currently selected)
rationale: Instant visual confirmation shows what the oven will do.
judge_comment: Photo cues make the selected setting clear at a glance, but this is more of an indicator than a substitution for a part.

title: Full-Width Grab Bar
new_elements: Full-width pull bar handle (Pulling anywhere along the bar releases the latch)
rationale: It needs no fine pressing and offers no wrong place to grab.
judge_comment: A full-width pull bar removes a minor fumble, but it only addresses the door and does little for operating the cooking controls.

title: Plate Is the Turntable
new_elements: Rotating three-arm spider (The user's own plate sits directly on a low rotating spider)
rationale: There is no fragile glass tray to handle or re-seat.
judge_comment: Using the user's own plate as the turntable is a clever substitution, but it only slightly helps with learning, and plate size and balance may cause problems.

title: Mechanical Sand-Bar Countdown
new_elements: Visible draining bead column (A clear tube of beads slowly drains as the cam turns, showing time left)
rationale: An hourglass metaphor shows time remaining without any digits.
judge_comment: A mechanical bead-drain timer is simple, cheap and easy to read, but it only displays time and does not simplify setting it.

title: Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Slide-out cooking drawer (Pull to open and push to close and start. There are no hinges or release button.)
rationale: A drawer is a universal piece of furniture that needs no instructions.
judge_comment: A drawer where closing starts the cook removes buttons and is intuitive, though RF sealing and spill containment in a drawer are harder.

title: Hidden Stirrer, No Tray
new_elements: Mode-stirrer fan in waveguide outlet (A rotating metal blade scatters the field, so food sits on a flat fixed floor.)
rationale: There is no tray to seat, lose or misalign, so the user just puts food in.
judge_comment: A mode stirrer replacing the tray is a real, widely used substitution that removes the tray-seating step, but it only marginally simplifies operation.

title: Solid-State Beam Steering
new_elements: Phased-array GaN RF sources (Several solid-state emitters adjust their phase to sweep hot spots electronically.); Multi-antenna solid-state RF module (Replaces the magnetron and the turntable.)
rationale: Even heating without user tricks such as stirring or repositioning removes a hidden learning curve.
judge_comment: Solid-state phased-array heating is technically credible and removes user workarounds, but it is costly and doesn't really address the operation interface.

title: Scan the Package
new_elements: Barcode reader on door edge (Reads the ready-meal barcode and loads the manufacturer's heating program.)
rationale: Users never have to read and translate the instructions on the box.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning removes instruction reading for ready meals, but only works for packaged food with available program data.

title: Soft-Close Self-Latching Door
new_elements: Hall-sensor interlock with soft-close latch (The door pulls itself shut, so a half-closed door never makes the oven seem to 'not work'.)
rationale: It eliminates the common confusion of an oven that won't start because the door is not quite shut.
judge_comment: A soft-close latch removes a real source of confusion about whether the door is shut, though it is a modest improvement.

title: Flat Floor, No Roller Ring
new_elements: Fixed ceramic floor over an under-floor rotating antenna (The antenna rotates beneath a flat ceramic floor, so there is no tray to assemble.)
rationale: There are no parts to seat correctly before use.
judge_comment: Flat-floor designs with a rotating antenna already exist, and they do remove the tray-seating step.

title: Recipe Tokens
new_elements: Drop-in plastic token slot (Tokens shaped like a cup, a plate or a snowflake mechanically set the cam program.)
rationale: Choosing a physical token is as simple as a child's shape-sorter.
judge_comment: Physical shape tokens make program selection intuitive and are mechanically simple, though they add loose parts that can be lost.

title: Dimming Light Countdown
new_elements: Time-proportional dimming cavity light (The interior light fades as time runs out, so the light doubles as the timer display.)
rationale: Remaining time is shown by an intuitive cue that needs no numbers.
judge_comment: Intuitive, numberless timer cue that is easy to build with a dimmable LED, but it does not simplify starting or setting the cook time.

title: Microwave Lunchbox
new_elements: Self-shielded RF lunchbox with integrated solid-state source (Close the lid to heat. The box itself is the cavity.)
rationale: The container and the oven are one object, which removes every step of transferring the food.
judge_comment: A radical one-object concept that removes steps, but self-shielded RF in a portable box with a solid-state source raises serious safety, cost and power-supply problems.

title: Bimetal Food Thermostat Stop
new_elements: Bimetal snap-disc that senses cavity exhaust temperature and trips the cycle (Rice-cooker logic: the cycle trips off when the exhaust air gets hot.)
rationale: Ultra-cheap automatic stopping lets users press go and walk away.
judge_comment: Walk-away operation is appealing, but exhaust temperature is a poor proxy for food doneness, and a microwave running empty or with varied loads would trip unreliably.

title: Pictogram Ring Dial
new_elements: Single dial with food pictograms and a combined time/power cam (Positions show a cup, plate, bowl and snowflake instead of numbers.)
rationale: One knob with pictures replaces two knobs with numbers.
judge_comment: Pictogram dial is easy to use and cheap, but it is an incremental idea rather than radical.

title: Magnetic Pull Handle Door
new_elements: Magnetic catch with full-width pull bar (Permanent magnets hold the door shut; a reed switch provides the interlock.)
rationale: The door opens like a fridge, with nothing to locate or press.
judge_comment: A magnetic pull door is simple and feasible, but it only removes the door-button step and leaves operation unchanged.

title: Delete the Power Knob
new_elements: Fixed full-power magnetron with timer-only control (The power control is removed entirely; defrost becomes 'short bursts' printed on the door.)
rationale: One fewer control means one fewer thing to learn or set wrong.
judge_comment: Removing the power control is trivially feasible and simplifies use, but defrosting by manual bursts shifts effort to the user and the idea is not very novel.

title: Pull-Cord Timer
new_elements: Retractable pull cord with marked beads (Pulling the cord out sets the time; it slowly retracts as time runs down.)
rationale: The remaining cord length shows the remaining time, with no numbers to read.
judge_comment: Pull-cord with retraction gives an intuitive, number-free time setting and display, though retraction mechanism and precision need engineering.

title: Food Probe Cutoff
new_elements: Shielded temperature probe with bimetal cutoff (User sticks the probe in the food and power stops at 70 °C.)
rationale: 'Stick it in and close the door' replaces guessing a time.
judge_comment: A probe with a bimetal cutoff is simple and intuitive, but metal probes in a microwave raise arcing and shielding challenges and the user must still place the probe.

title: Watch-and-Stop Mode
new_elements: Run-until-door-opened circuit with thermal-fuse 5 min cap (Cooking runs until the user opens the door; a hard safety cap prevents runaway.)
rationale: No time is set: the user watches and opens the door when it looks done.
judge_comment: Running until the door opens needs no setup and is easy to build, but it demands attention and the fuse cap is a blunt safety measure.

title: Push-to-Open Door
new_elements: Push-push touch latch (cabinet style) (Pressing anywhere on the door releases it.)
rationale: The whole door becomes the button, so there is no small target to find.
judge_comment: A push-push latch is simple and cheap and removes the small-button target, but it only simplifies door opening and is already common.

title: Kick-Plate Opener
new_elements: Large front bump plate below the door that releases the latch (Can be pressed with an elbow or a full hand.)
rationale: It works while carrying a plate or with weak fingers.
judge_comment: A bump plate for hands-full opening is accessible and plausible, though it only addresses opening and not operation.

title: Spoken Completion Chip
new_elements: Voice chip replacing the bell: 'Ready, careful it's hot' (A low-cost greeting-card sound IC triggered by the timer cam.)
rationale: Plain speech is unambiguous for elderly users.
judge_comment: A cheap voice IC is very feasible and clear for elderly users, but it only affects the end-of-cycle alert and not operation.

title: Number-of-Cups Crank
new_elements: Detented knob counting servings (1-4 cups) instead of minutes (The cam maps servings to time.)
rationale: People think in portions, not minutes.
judge_comment: Thinking in portions matches mental models and is easy to build with a cam, but it is imprecise across food types.

title: Hand-Hold Run Button
new_elements: Dead-man run button: cooks only while held (Suited to sub-minute warming tasks.)
rationale: Hold to warm and let go to stop, as intuitive as a tap.
judge_comment: A hold-to-run button is very intuitive and easily built, though it is not very radical and is impractical for longer cooking.

title: Close-Door-to-Cook
new_elements: Door-latch start switch (Closing the door starts a default reheat cycle and opening it stops the cycle.); Implicit start/stop (Shutting the door is the only command needed.)
rationale: Every user already closes the door, so making that action the start command needs no learning.
judge_comment: The zero-learning interaction is appealing, but accidental starts, including running empty, are a safety concern and a default cycle may not suit the food.

title: Status-Glow Door Frame
new_elements: Colour LED door frame (The door frame glows red while heating, amber near the end and green when done; it replaces the 25 W bulb.); Glanceable state (Shows progress from across the room.)
rationale: Colours that work like a traffic light need no explanation.
judge_comment: A traffic-light status frame is intuitive and plausible, but it only shows state and does not simplify operating the oven.

title: Talk-to-It Microwave
new_elements: Offline keyword speech recognition (Low-cost on-chip voice recognition with no internet connection.); Microphone and voice chip (Understands phrases such as 'warm my coffee'.); Natural language control (Replaces both knobs.)
rationale: Saying what you want is the most natural interface there is.
judge_comment: Voice control has no learning curve in principle, but it is a well-known concept, and it is not cheaper or simpler as the operator requires; noisy kitchens and limited vocabulary are drawbacks.

title: Popcorn Ear
new_elements: Acoustic pop detector (Microphone that counts popping sounds and stops when the gaps lengthen.); Sound-based doneness (Prevents burnt popcorn.)
rationale: The trickiest food to time takes care of itself.
judge_comment: Acoustic popcorn detection is concrete and workable, but it only covers one food and is already on the market in some models.

title: Three Fat Buttons
new_elements: Warm / Hot / Thaw buttons (Three large tactile buttons replace the 5-step power knob.); Intent-based power (Each button sets the duty cycle by the result the user wants.)
rationale: Three outcome words are simpler than five abstract power levels.
judge_comment: Outcome-labelled buttons clearly cut the learning curve and are easy to build, but they are an incremental simplification rather than a radical one.

title: Pop-Up Doneness Probe
new_elements: Microwave-safe pop-up thermometer (A wax-plug probe pops up at 70°C, like a turkey timer, with no electronics.); Passive doneness indication (Shows when the food is ready.)
rationale: When it pops, the food is done.
judge_comment: A passive pop-up thermometer is cheap and concrete, but it only signals doneness and does not control the oven, so the user still has to set it.

title: Handle-Twist Control
new_elements: Rotary door handle timer (After closing the door, twisting the handle sets the time and starts the oven.); Close-and-twist cooking (Combines door and timer into one control.)
rationale: One control in one place does everything.
judge_comment: Merging door and timer into one twist control is intuitive and novel, though the mechanical and safety interlock design is challenging.

title: Language-Free Pictograms
new_elements: Embossed pictogram fascia (Raised icons replace text labels and numbers.); Universal labelling (Readable by touch and sight.)
rationale: No reading or language is required.
judge_comment: Embossed icons are easy to build and help comprehension, but the idea is common and not radical.

title: Food Camera Recogniser
new_elements: Cavity camera with on-chip recognition (Identifies the food and sets the program; it also replaces the lamp's viewing role.); See-and-cook automation (Recognises the food and chooses time and power.)
rationale: The oven recognises lasagne by itself, so the user does not have to tell it anything.
judge_comment: Camera recognition removes all input and fits the zero-learning-curve need, though it is a known concept and accuracy and steam on the lens are real challenges.

title: Zero-Control Microwave
new_elements: Sensor fusion controller (Combines weight, steam and infrared readings and removes all knobs.); Fully autonomous heating (Closing the door is the only input.)
rationale: No controls means nothing to learn.
judge_comment: Removing all controls directly eliminates learning, but reliable autonomous heating from sensor fusion is technically hard and the substitution is loosely specified.

title: Weighing-Floor Auto Timer
new_elements: Mechanical clockwork timer knob (Base timer being substituted.); Load-cell cavity floor (Weighs the food and derives the heating time automatically.); Mass-to-energy heating estimation (Lookup table that converts grams to joules needed.)
rationale: The user never has to guess a time because the oven weighs the food and decides.
judge_comment: Weighing removes time guessing, but mass alone poorly predicts heating needs and the load cell must withstand the cavity environment; it also isn't much of a cheaper substitution.

title: Steam-Sniffer Auto Stop
new_elements: Clockwork timer and bell (Base timing and alert parts being substituted.); Exhaust humidity sensor (Stops heating when the steam burst shows the food is hot.); Detect doneness automatically (Ends the cycle on the food's actual state rather than elapsed time.)
rationale: The food tells the oven when it is done, so there are no settings to master.
judge_comment: Humidity-based auto-stop exists in sensor-cook models, but it fits zero-setting use well and is workable, though it handles dry foods poorly.

title: Magnetic Pull Door
new_elements: Door push-release button (Base door release being substituted.); Magnetic latch with pull edge (Opens like a fridge door with a single tug.)
rationale: Opens with the same pull motion as a fridge, which every user already knows.
judge_comment: A fridge-style pull door is intuitive and easy to build, though not radical.

title: Elbow Bump Door
new_elements: Door push-release button (Base door release being substituted.); Full-face press-to-open door (Pushing anywhere on the door pops it open, so hands can stay full.)
rationale: There is no small target to find; any push on the door works.
judge_comment: Pressing anywhere on the door to open it removes the need to find a button and helps full hands, though door mechanics and safety are a concern.

title: Warm-to-Hot Slider
new_elements: 5-step power cam knob (Base power control being substituted.); Single linear slider (Labelled only "warm" at one end and "hot" at the other.)
rationale: Two plain words replace five abstract power steps.
judge_comment: Plain-language slider is intuitive and cheap, though it still needs a separate timer.

title: Wave-to-Start
new_elements: Timer knob start action (Base start action being substituted.); IR proximity gesture sensor (A hand wave adds 30 s of heating.)
rationale: Starts with no button to find, even with dirty hands.
judge_comment: Waving to add 30 s is easy to do, but gestures are not obvious and could trigger by accident, so some learning is needed.

title: Color-Dot Packaging
new_elements: Timer and power knobs (Base controls being substituted.); Color-dot reader (Reads a printed dot on food packaging that encodes the program.)
rationale: The food package itself carries the instructions.
judge_comment: Packaging that carries the program removes the need to set anything, but it relies on food makers adopting it and does not help with food that is not in packaging.

title: Handle Is the Timer
new_elements: Separate timer knob (Base timer being substituted.); Twist door handle (Twisting the handle while closing the door sets the time.)
rationale: Closing the door and setting the time merge into one motion.
judge_comment: Merging door closing with time setting is clever and intuitive, but twist precision and the mapping from twist angle to time are unclear.

title: Projected Floor Arrow
new_elements: Printed knob labels (Base markings being substituted.); Pico projector guide (Projects a "place here" circle, then a countdown, onto the food.)
rationale: Instructions appear exactly where the user is looking.
judge_comment: A projector guide is engaging, but it adds cost and complexity, and it isn't a simpler substitute; its feasibility is hampered by steam and splatter inside or near the cavity.

title: Whole-Front Stop Panel
new_elements: Turning timer knob to zero to stop (Base stop method being substituted.); Capacitive front skin (Touching anywhere on the front stops heating.)
rationale: Stopping is instinctive and impossible to get wrong.
judge_comment: Whole-front touch-to-stop is easy and safe, but it covers only stopping, not the rest of operation, and accidental touches are a risk.

title: Hand-Crank Timer
new_elements: Rotary clockwork knob (Base timer being substituted.); Side crank (Each full turn of the crank winds on one minute.)
rationale: Users count turns, not dial marks.
judge_comment: A crank timer is intuitive and quirky, but it adds physical effort and is arguably no simpler than a dial.

title: Phone-Free NFC Sticker Cards
new_elements: Knob settings (Base controls being substituted.); Recipe cards with NFC (Tapping a picture card on the oven sets the cycle.)
rationale: Pick a picture card, tap it, and the cooking happens.
judge_comment: Tapping a picture card removes the need to learn settings, and NFC is cheap and proven, though it's an extra item to keep track of and not very radical.

title: Lift-Lid Top Loader
new_elements: Side-hinged door + release button (Base door system being substituted.); Rice-cooker-style top lid (Lift the lid to load; lowering it starts the default cycle.)
rationale: Borrows the lift-and-drop interaction of a familiar rice cooker.
judge_comment: A rice-cooker-style lid is a radical and familiar interaction that starts cooking automatically, but a top-loading cavity raises problems with spills, safety, and RF sealing.

title: Curie-Point Drink Puck
new_elements: Curie-point ferrite stirring puck (A ceramic-coated puck placed in the cup loses its magnetism at 70 °C, which opens a floor reed switch to stop heating.); Curie-temperature magnetic switching (The ferrite becomes non-magnetic at a fixed temperature.)
rationale: The user drops the puck in the milk and closes the door, and the drink is always perfectly hot with no setting at all.
judge_comment: The Curie puck is a wildly inventive idea, but a ferrite puck in a microwave would heat and arc, and the reed switch would need to sit in the cavity floor.

title: Push-to-Open Touch Latch
new_elements: Push-push touch latch door (A cabinet-style click latch: push the door to open it and push it again to close.)
rationale: There is no hidden button to find, because the door itself is the control.
judge_comment: Push-to-open latches are simple and cheap and remove the hidden button, but they only affect opening and do not address operation overall.

title: Green-Glow Done Lamp
new_elements: Bicolour cavity lamp (amber cooking, green done) (The timer cam switches the lamp filter colour at zero instead of striking a bell.)
rationale: It uses the universal traffic-light language for 'ready', which needs no learning.
judge_comment: A simple, feasible done-signal that is intuitive, but it only modestly addresses operation and is not radical.

title: RF-Powered Neon Witness Bulb
new_elements: Wireless neon glow tube in cavity roof (A gas tube is lit directly by the microwave field, so it glows only while heating.)
rationale: Glowing means cooking and dark means not cooking, a self-evident status signal with no wiring.
judge_comment: A neon bulb lit by the field is a self-evident, wire-free cooking indicator and is plausible, though it needs a safe design and its brightness is uncertain.

title: Shielded Defrost Box
new_elements: Perforated-metal defrost lidded box (A calibrated aperture lid passes about 30% of the field, giving low power without any power knob.); Partial aperture attenuation (Hole size and density set how much RF reaches the food.)
rationale: Defrosting simply means using the defrost box, with no settings to remember.
judge_comment: Passive RF attenuation to replace the power knob is clever and cheap, but a partial aperture gives uneven heating and a lidded box adds a step users must learn.

title: Say-the-Time Voice Chip
new_elements: Offline keyword voice module (A low-cost speech chip recognises phrases like 'one minute' or 'defrost' and drives a relay timer.)
rationale: Talking needs no learning at all.
judge_comment: Offline voice commands need no learning, though they are not very novel, and noise and accents make recognition less reliable.

title: Solid-State GaN RF Source
new_elements: GaN solid-state RF amplifier module (A low-voltage transistor RF source with continuous power control replaces the magnetron and the HV chain.); Gallium-nitride RF power transistors (Efficient high-frequency semiconductors operating at 2.45 GHz.)
rationale: Smooth power control lets the oven pick the gentle setting itself, so users stop juggling power levels.
judge_comment: Solid-state RF gives fine power control that enables automatic gentle heating, but the link to simpler operation is indirect and the parts are costly today.

title: Spin-the-Tray to Set Time
new_elements: Hand-wound turntable timer clutch (The user turns the tray backward to wind the time, and the motor unwinds it while cooking.)
rationale: The food plate is the only control, with nothing on the outside to learn.
judge_comment: Using the tray as the only control is a clever way to remove the interface, but a mechanical clutch under a heavy rotating glass tray is awkward and the door-open and safety interlocks are unclear.

title: Ice-Sensing Auto Defrost
new_elements: Reflected-power diode detector in waveguide (Frozen food absorbs poorly, so high reflection automatically switches the oven to a gentle duty cycle.); Load-impedance sensing via reflected RF (The dielectric loss of ice differs strongly from that of water.)
rationale: The oven knows it's defrosting, so the user doesn't have to.
judge_comment: Sensing the load from reflected power removes the defrost decision and is physically grounded, though reflection also varies with load shape and size, making it hard to do reliably.

title: Why-It-Stopped Flag
new_elements: Visible overheat tell-tale flag (The bimetal cutout also flips an orange window flag that reads 'cooling - wait'.)
rationale: Users never wonder why the oven died, because it explains itself.
judge_comment: A cheap, plausible mechanical flag that explains a confusing shutdown, though it is incremental and addresses an edge case.

title: Load-Current Auto Timer
new_elements: Anode-current integrating energy counter (Measures the energy actually absorbed and stops once the delivered dose suits the portion.)
rationale: Big or small portions just work, with no scale and no timing knowledge needed.
judge_comment: Auto-dosing by absorbed energy would remove the need for timing knowledge, but anode current does not reliably measure food load or doneness.

title: Gravity Flap Door
new_elements: Top-hinged self-closing flap (Lift to load; gravity swings it shut and closes the interlocks.)
rationale: The door can't be left ajar and needs no latching skill.
judge_comment: A self-closing flap is simple and feasible and prevents ajar use, though it only marginally addresses the learning curve and may be awkward with hot dishes.

title: One-Button +30s
new_elements: Single giant push button (Each press adds 30 seconds at full power; replaces both knobs.)
rationale: One button with one meaning is impossible to misunderstand.
judge_comment: A single +30s button is extremely simple and feasible, but it is a common existing pattern and still requires judging time.

title: Voice Command Heating
new_elements: Offline voice keyword module (Understands phrases like 'heat my coffee'.)
rationale: Natural speech replaces knobs entirely.
judge_comment: Offline voice keywords are feasible and need no learning, but this is a familiar idea with noise and accent issues.

title: Reed-Switch Interlocks
new_elements: Sealed magnetic reed interlocks (Contactless door sensing with no wear and no welding.)
rationale: The door works with a light, forgiving push and never jams on a misaligned latch.
judge_comment: Technically sound and a real substitution, but it is an invisible internal change that does little for the user's learning curve and is not radical.

title: Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Pull-out drawer cavity (The food sits in a drawer; the choke runs along the drawer front.)
rationale: Loading from above is natural, so there is no reaching in and no spills.
judge_comment: Drawer microwaves already exist, so it is only moderately novel, but loading is intuitive and the choke along the drawer front is plausible.

title: Thermochromic Overheat Skin
new_elements: Thermochromic casing panel (Turns red when the vents are blocked and the internals are overheating.)
rationale: It shows the problem in plain colour without any error codes.
judge_comment: A colour-change warning is simple and needs no code reading, but overheating is a rare event and it does little for everyday operation.

title: Magnetic-Breakaway Cord
new_elements: Magnetic breakaway power connector (Snaps off safely if the cord is yanked.)
rationale: Connecting power is effortless, and the oven cannot be tipped over by tripping on the cord.
judge_comment: Magnetic breakaway connectors are proven on appliances, but they only marginally ease operation and do little for the no-learning-curve need.

title: Susceptor Crisp Tray
new_elements: Built-in susceptor ceramic tray (A microwave-absorbing coating gets hot enough to brown food.)
rationale: Crisp results come with no separate grill mode to learn.
judge_comment: Susceptor trays already exist and are very feasible, but they add a crisping capability rather than reducing learning for basic operation.

title: Fixed-Time Compartments
new_elements: Three labelled cavities (30 s / 1 min / 3 min) (The user picks a slot instead of a time.)
rationale: Spatial choice is more intuitive than turning a dial.
judge_comment: Spatial choice removes the dial, but three separate cavities with their own magnetron or waveguide feeds are costly and bulky.

title: Dielectric Ice Sensing Defrost
new_elements: Auto-detects frozen food (Ice has a distinct RF reflection, so defrost runs automatically.)
rationale: No separate defrost mode needs to be understood.
judge_comment: Auto-detecting frozen food removes a mode, but reliable RF sensing of ice is hard and it isn't really a substitution.

title: Induction-Linked Hybrid Plate
new_elements: Induction coil under ferritic tray (The same plate both microwaves and sears from below.)
rationale: One plate gives crisp and hot results with no mode switching.
judge_comment: Combining induction and microwave in one plate is concrete and interesting, but a ferritic tray in a microwave is hard to engineer and the idea does not really address the no-learning-curve need.

title: Drawer Microwave
new_elements: Pull-out cavity drawer (Shielded drawer on rollers with choke-flange seal; no hinges or latch button.)
rationale: Pulling a drawer is universally understood and lets users drop food in from above.
judge_comment: A drawer is intuitive for loading, but it doesn't address operating the controls, and microwave leakage through a rolling drawer seal is a serious engineering challenge.

title: Magnetic Pull Door
new_elements: Magnet catch with reed interlock (Fridge-style magnet holds the door shut and a reed switch cuts power on opening.)
rationale: It opens exactly like a fridge, with no hidden button to find or press hard.
judge_comment: A fridge-style magnetic door is simple and plausible, but it is an incremental change that only covers opening the door.

title: Full-Face Push Door
new_elements: Push-anywhere door panel (The whole door face is a push-to-release touch latch, like push-open cabinets.)
rationale: Users can open it with an elbow or full hands, and there is no small button to locate.
judge_comment: A push-anywhere door is easy to use and buildable with a push latch, but it only simplifies opening and not the cooking operation.

title: Pull-Down Handle Opener
new_elements: Lever handle latch (Pulling the door handle itself lifts the hooks, like a car door.)
rationale: One natural motion opens the door instead of a push-then-pull sequence.
judge_comment: Pull handle opening is simple and easy to build, but many microwaves already use this and the gain in ease of use is small.

title: Transparent Conductive Door
new_elements: ITO/silver-nanowire shielding glass (An optically clear conductive coating replaces the perforated mesh.)
rationale: A crystal-clear view lets users judge doneness by eye, as with a pot.
judge_comment: Transparent conductive shielding is a clever substitution, but it does little for operational simplicity and microwave-grade attenuation and cost remain hard.

title: Listening Popcorn Stop
new_elements: Acoustic pop-rate microphone (Stops heating when pops fall below 1 per 2 s.)
rationale: Users get perfect popcorn without knowing any time.
judge_comment: Acoustic popcorn sensing already exists in commercial microwaves, and it only addresses one use case.

title: Bimetal Food Probe
new_elements: Shielded bimetal probe switch (Stick it in the food; it opens the circuit at 75°C with no electronics.)
rationale: Stick-in-and-close is a single, obvious step.
judge_comment: A bimetal probe in a microwave field is a clever electronics-free idea, but metal in the cavity risks arcing and a probe adds a step.

title: Water Ballast Power Cup
new_elements: Removable water dummy-load cup (A cup in a side alcove absorbs about half the power for gentle heating.)
rationale: 'Cup in = gentle' is a physical rule users can see.
judge_comment: Original physical power-control metaphor, but handling a water cup adds steps and is not really a zero-learning-curve operation.

title: Food-Shaped Detents
new_elements: Raised tactile food-icon knob (Embossed shapes and strong detents replace printed minute numbers.)
rationale: Low-vision users can operate it by touch alone.
judge_comment: Tactile icon knob helps accessibility and is simple, though food icons may be ambiguous and it's less about no learning curve generally.

title: Thermostat Keep-Warm End
new_elements: Holds food at serving temperature (After reaching temperature, the oven pulses gently instead of stopping.)
rationale: Users cannot get timing wrong; the food is simply ready whenever they come back.
judge_comment: Temperature-hold removes timing errors, but it substitutes an end behavior rather than a part and needs reliable sensing.

title: Talking Ready Voice
new_elements: Recorded voice prompt chip (Says 'Your food is ready, the dish is hot' instead of ringing the bell.)
rationale: Plain speech replaces an abstract signal.
judge_comment: Voice message is cheap and easy to implement but only addresses the end signal, not operation, and is hardly radical.

title: Talking Bell
new_elements: Voice chip speaker (Replaces the mechanical bell with a spoken message such as "Ready, it's hot."); Plain-language status (Explains what is happening instead of just ringing.)
rationale: Spoken words need no interpretation.
judge_comment: A voice message is cheap and clear, but it only improves the end-of-cycle signal and not how the user sets up the cook.

title: Touch-Anywhere Door
new_elements: Capacitive door skin (Touching anywhere on the door releases it, replacing the push button.); Target-free opening (There is no button to locate.)
rationale: The user does not need to find a specific control to open the door.
judge_comment: It removes the need to find a button, but accidental opening is a risk and the benefit is small.

title: RF Load Sensing Defrost
new_elements: RF reflection dielectric sensing (Detects whether the food is frozen or thawed from its RF signature.); Automatic defrost mode (Switches power profile on its own when ice is detected.)
rationale: The user never has to choose a defrost setting.
judge_comment: Auto-detecting frozen food removes a real decision and is plausible with reflection sensing, though it is not very cheap or simple.

title: Natural Voice Command
new_elements: Offline speech recognition (Understands requests like "warm my soup" without a network connection.); Conversational control (The user says what they want in their own words.)
rationale: Speaking normally requires no training.
judge_comment: Natural speech needs no learning, but offline understanding of free-form requests in a noisy kitchen is challenging and the idea is already common.

title: Wave-to-Start
new_elements: Proximity gesture sensor (A hand wave starts or stops cooking.); Touchless control (Works even when hands are full or messy.)
rationale: A single wave is the only gesture to remember.
judge_comment: Simple single gesture, but it only starts or stops and does not address setting time or power, and may cause accidental starts.

title: Barcode Handle Scanner
new_elements: Handle barcode reader (Reads the food package as it is placed inside.); Package-defined cooking (Uses the manufacturer's heating profile.)
rationale: There is no need to read the instructions on the box.
judge_comment: Barcode scanning of packages is plausible and removes reading instructions, but it is a known concept and depends on a database or the barcode carrying heating data.

title: Dedicated Mug Well
new_elements: Mug-shaped pocket (A side well that heats any drink to drinking temperature.); Single-purpose drink heating (Dropping a mug in starts heating to a fixed temperature.)
rationale: The most common task becomes a no-settings action.
judge_comment: A dedicated drink well simplifies the most common task but only covers one use case and adds a separate heating zone.

title: Pause-on-Open Resume-on-Close
new_elements: Electronic interlock memory (Replaces the clockwork timer, which keeps no state when the door opens.); Seamless stir-and-continue (Closing the door after stirring resumes the remaining time.)
rationale: No restart is needed after checking or stirring the food.
judge_comment: Pause and resume on door open is already standard in most modern microwaves, so it is easy to build but not radical.

title: Wireless Probe Plate
new_elements: Sensor plate (A plate with a thermocouple, harvesting RF energy, replaces the turntable.); Contact temperature sensing (Measures how hot the food actually is.)
rationale: Cooking stops at exactly the right temperature without the user doing anything.
judge_comment: Auto-stop at target temperature removes all settings, but an RF-harvesting thermocouple plate inside a microwave cavity is very hard (arcing, metal, wireless reliability).

title: Door Screen Webcam View
new_elements: E-paper door with camera (Shows the interior and the remaining time as a filling bar.); Visual countdown (A bar graphic replaces the timer numbers.)
rationale: A filling bar is understood instantly.
judge_comment: A filling bar is intuitive, but a camera and e-paper door add cost and complexity and do not address the input side of operation.

title: Embossed Floor Guide
new_elements: Cavity floor icons (Floor zones marked mug, plate and bowl; placement sets the power profile.); Placement-as-setting (Where the dish sits decides how it is heated.)
rationale: Putting the food down is the only setting.
judge_comment: Placement-as-setting is clever and learning-free, but detecting the dish and setting different power by zone is technically doubtful in a microwave cavity.

title: Elbow Panel Door
new_elements: Large lower bump panel (An elbow or hip press opens the door, replacing the small push button.); Hands-full access (Opens the door while carrying a plate.)
rationale: A large target is easy for anyone to hit.
judge_comment: Easy and practical door opening, but it covers only one part of operation and not the setting of cook time.

title: Sand-Timer Window
new_elements: Visible flowing-bead timer (A mechanical bead column drains as time passes, replacing the clockwork dial face.); Analog time-left display (Time remaining is visible as a draining column.)
rationale: Everyone understands an hourglass.
judge_comment: A visual draining timer is intuitive and easy to build, but it only improves the time display and not the operation itself.

title: Dielectric Portion Sensing
new_elements: Magnetron impedance monitoring (Infers load size from reflected power.); Sensorless portion detection (Adjusts heating to the amount of food with no extra hardware.)
rationale: The amount of food is handled automatically at low cost.
judge_comment: Substitutes sensing hardware with impedance monitoring to remove portion inputs, but reliably inferring load from reflected power is technically doubtful.

title: Pop-Open Door Instead of Bell
new_elements: Solenoid door kicker (The door gently swings open when cooking ends.); Unmissable done signal (Replaces the mechanical bell and the push-release button.)
rationale: An open door says 'take your food' without the user needing to interpret anything.
judge_comment: A solenoid door kicker is a clear and simple done signal, but it is a minor tweak that does not address how to operate the microwave.

title: Voice: 'Warm My Coffee'
new_elements: Offline voice module (Recognises plain phrases such as 'warm my coffee' or 'defrost chicken'.); Natural-language command (Replaces the knobs.)
rationale: Talking needs no instruction manual.
judge_comment: Voice control is intuitive and feasible with offline modules, but it is already on the market and not very radical.

title: Time-of-Day Habit Learner
new_elements: Habit-learning controller (Learns that 7 am means coffee and 1 pm means a leftover plate.); Predictive default program (Pre-selects the likely program.)
rationale: The microwave adapts to the user instead of the reverse.
judge_comment: Habit learning directly reduces the need to learn the interface, but it adds rather than substitutes parts and is a fairly familiar smart-appliance concept.
